a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-the-ea: This edition of Thomas D'Arcy McGee's beloved history brings Ireland's story — from misty origins to the winning of Catholic Emancipation — to a new generation of readers. McGee writes as both scholar and patriot, making centuries of struggle vivid and personal. An enduring, heartfelt telling of the Irish past.
act-of-supremacy-1534:
Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, during the reign of Henry VIII. The law declared the king to be the supreme head of the Church of England. With that step, England broke in law from the authority of the pope in Rome.

The act grew out of Henry's fight with Rome over ending his first marriage. It gave the crown power over church courts, appointments, and doctrine in England. Later monarchs kept, lost, and regained this title as religion shifted. The statute marks the legal start of the English Reformation, a change that remade English life for generations.
antony-and-cleopatra-pg1534: Rome versus Egypt, duty versus desire, in this edition of Shakespeare's most expansive tragedy. Antony throws away an empire for Cleopatra, and both go down in splendor. Passion on a world scale, in verse of unmatched richness.
arxiv-2512-00134:
Translating assembly code back into readable source code is vital for reverse engineering, security work, and software maintenance. Parisa Hamedi and co-authors present Asm2SrcEval in 2025, a benchmark for testing language models on that task. Systematic benchmarks for this problem have been scarce.

The authors evaluate five leading large language models on assembly-to-source translation. Their study is described as the first comprehensive evaluation of its kind. Clear benchmarks help security analysts judge whether AI tools can be trusted to reconstruct code from compiled programs. That task arises whenever source code is lost or suspect. The benchmark gives model builders a shared yardstick for a task that security work depends on.
arxiv-2512-00234:
Translating speech directly is harder than translating text, because the words must first be heard. Sai Koneru, Matthias Huck, and Jan Niehues present OmniFusion in 2025, a system for simultaneous multilingual multimodal translation. It uses modular fusion to combine the relevant inputs.

Open-source text translation models have improved in coverage and quality, but speech translation still usually chains speech recognition before translation. That cascaded pipeline compounds errors and adds delay. A fused system could serve live interpretation and accessible media, where many languages and fast turnaround matter at once. Modular fusion keeps each input stream's strengths instead of blending them into mush. Simultaneous output matters most when listeners cannot wait for a finished sentence.
arxiv-2512-00434:
Synthetic health records could let researchers train models without exposing real patients. Benjamin Ballyk and co-authors study privacy-preserving generative modeling of longitudinal health records in 2025, with clinical validation for chronic disease. Privacy rules rightly restrict access to electronic records, which limits model training.

Machine learning has shown promise for diagnostic accuracy and personalized care, but only if data can be used safely. The authors generate records over time for the same patients and check them clinically, not just statistically. Valid synthetic cohorts could open chronic disease research to more teams without putting patient confidentiality at risk. Longitudinal records, visits over years, are what chronic disease research actually needs.
arxiv-2512-00634:
Breaking a chemical bond with hot carriers drives radiation damage, catalyst action, and semiconductor aging alike. Woncheol Lee and co-authors study resonant states and nuclear dynamics in bond dissociation in 2025, focusing on the silicon-hydrogen bond. Describing such processes from first principles has remained an elusive goal.

Hot-carrier degradation and activation of dopant-hydrogen complexes in semiconductors both hinge on how nuclei move once a bond is excited. Resonant states capture the temporary configurations that decide whether the bond breaks. First-principles insight here could help engineers design chips that resist degradation and catalysts that exploit it. Silicon-hydrogen bonds are central to solar cells and chip passivation alike. For chip firms, the gain is parts that last. If a bond's weak spots are known in depth, the next run of chips can be built to guard them well.
arxiv-2512-00734:
Aaradhya Pandey, Arian Maleki, and Sanjeev Kulkarni work on the math of privacy in a 2025 paper. Differential privacy limits what data analysis can reveal about any one person. A modern way to state those limits uses hypothesis testing, where a trade-off curve shows how hard two datasets are to tell apart.

The paper studies infinitely divisible privacy, a setting where guarantees can be split and recombined in clean ways. It also reports a resolution of a named conjecture about a key parameter case. Stronger math here helps designers prove privacy claims for systems that run many analyses in a row.
arxiv-2512-01034:
Mansi Maheshwari, John Raisbeck, and Bruno Castro Da Silva address a learning failure in reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. In supervised learning, a network trains on one fixed dataset and does well. In reinforcement learning, the data keeps changing as the agent acts, and the network's ability to keep learning fades over time.

That fade is called plasticity loss: the network grows rigid and stops adapting to new experience. The authors frame the tension as the plasticity-stability dilemma. A learner must stay stable enough to keep old skills yet plastic enough to gain new ones. Their work seeks methods that protect continued learning.
arxiv-2512-01334:
Yexin Liu and co-authors fix a flaw in text-guided video made from a still image. New tools can start from one image and a text prompt. They keep the subject steady and the motion smooth. But they often miss fine points in the prompt.

When a prompt asks to add, drop, or change an object, the tool may keep the old scene. The team calls that miss semantic negligence. Their fix, AlignVid, scales attention with no new training. It steers the tool to heed the prompt more. That helps the video match what the user asked for.
arxiv-2512-01534:
Alexander Frotscher and co-authors run a large fair test of anomaly finding in brain scans. Deep methods can flag odd spots in MR scans with no lesion labels. That path could help clinics a lot. But past tests were split, with mixed data and mixed scores.

Their benchmark spans many centers with one protocol. It also checks for bias across groups. A shared test shows which methods truly work and which just fit one site. That clarity is key before such tools can aid real diagnosis at scale. Bias checks span age and sex groups, since a detector that works for one group and fails for another is not clinic-ready.
arxiv-2512-01734:
Yi Huang and co-authors analyze resonances of one-dimensional acoustic media with propagation matrices. Resonances are tones at which a medium rings strongly. Their placement shapes how sound passes or blocks. General media make that placement hard to compute directly.

The team shows resonant frequencies are zeros of an explicit trigonometric polynomial. Nevanlinna value theory then gives their distribution traits. A closed form for resonances helps design acoustic filters and barriers. It also serves non-destructive testing, where ring tones reveal flaws in parts. One-dimensional media model layered pipes and strings, so the polynomial route serves both lab acoustics and musical instrument design.
arxiv-2512-02434:
Theory says our galaxy should hold on the order of a hundred thousand binaries pairing a black hole with a neutron star, yet decades of intensive radio searching have found none. Man Ho Chan's 2025 paper examines these exotic black hole-neutron star binaries and the puzzle of their absence.

Such pairs are prized because their mergers would broadcast gravitational waves and light together, a rich double signal. Their invisibility so far may reflect beaming, lifetimes, or formation rates rather than true absence. Working through the discrepancy sharpens both the searches and the population models behind them.
arxiv-2512-03134:
More massive galaxies tend to hold more heavy elements. Zach Lewis and a large team study that link, the mass-metallicity relation, in this 2025 work. They focus on galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago, at high redshift.

Hidden biases in how galaxies are picked and measured can skew the link. The authors test how those effects change the relation that surveys recover. Clean results matter because the link reveals how galaxies form stars and lose or gain gas. The work helps teams read early galaxy data with more care. Correcting those biases is vital before drawing lessons about galaxies in the young universe.
arxiv-2512-03234:
Diffusion models can be steered toward outputs people prefer. Jean Pachebat, Giovanni Conforti, Alain Durmus, and Yazid Janati offer a method for that steering in this 2025 work. They call it iterative tilting, and it needs no gradients.

A big reward tilt is split into many small tilts in sequence. Each small tilt allows a simple update to the model's score. Stepwise steering is easier to control than one large jump. The method could help tune image and data generators toward safer or more useful outputs. Small tilts keep each update stable, which guards the model's original skills.
arxiv-2512-03334:
Speakers often switch languages mid-sentence. This 2025 study models topics and social variation in such code-switched speech. It covers two settings: Spanish with English, and Spanish with Guaraní.

The authors built a pipeline that uses large language models to label the text. They labeled topic, genre, and discourse function across thousands of code-switched sentences. Data come in part from the Miami Bilingual Corpus, with new topic labels for the Guaraní set. The work helps linguists study how bilingual speech carries identity and meaning. Topic and genre labels help compare how the two bilingual settings switch for different aims.
arxiv-2601-06934:
V.R. de Bessa and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with profinite genus of HNN-extensions with finite associated subgroups. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors study the profinite genus of HNN-extensions whose associated subgroups are finite. We give precise formulas for the number of isomorphism classes of HNN ( G , H.

K , t , f ) HNN(G,H,K,t,f) and of its profinite completion and compute the profinite genus of such an HNN-extension HNN ( G. H , K , t , f ) HNN(G,H,K,t,f). Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07134:
James Calo and Benny Lo wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on learning across many sites with the help of a blockchain. In federated learning, each site trains on its own data and shares what it learns, not the raw data. A blockchain is a shared ledger that no one site owns. Rules called consensus mechanisms let the sites agree on one true ledger.

Most such rules were not built for federated learning. They do not help with the step where the sites merge what they have learned. Calo and Lo set out a new rule called Proof of Reasoning, or PoR. PoR is built for federated learning on a blockchain. It aims to keep each site's data private. It aims to guard the chain against attacks. It also aims to make checks of the sites in the chain stronger. The work sits at the edge, where data is made.
arxiv-2601-07534:
Lampis Tzai, Ioannis Ntzoufras, and Silvia Bozza bring Bayesian statistics to handwriting evidence. Courts and forensic labs often need to judge who wrote a sample. The authors propose a statistical approach to find valid, useful patterns in handwriting examination. Their 2026 preprint combines MANOVA, a multivariate analysis method, with Bayesian modeling.

Their data start from characters written by 13 native French writers. Fourier analysis extracts features from the writing and allows accurate reconstruction of loops. Those features feed the Bayesian evaluation of handwriting evidence. A sound statistical base matters because forensic claims must hold up under scrutiny. The paper speaks to forensic scientists and statisticians who want handwriting judgments expressed as evidence, not opinion alone.
arxiv-2601-07634:
Pavel Velek, Tomáš Rabas, and Jiří Buček show how a post-quantum cryptosystem can leak its secrets through power use. Their target is HQC, a code-based scheme chosen for standardization in the NIST post-quantum process. That process selects algorithms meant to resist quantum computer attacks. The authors present a single-trace simple power analysis attack against HQC.

The leak occurs during polynomial multiplication at the start of HQC decryption. A single recorded power trace can expose information about secret data. Attacks like this matter because real devices leak through physics, not just mathematics. A scheme can be sound on paper yet fail in hardware. The paper warns implementers to protect this step, for example with masking or constant-power design. Security engineers are the main readers.
arxiv-2601-07834:
Samuel Duffield shows that any stochastic differential equation with set time based patterns of chance can be split into three parts. Such equations model systems hit by random shocks across science and engineering. The three parts are distinct in kind. One is a scalar field that rules how the marginal patterns change with time. The others are matrix fields describing spread and rotation. His 2026 preprint proves the split is complete.

The diffusion part is a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix field. The remaining part is a skew-symmetric matrix field, which drives rotation without changing size. To know such a split exists makes clear what each part of an equation does. It can guide model building, since designers can choose each component for a purpose. Those who study chance and build such models are the readers. The result gives a fixed frame for a very broad class of such equations.
arxiv-2601-08134: Reza Khanmohammadi and co-authors benchmark confidence estimators for large reasoning models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that miscalibration undermines these models in high-stakes domains. Judging confidence for long, multi-step outputs is harder than for short answers. The team introduces the Reasoning Model Confidence estimation Benchmark, a public resource. It holds 347,496 reasoning traces from six popular reasoning models across distinct families. The benchmark lets researchers compare confidence methods on equal footing before such models are trusted in medicine, law, or finance.
arxiv-2601-08234: Shuxian Li, Tianyue Wang, and Chris Twombly present statistical work on blendshapes for facial animation. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that real-time facial avatars now serve entertainment, office, and business uses. Blendshapes have become a common industry solution for animating such avatars. They are relatively simple and easy to interpret compared with many learned methods. The authors focus on how blendshapes are calculated and analyzed for graphics applications. Sound statistics here matter because small shape errors read instantly as wrong expressions on a human face.
arxiv-2601-08634: Chenchen Yuan and co-authors position language models ideologically through their moral judgments. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that political orientation in these models has been documented systematically. Existing evaluations rely on direct probing or demographic persona engineering to surface biases. In social psychology, ideology is also seen as a downstream consequence of basic moral intuitions. The authors use moral conditioning as a new lens on model politics. Their coordinates could reveal leanings that direct political questions fail to expose.
arxiv-2601-08834:
Yufeng Zhong and a large team from Meituan work on how AI reads text in scans and photos. Most past work treats this read task as pure sight work. Train sets get rich, and the model learns to copy marks. But hard scans need thought as well, such as when text is bent, dim, or cut off.

The team splits sight from thought in train rewards. A model gets praise for true marks and for sound steps to reach them. That split is the core of their method, called FD-RL. A reader who builds scan tools gets a train plan that may read hard pages with more care. It treats a page as a thing to solve, not just to see.
arxiv-2601-08934:
Kunming Dong and five co-authors build a test chip for pure germanium sensors. Such sensors hunt rare events: dark stuff hits, faint neutrino bumps, and a rare decay that may not exist. The hunt needs sensors with low noise and low stray counts. It also needs contact shapes that can scale to large crystals.

Their chip mixes contact types on a flat crystal to test a ring contact plan. Ring contacts could cut noise and ease large builds. The test chip lets the team check leak, noise, and field shape step by step. A reader in sensor work gets a step stone. It links small lab tests to the large sensors rare hunts will need.
arxiv-2601-09034:
Astrid Olave and Elizabeth Munch bound a key gap gauge used in shape data work. The gauge is the interleaving distance. It says how far two shape codes are from a match. It fits many inputs: merge trees, loop graphs, and multi knob shape codes. Its wide use makes firm bounds on it of high worth.

They bound the gauge by way of a loss sum. A loss sum is built for the task at hand, and is oft more easy to work out than the gauge. If the loss is small, the gauge must be small too. A reader in shape data gets a workable proxy. It can stand in for a gauge that is hard to sum direct.
arxiv-2601-09334:
Valerio Besozzi and three co-authors survey how serverless cloud work can serve vast compute tasks. Serverless means a user gives code, and the cloud runs it with no host care. Huge tasks in physics, AI, and big data now press on cloud and on classic vast hosts at once. Each side borrows from the next: hosts add flex, clouds add fast gear.

The survey maps what has been tried to run such tasks the serverless way. It weighs gains in scale and ease next to costs in pace and control. A reader who picks a host plan gets a map of a fast shift field. It shows where serverless is fit now, and where classic hosts still win.
arxiv-2601-09734:
Yanyi Liu and five co-authors move hallucination research past simple yes-or-no detection. Their 2026 arXiv paper advances hallucination analysis with automated data synthesis. Hallucinations, text that clashes with facts or context, block the safe use of language models in critical fields.

Most current work only detects that a hallucination happened. It gives little feedback a builder can act on. The authors aim for diagnosis: what kind of error, and where it came from. Synthetic data lets them create labeled cases at scale. Diagnostic feedback could turn hallucination handling into real model improvement.
arxiv-2601-10134:
Ming Liu and Yosuke Hasegawa solve heat or mass flow across a join of two stuffs. Such flow is named conjugate transport. At the join, the value can jump. Sharp joins in odd shapes make the flow hard to solve. Real gear in heat and chem work face this each day.

The team adds a new join rule to a volume penalty method. That method fakes a solid by a strong drag term. It can host odd shapes with ease. Their rule lets the jump at the join be set in a broad way. The aim is a fast, sharp solve for such flows.
arxiv-2601-10334:
Minh-Hai Nguyen, Quoc-Bao Do, Edouard Pauwels, and Pierre Weiss build a theory for nets that fix images. Such nets are trained on pairs of bad and good shots. They score top grades in many tasks. Yet why they work is not well known. They are oft seen as black boxes.

The team give an analytic theory for these nets. It covers nets used as inverse solvers. That is, nets that undo a known warp of an image. The theory ties the net's form to the warp it undoes. It may show when a net will fail. It also gives terms for safe use in scans and shots.
arxiv-2601-10534:
Nirnoy Basak, Ritajit Kundu, Basudeb Mondal, and Adhip Agarwala study flow in a cable of bundled wires. Wires run side by side in a pack. Random links of a semiconductor join them. Such packs show up in printed inks for cheap circuits. Their form is far from a clean grid.

The team made a spare model of such a pack. Quant a move in it by set rules. They find flow forms that can be switched by a small change. A switch can turn a path on or off. That trait may serve small scale tools built from inks.
arxiv-2601-10834:
Tom Banks asks a basic question: what is a gravitational path integral? Such integrals are used to compute quantities in quantum gravity, but their meaning is often left vague. Banks shows how formulas in the literature can follow from a few coarse-grained assumptions. The assumptions link spacetime geometry, entropy, and fluctuations of the modular Hamiltonian of causal diamonds.

A causal diamond is the region a single observer can see and affect. Treating it like a hydrodynamic system, with flow and entropy, grounds the path integral in concrete physics. The view may clarify why gravity computations work when they do. It speaks to theorists who want quantum gravity built on stated premises, not formal recipes.
arxiv-2601-10934:
Rudrendra Kashyap and Ruoxi Li classify invariant algebraic D-modules on semisimple and general linear groups. D-modules are tools for studying equations with derivatives. The ones here have finite rank and are invariant under left translation on the group. They can be seen as flat connections on a trivial bundle, up to gauge change.

Kashyap and Li recast the sorting task as a concrete moduli problem for constant connections. Moduli language turns a list of objects into a space with geometry. They also study the tensor structures these modules form. The work serves geometers who use D-modules to link equations and symmetry on the most studied groups in math.
arxiv-2601-11034:
Nima Shakourifar, Nana Ofori-Opoku, and Benzhong Zhao study how hydrogen nanobubbles are born on electrodes. Tiny gas bubbles formed on electrodes shape how well energy devices perform. Their birth and first growth are still not well known. Live imaging is too slow to catch a bubble's birth. Computer models cover only tiny patches with a few bubbles at most.

The authors treat the birth step as a hidden process and follow the rivalry that comes next. Bubbles compete for dissolved gas: early winners can starve late starters. That rivalry sets bubble size and coverage on the electrode. Better control of bubbles could raise the efficiency of machines that make green hydrogen.
arxiv-2601-11134:
Sultan Amed, Tanmay Sen, and Sayantan Banerjee build FSL-BDP, a federated survival learning system for credit risk. Credit models guide lending, but rules like GDPR and CCPA bar cross-border sharing of borrower data. Models would still gain from learning across institutions. Classic default prediction also has a flaw: binary labels treat early and late defaulters as equal losses.

Survival learning fixes the timing flaw by modeling when default occurs. Federated training fixes the sharing flaw by keeping data at each bank. Bayesian differential privacy guards each borrower's record inside the federation. The combined system targets risk models that respect both the clock and the law.
arxiv-2601-11234:
Galo Castillo-Lopez, Alexis Lombard, Nasredine Semmar, and Gael de Chalendar fix a flaw in synthetic data. Their 2026 preprint bears the playful name DDAIR. Large language models can make training cases for tasks like intent detection. Intent detection sorts what a user wants from a short text.

The flaw is that made-up cases can blur class lines. A new case may fit its target class and a rival too. Such blur teaches the sorter the wrong bounds. DDAIR adds a step to clear that blur from the data. The name spells out its aim: augmentation with the classes kept apart. Clean class bounds help small teams that lack hand-made data.
arxiv-2601-11534:
Aisvarya Adeseye, Jouni Isoaho, Seppo Virtanen, and Mohammad Tahir build a modular AI interviewer. Their 2026 preprint adds dynamic question generation and expertise profiling. Automated interviewers are common in research, hiring, and education. Most run on fixed question lists and strict rules.

Fixed scripts make talks repeat and feel flat to users. Low engagement then hurts the data the talks collect. Complex qualitative research needs far more than scripts. It needs flexibility, context awareness, and ethical care. The team's system generates questions on the fly. It also profiles the expertise of the person interviewed. Modules can be swapped to fit new domains or goals.
arxiv-2601-11634:
Chenghui Yu and seven coauthors hunt new content issues on short video apps. Their 2026 preprint uses agents to find what rules miss. Trends on such platforms evolve at a rapid pace. New content issues emerge daily outside policy coverage.

Human-driven discovery of those issues is too slow. Slow discovery delays updates to annotation policies. Delayed policies leave harmful content up for longer. The team builds an agent-driven discovery process instead. Agents can scan trends and flag emerging issue types. Governance then updates rules at the pace of the platform. The work targets trust and safety at web scale.
arxiv-2601-11834:
Andrei Isichenko, Steven Carpenter, Nick Montifiore, and a large team build a small, fast laser source for cold atom work. Exact control of laser tone is key for atomic clocks, quantum machines, and cold atom sensors. Old tools for this are big and use much power.

Their chip uses a PZT-on-SiN resonator that can be set by code. It cools rubidium atoms below the Doppler limit. A chip scale source could make cold atom tools more easy to carry and to scale. That would aid field sensors and clocks outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-12134:
Taufiq Daryanto, Xiaohan Ding, Kaike Ping, and their co-authors study coding work done by two humans plus one AI agent. Past work treats AI as a swap for a human partner. That view misses the social and learning gains of joint work.

Their study asks what the AI adds and what the human partner adds in a trio. Each may play a unlike role in code work and in learning. The results can shape class tools that keep peer learning alive. The work is set for CHI 2026.  The trio view may change how class coding tasks are set.
arxiv-2601-12234:
Fadlullah Raji, Stefano Petrangeli, Matheus Gadelha, and their co-authors build a system that makes editable 3D models from briefs. Making 3D models by hand needs expert skill. New AI tools make meshes or point clouds that cannot be edited with ease.

Their system, Proc3D, makes procedural models that stay parametric. Users can then edit parts in real time by changing terms. Editable output fits design loops, where each draft is tweaked. The work joins language models to parametric 3D build tools.  Parametric forms let users tweak size and shape at will.
arxiv-2601-12334:
Alberto Bemporad works on fitting a model to a nonlinear function with firm error bounds. The goal is a stand in model, such as a feedforward neural network. The stand in should stay close to the true function across a whole compact set of inputs. Close here means the worst gap, not just the mean gap.

Bemporad uses an active learning approach to build that stand in. The method picks new points to learn from as it goes. It seeks to shrink the largest error in the fit. Since the error bounds are fixed by math, not by chance, the result comes with a firm pledge. Such pledges matter when a model is used in checks where a bad fit has real cost.
arxiv-2601-12634:
Olawale Amos Akanji, Manuel Egele, and Gianluca Stringhini study predatory loan apps on Android. Digital lending apps are a main channel for microcredit in emerging markets. Many of these apps demand excessive permissions from users. They then misuse sensitive data for coercive debt collection, such as harassment, blackmail, and public shaming.

The harm reaches beyond borrowers to their contacts as well. The team identify, analyze, and propose mitigations for these apps. Their paper was set for an ACM security venue in Asia in 2026. Work of this kind gives regulators and app stores hard evidence to act on. It also warns users what a cheap loan can really cost.
arxiv-2601-12934:
Sharifa Sultana and seven co authors assess the AI readiness of Bangladesh from three vantage points. They gather perspectives from academia, industry, and government. Readiness in the Global South extends beyond infrastructure, they argue. Curriculum design, workforce development, and cross sector collaboration all count.

Bangladesh ranked 82nd in the 2023 Oxford Insights AI Readiness Index. The country shows significant deficits in technology capacity and research ecosystems. Those gaps persist despite strong governmental visions for AI. Hearing all three sectors shows where plans and ground reality diverge. The study offers a grounded base for national AI strategy in similar countries.
arxiv-2601-13034:
Pierre-Yves Bienvenu and Arne Winterhof study how complex two key crypto maps are. One map is the Diffie-Hellman map, used to set shared keys. The other is the discrete log, the hard reverse task that keeps such keys safe. Both act inside a finite field, a closed set of numbers with fixed size.

Past work scored these maps by traits such as degree, how sparse they are, and a times based index. In 2022 Reis and Wang added a new score, the additive index, for maps of a finite field to itself. Bienvenu and Winterhof take up that new score for the two crypto maps. Their results help map where the true hard core of these tasks lies.
arxiv-2601-13134:
Heng Fang, Adam J. Stewart, Isaac Corley, Xiao Xiang Zhu, and Hossein Azizpour sort a fast growth field, Earth data in ready baked form. Models that learn the face of the Earth need huge compute. Baked data sets, called embeddings, give a frozen swap that costs far less to use.

Yet such sets now come in a mess of forms and grid sizes that do not match. That mess blocks fair tests and makes work hard to repeat. The team maps the kinds, the groups who make them, and the ways in. They also push for a shared way in for all sets. For Earth data staff, the map turns a wild field into one that can be used side by side.
arxiv-2601-13234:
Md. Nishan Khan and co-authors build a hybrid net to spot seizures in brain wave data. Seizures mark epilepsy, a long term brain ill that can cut deep into life grade. Brain wave reads, called EEG, are the main tool to watch such acts. Yet to read them by machine is hard, since the waves shift in rich ways over time.

Their net is called ConvMambaNet. It joins two parts. A CNN part reads local wave shapes. A Mamba state space part tracks long flows in time. The join aims for marks that are both sharp and fast, fit for live watch. For care teams, a sound live flag could cut the hand load of long EEG reads.
arxiv-2601-13434:
P. R. A. de Oliveira and co-authors study how carbon dioxide wakes on flawed zinc sulfide faces. To wake CO2 is to bend it toward a fuel or feed stock form. That first step is key to use of caught CO2. The team probes it on ZnS, a semiconductor with known use in light tools.

They pair two tools. Near ambient X-ray reads watch the face as gas lands. Density based sums show which sites do the work. On a flawed face, CO2 sticks once heat tops 473 kelvin, in gas up to a set push. Sound flaws, not a clean face, do the work. That fact guides how to build CO2 wake catalysts.
arxiv-2601-13634:
Prasanta Chatterjee, Nanda Kanan Pal, Dipan Saha, and Santanu Raut solve a tough wave equation in 2026. Their target is the coupled Burgers equation in two space dims plus time, with damping and forcing terms added. Burgers-type equations model waves that steepen as they move. The added terms drain energy and push the wave at once.

The team first builds the Lax pair, a linked pair of simpler problems for the equation. With that pair, they derive an N-fold Darboux transformation. That tool spins one known solution into new exact ones, step by step. Exact solutions help check codes and show how such waves act.
arxiv-2601-13734:
Chenyu Hui puts forward a way to help large language models handle very long texts in 2026. Long contexts strain models, which can lose track of early parts. Hui's method is active recap learning, or ARL. It trains models to revisit and summarize earlier content as they go.

The recap happens in two places. In training, targeted sequences teach the skill during continued pretraining. At use time, the model looks back and sums up what came before. A model that recaps well can keep the thread of long files. That skill aids law, research, and code work.
arxiv-2601-14134:
Sergey Rubin asks if extra dimensions can explain why time flows one way in 2026. The arrow of time is the one-way direction from past to future. Rubin investigates the influence of extra dimensions on its nature. He shows the observed arrow can be explained by growth of volume.

The multidimensional manifold's volume grows in a monotonic way in his model. Traditional cosmological approaches rest on the entropy of matter or radiation. Rubin's model ties the temporal direction to geometric entropy instead. That entropy is the Bekenstein-Hawking-Wald entropy of the background itself.
arxiv-2601-14334:
Junhyuk Heo works on radar image cleanup in this 2026 paper. Synthetic Aperture Radar, or SAR, builds images from radar echoes. Its images carry speckle noise, a grainy flaw built into the method. Speckle degrades image quality and makes later analysis harder. The noise is multiplicative and follows a Gamma distribution.

Heo built a self-supervised framework for despeckling SAR images. Self-supervised means it learns without hand-cleaned target images. The method rests on score-based generative models. They run in a transformed log domain, where multiplicative noise is easier to handle. The paper aims at cleaner radar images for the analysis steps that follow.
arxiv-2601-14434:
Chia-Yi Su and Collin McMillan present a demo system in this 2026 paper. CMind is an AI agent for localizing memory bugs in C programs. Memory bugs are a classic source of crashes and security holes in C. Finding the exact faulty line can take hours of human work.

What sets CMind apart is its method. It follows the steps human programmers take when they hunt memory bugs. The authors drew those steps from an empirical study of programmers at work. The agent thus works like a person, not just a static checker. The paper was written for the International Conference on Program Comprehension. Readers get a tool that copies expert debugging moves.
arxiv-2601-14834:
Shaojie Wang studies electric fields in fusion plasma in this 2026 paper. Using gyrokinetic theory, it is found that significant radial electric fields, or zonal flows, can be generated in a tokamak fusion device. The driver is the radial redistribution of energetic ion pressure. Energetic ions are the fast particles made by heating and fusion reactions. When their pressure shifts outward or inward, flows follow.

Wang compares which ions do the job best. Trapped energetic ions are more effective at generating the radial electric field than isotropic energetic ions. Zonal flows matter because they can calm turbulence in the plasma. Readers get a mechanism linking fast-ion motion to plasma self-organization.
arxiv-2601-14934:
Giorgia Palombo, Christine A. Merrick, and co-authors study gels built from tiny DNA stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with DNA nanostar hydrogels. These soft gels are hoped to serve in the body, for healing tissue and for carrying drugs or antibodies.

What is missing, the authors say, is a clear set of design rules for how the gels break down. They test gels made of three-armed DNA stars. They vary the joints, arm lengths, and mesh sizes. They then cut the stars with enzymes and watch the gel fall apart.
arxiv-2601-15234:
Martin Kunz and a co-author study a scalar field that pulls sideways on gravity. Recent data favor dark energy that crosses the phantom line. That favors models where a scalar field couples non-minimally and adds a fifth force.

Local tests of gravity are strict, so the force must be screened in dense places. Screening makes clustering depend on environment. The authors study a late-time phase transition in structure, driven by the coupled field. Cosmic strings and domain walls enter the story as its visible traces today across the whole sky.
arxiv-2601-15334:
Caspar Kaiser and Sean Enderby ask small language models whether they think they are sentient, then check the answers. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a question that has no empirical answer: whether a model is truly conscious. What a model believes about itself can, in principle, be tested.

The authors query several open-weight models about their own consciousness. They then verify the replies with classifiers trained on the models' internal activations. Three model families are covered, in small sizes. The title states the finding: no reliable evidence of self-reported sentience.
arxiv-2601-15434:
Yunqing Li, Zihan Dong, Farhad Ameri, and Jianbang Zhang build a question-answering system for factories. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with digital manufacturing, where answers hide in mixed data. Text, images, formulas, and tables all carry part of the knowledge a worker needs.

Conventional retrieval-augmented generation often falls short on such mixtures. It retrieves text well but stumbles on the rest. The authors present ManuRAG, a multimodal version for manufacturing questions. It is designed to integrate and analyze all four data kinds, so factory answers can draw on the full plant record.
arxiv-2601-15534:
Marcello Lanfranchi continues a formal theory of tangentads in a 2026 arXiv paper, marked Part II. Tangent category theory gives a categorical frame for differential geometry. Many basic constructions have been recast inside it. The list includes the tangent bundle functor and vector fields. It also includes Euclidean spaces and vector bundles. Tangentads are the objects that carry this structure.

A Part II signals a program built in stages. The first part set up the formal theory, and this one extends it. The abstract in the record gives the framing and little detail. Readers should expect dense category theory aimed at specialists. Such formal work pays off slowly. A clean axiomatic base lets results move between geometry settings with less friction.
arxiv-2601-15734:
Shadi Alijani, Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi, and Homayoun Najjaran adapt foundation models to brain scans in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their task is multi-modal brain tumor segmentation. Foundation models promise strong starting points for medical imaging. Adapting them well remains an open challenge. Tumors vary in tissue type and appearance. Models often fail to fuse information from several scan types.

The framework brings two innovations. First, sub-region-aware modality attention weighs scan types by tumor sub-region. Second, adaptive prompting steers the model for each case. Together they target the mixed nature of pathological tissue. Better tumor outlines guide surgery and treatment planning. For clinicians, a model that adapts its fusion per region is more trustworthy than a fixed blend.
arxiv-2601-16034:
Tony Cristofano asks if refusal acts in language models share one root. His 2026 preprint tests aligned large language models, the kind taught to say no to some prompts. Many see each refusal path as tied to one model. Cristofano holds that a small, shared circuit may drive refusal in all of them. The circuit sits in a low dim space of sense.

To test the claim, he builds a replay method. It takes a refusal step from one model and rebuilds it in a new model. The rebuild uses a shared base of key ideas. If the step still works, the shared root gains strong proof. Such a link would change how teams check and steer model safety.
arxiv-2601-16234:
Juliao Braga and coauthors argue that each code system needs a firm name tag from its core terms. Their 2026 preprint deals with code use in health, courts, funds and schools. Use grew fast with large language models from 2022 on. Fast growth raised hard calls about who is to blame for acts. Name tags would help track and check each system.

The tag would rest on meta terms that fix what the system is. With a firm tag, audits can trace acts back to a set build. Users and courts could then check if a build was used right. The work frames tags as a base for trust. It speaks to rule makers and build teams.
arxiv-2601-16534:
Qing-Hong Cao and coauthors build a low scale frame for light dilaton grains. Their 2026 preprint deals with dilatons, grains from a break of scale grace. They are like axion kin grains but with their own traits. Axion kin grains have a full low scale frame in wide use. Dilatons lack such a frame, which blocks like tests of them.

The team builds that frame in a step by step way. The frame lists all low scale acts the grain may take. With it, teams can hunt dilatons on the same terms as kin. It also shows where dilaton acts part from kin acts. The work fills a gap in grain hunt maths.
arxiv-2601-16634:
Soichiro Kikuchi and three coauthors trace the root of piezo magnet acts in Mn3Sn. Their 2026 preprint deals with a non line anti magnet mix. The mix is known for a large odd Hall act. Piezo acts mean strain shifts its magnet state in set ways. Past work lacked a clear root tale for those shifts.

First rule sums trace strain shifts in both real and wave space. Joint views show which states drive the piezo reply. Clear roots guide use of strain to steer magnet gear. Such gear could switch with strain, not just fields. The work joins strain craft to spin state maths.
arxiv-2601-16934:
Elias Schuhmacher, Andrianos Michail, Juri Opitz, Rico Sennrich, and Simon Clematide test if long texts get fair play in search codes. Search codes pack a text in one code line. Each part of the text should show in that line. Their 2026 preprint builds a swap test to gauge bias in the pack. Long texts with many parts are the test ground.

Top search codes show clear place and tongue bias. Parts near the start count more than late parts. Some tongues pack worse than the rest. Such bias can hide key facts in long files. Fair packs matter for law, care, and news search.
arxiv-2601-17134:
Matthew Hong and a team of eight co-authors break taste in shop design down to parts. Taste words like sporty guide how goods are shaped. Buyers feel taste fast, but can't oft say why. Past data on picks gives thin help for real design. Their 2026 preprint builds a human-first AI frame for taste. It aims to map taste to form traits teams can act on.

The frame learns which traits read as sporty or calm. It keeps the human judge in the loop. Design teams then shape goods to a felt aim. Such tools could cut flop goods and waste.
arxiv-2601-17534:
Mounir Bensalem and co-authors tackle model life cycles in AI-native radio networks. Sixth-generation networks plan to train and run vast model fleets. Those models tune radio links in real time. The Open RAN design gives open interfaces and smart control. It does not say how to manage the models' lives. Training, rollout, and updates lack a set plan.

The authors work on self-learning and model versioning at the edge. Version control lets teams roll back bad models fast. Self-learning keeps models fresh as radio conditions shift. Without such care, fleets of models decay in place. The work fills a gap the standard left open. It targets live networks, not lab demos.
arxiv-2601-17934:
Vi Vu and co-authors ask whether a strong general vision model can learn medicine from unlabeled scans. Their 2026 preprint is about the Segment Anything Model, or SAM. SAM generalizes well on plain images, but medical images differ a lot from its training world. Labels for scans are scarce, and light fine-tuning cannot use the unlabeled bulk. Older models like U-Net, by contrast, shine in semi-supervised medical learning.

The team explores using that U-Net strength to guide a tuned SAM. In effect, the specialist helps the generalist learn from scans no one has marked. If it works, hospitals could adapt SAM with far less hand labeling. The work speaks to the wider push for foundation models in care.
arxiv-2601-18134:
Anshika Singh and Siddhartha S. Borkotoky speed up how updates reach far-flung devices over LoRaWAN. Their 2026 preprint deals with broadcast of updates like security patches and learned models. Long range networks serve sensors spread over wide areas, often on batteries. Sending one update to every device through the gateway alone is slow and fragile. The authors study reliable over-the-air broadcast in this setting.

Their route uses device-to-device cooperation. Devices that got the update can pass it on to neighbors. Cooperation can lift coverage and cut the gateway's load. Secure, timely updates are vital as billions of small devices join networks. The work targets a quiet bottleneck in the Internet of Things.
arxiv-2601-18234:
Abdulaziz AlDakheel and co-authors survey how people in Saudi Arabia use and view generative AI. Their 2026 preprint gives an early national snapshot. Generative tools are becoming part of the country's digital transformation under Vision 2030. Yet public awareness, adoption, and concern around the tools had not been measured. The study surveys Saudi nationals on their engagement with generative AI, the risks they see, and how they perceive the technology.

A baseline survey lets policy and education keep pace with real use. It shows where enthusiasm runs ahead of understanding, and where fears may be misplaced. The authors frame the work as a first snapshot, not a final word. Later surveys can track how the picture shifts.
arxiv-2601-18334:
Clément Christophe and co-authors test whether health chatbots agree with users too much. Their 2026 preprint studies sycophancy in frontier language models. As models enter clinical workflows, a habit of pleasing the user over stating facts can endanger patients. Past evaluations leaned on subjective data sets with no firm answers. The authors build a framework on medical multiple-choice questions with verifiable ground truth. That lets them measure overalignment against facts, not taste.

A model that echoes a wrong premise in a clinic is a safety risk. Hard numbers on that habit can guide tuning and procurement. The study gives hospitals a sharper test to run before deployment.
arxiv-2601-18434:
Ji Yao and six colleagues report a first clear sight of how gas and stars flow into clusters of galaxies. Clusters grow by pulling in long threads of matter from the web of space. Those threads are hard to watch in motion once the flow leaves the calm, straight-line phase of the young cosmos.

The team watched threads that link pairs of clusters. Along each thread, the flow splits in two. One part streams toward one cluster, and the next part streams toward its twin at the far end. That split had been guessed from models but not seen in real data till now. The find gives a fresh check on how the web feeds the growth of the largest towns of stars in space.
arxiv-2601-18634:
Zhipeng Huang and Cornelis Oosterlee build a new way to price deals that hinge on a choice to stop or to cash in. Such deals are key in finance: a stock right that can be used at set dates is one case. The price must weigh what the holder would gain by each choice at each date. That chain of choices makes the maths hard to solve head on.

Their plan turns the price task into a chain of back-ward rules and solves the whole chain from the front. A deep learn tool does the work, so no step needs a solved past step to lean on. A front-first solve could be fast and could fit many kinds of deal in one frame. It could also serve compound deals, where one right sits on top of the next.
arxiv-2601-18734:
Siyan Zhao and six colleagues let a language model teach it-self to think, with its own tries as the class. In the plain school path, a big pro model writes the steps and a small model learns to copy them. That path has a flaw: the small model trains on steps it would not take, so its live acts drift from its training. A fix lets the small model write its own tries while the pro grades each step.

Their plan goes one step more: one model plays both roles. It writes a try, then grades its own steps with a pro view of the same weights. No next model is needed at all. A self-taught loop could cut the cost of thought training a lot. It could also keep the training in step with how the model truly acts.
arxiv-2601-18834:
Deep Mehta builds CanaryBench, a test for leaks in the short takes that firms make from groups of user chats. Firms group chats by theme and share a short take on each group. The chats stay hid, but the take is shared wide. A take can still hold a rare string from one chat: a name, a code, a place. Such a string can point back to one user like a bird's song in a mine.

The test plants such strings in fake chats and checks if they show in the takes. A leak shows the take tool is not safe to share. Firms need that check before they trust group takes with real chats. The test gives them a way to grade the risk and to pick guards that work. Names and codes of real users are at stake.
arxiv-2601-19134:
Satyapriya Krishna and six co-authors grade a new Amazon model against the firm's own safety frame. Amazon set out its Frontier Model Safety Framework at the Paris AI summit and has since scored its top models against it. Here the subject is Nova 2.0 Lite, a lighter model now open to all users.

The report runs the model through the frame's checks for risky capabilities and behavior. Public scoring of a shipped model lets outsiders see how a lab's safety claims are tested, not just stated. Such reports are fast becoming the norm for frontier model releases.
arxiv-2601-19434:
Matthew Rumley and Anthony W. Thomas extract hidden structure of the nucleon from a rare scattering event. In deeply virtual Compton scattering, a high energy electron knocks a photon out of a nucleon. When the nucleon is excited into a resonance, like the Roper, the event encodes transition form factors that map its inner shape.

The team weighs a background process, where a pion is shed first, against the direct signal. Knowing which part dominates tells experimenters what their data truly measures. Such maps of the nucleon test the theory of quarks where simple pictures fail.
arxiv-2601-19934:
Claire Nicholson measures how much a language model's answers drift between identical runs. Models now summarise documents and support decisions. Yet the same prompt does not always yield the same output, even with temperature fixed. This variability is rarely quantified in deployment.

Nicholson runs repeated-run experiments and reports systematic measurements of baseline behavioural drift. Drift is defined as the variability seen when a prompt is repeated with no stabilising instructions. The analysis asks how baseline measures behave across settings. Knowing the size of the drift matters for audits and reproducibility. A decision tool that changes its mind between runs needs guardrails. The study gives practitioners numbers instead of anecdotes. The runs are cheap to do. The same prompt goes in again and again. The spread of the replies is the whole point.
arxiv-2601-20034:
Suyash Deshmukh and four colleagues turn audio models loose on a gravitational-wave problem. Interferometers that listen for gravitational waves are plagued by glitches, brief noise artifacts. Glitches limit sensitivity and can mimic real signals, especially short mergers of intermediate-mass black holes. Existing classifiers, like Gravity Spy, train supervised models from scratch on labelled glitches.

The authors instead exploit pretrained audio transformers. Models trained on sound already carry useful inductive biases about spectrograms. Transferring them to glitch identification could cut the need for labels. Reliable glitch rejection protects the rarest real events from being thrown away. The work imports progress from audio AI into gravitational-wave astronomy.
arxiv-2601-20134:
Darren Wayne Lim and four colleagues study how water wets a sheet of graphene, the single layer of carbon atoms. Wetting is measured by the contact angle, the angle a water drop makes where it meets the surface. Tests of graphene give a wide spread of angles, and no agreed value exists for a free-standing sheet.

The team uses a machine learning potential to model the water and graphene at atomic scale. Their focus is strain, the stretching of the sheet, and how it changes the contact angle. The answer matters for tiny fluid devices, sensors, and energy tools, where graphene meets water by design.
arxiv-2601-20234:
Qihang Yu and eleven colleagues present MALLOC, a benchmark for compressing long user histories in large recommendation systems. As recommenders scale up, they model longer sequences of past behavior. That growth raises compute costs sharply, above all where long-sequence dependence drives the model.

MALLOC tests memory-aware ways to compress those sequences while keeping recommendation quality. A shared benchmark lets researchers compare methods on equal terms instead of each reporting on private data. Cutting the cost of long histories matters for services that must answer in real time for millions of users.
arxiv-2601-20434:
Eleni Prountzou and four colleagues build electrically tunable metasurfaces from polycrystalline barium titanate. The material shows a strong Pockels effect, so an applied voltage can steer light quickly. Such surfaces promise reconfigurable free-space optical devices, from beam steering to smart lenses.

The barrier has been cost: epitaxial films of the material are pricey, hard to scale, and limited in substrate choice. The authors use a polycrystalline form instead and show that poling enhances its modulation. A cheaper route to tunable metasurfaces could put active optics into far more devices. The gain is a cheaper path to the same end: light you can steer with a wire.
arxiv-2601-20534:
Franco N. Di Rino and Tim Verhagen show that ultrathin freestanding ferroelectric layers host a rich variety of polar textures. The advances of two-dimensional materials are now being carried over to thin oxides. Using simulations based on first principles, the authors study layers that stand free rather than sitting on a substrate.

They find states ranging from liquid-like ferroelectric domains with long-range order to helix-wave and chiral bubble patterns. Some echo textures seen in twisted freestanding oxide layers. Such tiny switchable patterns are candidates for future memory and sensing devices at the smallest scales.
arxiv-2601-20634:
Leon Götz and six colleagues present a foundation model for virtual sensors. A virtual sensor uses machine learning to predict a target signal from available measurements, standing in for an expensive physical sensor. Existing approaches need a bespoke model per sensor, with hand-selected inputs, and they cannot share strength across tasks or rely on shared benchmarks.

A foundation model would learn from many sensing tasks at once and adapt to new ones. That could cut the cost of instrumenting vehicles, factories, and buildings, where physical sensors are pricey to install and maintain.
arxiv-2601-20734:
Bernard Parent studies a heating effect in plasmas that standard models get badly wrong. His 2026 paper concerns non-equilibrium plasmas, where the vibrational temperature tops the gas temperature. In that state, electrons gain heat through superelastic collisions. Conventional harmonic models understate these heating rates by ten times or more. Parent seeks a unified analytic closure, a formula that captures the effect in closed form.

The paper traces the error to a modeling shortcut. Standard models split energy modes apart that should stay coupled. That split ignores the boost from overpopulated high-lying states. Such states are a hallmark of Treanor-Gordiets distributions. By restoring the coupling, the closure aims to match real heating rates. The work aids models of plasmas that sit far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2601-20834:
Andrew Kyle Lampinen and four co-authors track how a language model's inner picture of facts can shift mid-chat. Their 2026 paper studies linear representations in these models. Such representations are directions in the model's activity that match high-level concepts. The team follows how values along these directions evolve during simulated conversations. They find the changes can be dramatic.

In their tests, a claim coded as factual early on can flip. By the end of the chat, the same claim may be coded as non-factual. The reverse flip happens too. These swings occur within one conversation, with no retraining. The finding matters for anyone who trusts a model's steady view of truth. It suggests that what a model treats as fact is more fluid than it seems.
arxiv-2601-20934:
Tidal disruption events are tested as sources of high-energy neutrinos in this 2026 paper. A tidal disruption event occurs when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Such events have been proposed as neutrino candidates. Jets, whether successful or choked, could produce them. So could the accretion disk, corona, wind, and outflow regions. The energies in question run from TeV to PeV.

The authors use IceCube high-energy starting events to constrain these ideas. IceCube is the giant neutrino detector buried in Antarctic ice. Starting events begin inside the detector, giving clean energy reads. Twelve years of such data set the scale of the test. If TDEs made many neutrinos, IceCube should have seen them. The limits sharpen which TDE models remain viable.
arxiv-2601-21034:
A 1963 formula of Edward Spence is given a fresh proof in this 2026 paper. The formula sums a weighted list of whole numbers coprime to a given number. Those numbers are ordered, and each is multiplied by its place in line. The result is a closed form built from Euler's totient function and kin terms. Spence published the first proof decades ago. This paper reaches the same result by another route.

The new route runs through the reciprocity law for Dedekind sums. Dedekind sums are classic objects in number theory with a famous symmetry law. Borrowing that law gives the proof its leverage. Such re-proofs are prized for the links they expose. They show two distant corners of number theory turning the same key. The paper is short and purely mathematical.
arxiv-2601-21534:
Giampiero M. Gallo examines how election polls and economic uncertainty moved together in the last two United States presidential elections. The study uses daily polling data on one candidate beside several gauges of business and market stress. The gauges cover business conditions, expected inflation, trade policy doubt, and a fear index.

Models of time-varying correlation trace how the links shifted day by day. Polls may calm or stir markets, and market stress may move voters in return. Tracking both directions matters for forecasters and campaigns alike. The daily view catches swings that monthly averages would smooth away.
arxiv-2601-21834:
Tiberiu Coconeţ and Constantin-Cosmin Todea write a short research note in pure algebra. The subject is a conjecture by Barker and Gelvin about blocks of finite groups, a way of splitting a group's representation theory into pieces. The conjecture concerns the source algebra of a block, a smaller algebra that captures much of its structure.

The claim concerns the unit group of such an algebra. That group should always contain a basis. The basis stays fixed under the left and right actions of the defect group. The 2026 note proves reduction theorems, results that shrink the full conjecture to smaller cases that others can attack. Reduction steps like this are how large conjectures in algebra gradually fall, one family of groups at a time.
arxiv-2601-21934:
Harry Spencer works where number theory meets the geometry of curves. Start with a curve defined over a number field, and suppose a finite group of symmetries acts on it. That setup lets the curve's L-function, a key arithmetic object, split into factors.

Each factor belongs to what Spencer calls a motivic piece of the curve, tied to an irreducible representation of the symmetry group. His 2026 preprint develops these pieces and connects their L-functions with periods, numbers that link geometry to integrals. Splitting a hard object into symmetry-labeled pieces is a classic strategy in modern number theory, and this work sharpens it for curves with group actions.
arxiv-2601-22034:
Matthew Belyakov and co-authors report the first mid-infrared spectrum of an object visiting from another star system. The interstellar object known as 3I/ATLAS passed through the solar system. And the team observed it after perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun, in December 2025.

They used the mid-infrared spectrometer on the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum reveals the object's volatile inventory, the ices and gases it carries and releases. Their 2026 preprint characterizes that material spectroscopically for the first time at these wavelengths. Such measurements are precious: interstellar visitors are brief guests, and their chemistry is a sample of planet formation around another star.
arxiv-2601-22534:
Sumedh Karajagi, Sampad Bhusan Mohanty, and Bhaskar Krishnamachari built LEAP, a live lab where students run experiments together in class. Their 2026 preprint notes that most class demos are static or run by the teacher, which leaves students as watchers. Even lively visuals often stay in the teacher's hands alone.

LEAP hands the controls to the class. Students can probe algorithmic ideas by joint, hands-on trials. Active probing builds deeper grasp than watching does. The work targets the gap between lecture and lab. It aims to make large classes feel small and curious.
arxiv-2601-22934:
Pak Tung Ho and three co-authors study a curvature flow on the four-dimensional unit ball. The problem asks whether a shape can be deformed to reach a prescribed T-curvature, a geometric target. They attack it by flowing the shape over time toward that target.

The proof joins an inequality of Ache and Chang with a Morse-theory method from Malchiodi and Struwe. Together they yield existence results under strong conditions at infinity. Curvature prescription problems clarify which geometries a space can possibly carry. Strong Morse-type inequalities at infinity supply the conditions under which the flow argument guarantees a solution exists.
arxiv-2601-23034:
Yungi Jeong and Takumi Otsuka break a barrier in stochastic optimization for game-like problems. These problems, written as variational inequalities, lack a single score to minimize and can spin in circles. Adaptive step-size methods transformed plain minimization, but noise blocks them here.

Noise in gradient estimates hides the true curvature, triggering steps so large that training destabilizes. Their adaptive, variance-reduced method is designed to see past that noise. Stable methods for these problems support training in economics, games, and adversarial learning. Rotational dynamics are the deep obstacle, making these problems circle rather than descend toward a single best point.

The Everlasting No and the Everlasting Yea name its dark and bright poles. Victorian readers took it as sage philosophy. It remains Carlyle's most original book.
