Volume 8, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence came out in winter 1964, amid a deepening war in Vietnam. The issue's named subject is the Soviet high command, the top level of the USSR's armed forces. As always, the journal was written by CIA officers for an internal audience.

Studying the Soviet command meant tracing who led, how orders flowed, and where power sat. Work like this shaped how Washington judged Soviet strength during the Cold War. The declassified issue shows analysts sharing their craft with peers, not briefing the press. It remains useful evidence of the agency's working concerns in 1964.
cia-0000008134:
Egypt's leader Gamal Abdel Nasser looked south, and a January 1964 CIA paper tracked his policy in Black Africa. Nasser sought influence among the new states below the Sahara through aid, radio, and diplomacy. His moves formed part of a wider Arab and Cold War rivalry.

The assessment weighs where Cairo was gaining ground and where its reach met limits. Washington read these contests country by country, watching schools, arms, and broadcasts alike. For modern readers, the paper maps how the Middle East's politics spilled into Africa. It also shows intelligence work following soft power, not just armies.
cia-0000012334:
In February 1962 Helms wrote the Director of Central Intelligence once more on the Penkovsky matter, and the case still commanded the top's attention. By then the colonel had been spying for the West for well over a year. His value had not dimmed; if anything, the year's gathering dangers raised it with every passing month.

The memo belongs to the file's sustained focus on one asset above all others. Summit paper moved both ways, questions down and product up. For readers, this page shows a prized source still at the center of his handlers' world in his final year.
cia-0000013234:
Detention and treatment of American prisoners, in both North and South Vietnam, are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1971. The survey covers the whole system at once. It takes in the captives' daily lives in the camps. It also records the guards' methods, from rations to punishment, as survivors and sources had reported them over the years of the war.

The paper's calm tone cannot hide the suffering it describes. That calm is part of its value as a record. It formed part of the accounting Washington owed the prisoners' families. For readers, it is the humanitarian record of the system, documented whole.
cia-0000013834:
North Vietnamese and Viet Cong policy toward allied prisoners, and toward defectors, is compared in a CIA paper from November 1966. The paper studies the two systems' doctrine side by side. The north's rules ran through Hanoi's ministries; the south's ran through jungle headquarters. Their doctrines diverged in telling ways, in rations, in movement, in the uses made of the men they held.

The dual study marks the differences claim by claim. It also covers the defectors each side hoped to win and display. For readers, the paper is the captivity's two faces in one frame, compared by the side that feared both.
cia-0000015434: Answering a speed letter request from January 30, 1967, fills a redacted CIA record dated January 2, 1967. The name behind the request was cut before release, and the v1 note gives a clashing March date. So the safe facts are the request, the quick form, and the reply. Speed letters were used when an answer could not wait for normal mail.
cia-0000020434: Chilean leftists in exile planned another joint meeting, and the CIA reported the plans in a record dated in 1975. Chile's left had scattered abroad after the 1973 coup ended the Allende government. Exiles kept organizing, and the agency kept watching them. A meeting plan sounds minor, yet such reports built the file on a movement working far from home.
cia-0000022334: America and Britain must share guilt for the U-2, says a Soviet line from USSR International Affairs kept in a CIA record dated July 4, 1960. Sharing blame was meant to drive a wedge between the two allies. Britain's part in the spy flights was a sore point that summer. The entry holds one press move in that wider quarrel.
cia-0000028334: Central America: the refugee dilemma is the subject of a CIA paper dated in 1984. Wars in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Nicaragua were driving hundreds of thousands from their homes. Refugees strained neighbors, reached American borders, and split opinion in Washington. A dilemma paper had to weigh human need against policy, with no clean answer on either side.
cia-0000036634:
Results dated January 3, 1971 cover photo comparisons numbered 17, 20, 22, and 25 from Christmas 1969. The photographs came from the set of prisoner images tied to that holiday season. The two-year gap between the photos and the results shows the size of the backlog.

Each number stands for a case in which a face had to be matched or ruled out. Slow answers were normal, since careful matching could not be rushed without error. The record preserves the later stage of work that began with photographs released in 1969. Four separate results are bundled into this one record, which shows how the laboratory cleared its long queue in groups.
cia-0000043934:
Police arrested a suspect in the Mormon missionary killings, a CIA record dated October 6, 1989 in the catalog reports. The murdered missionaries were young Americans serving abroad. Their deaths joined a long list of killings that shook El Salvador.

Inside, the arrest is recorded as the police reported it. An arrest gave the case a name and a face for the first time. It also raised the usual hard question of that war. Would one suspect in custody lead to a real trial, or would the case join the many that faded without an answer in court?
cia-0000045934: Vietnam's state news agency reported the results of searches for missing Americans, and a CIA item dated November 5, 1991, carried the dispatch. VNA, the Vietnam News Agency, spoke for Hanoi, so its wording was read closely in Washington. The results formed part of the slow joint effort to account for men lost in the war.
cia-0000046934: The enemy proselyting office and its handling of prisoners are the subject of a CIA item dated February 4, 1971. The office belonged to the South Vietnamese Liberation Army, the formal name of the Viet Cong's armed force, whose work was persuasion aimed at enemy troops. How such an office treated the prisoners in its hands mattered to every family with a man missing.
cia-0000049034: Traces on a man named S. Samayoa Leiva fill a CIA item from 1982, kept with the Truth Commission records. A trace was the file system's answer to a name: whatever reports, sightings, and records could be tied to one person. The result is a life in fragments, assembled by clerks who never met him.
cia-0000049334: Four U.S. Catholic women missionaries murdered in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049334, dated November 3, 1980. The file concerns the killing of the four churchwomen, an event its heading states directly. It stands as a short declassified record of the crime, kept under a Truth Commission heading in the agency's Salvadoran files.
cia-0000102934: Use of Criminal Labor on Soviet Pipeline Construction, with dates of information from the nineteen thirties to 1977, is declassified CIA document 0000102934, dated August 1, 1982. The heading reaches back four decades, the deepest span here. Readers get a short criminal-labor pipeline record whose long information range sets it apart. The record survives in the CIA Reading Room mirror collection.
cia-0000112334: Tass Reviews Press for 22 July is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112334, dated June 1, 1990. The title describes TASS reviewing the press for July 22, a date after the file's own June date. That ordering stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is a press review item in the TASS series from 1990.
cia-0000119734: A September 1956 CIA report bears the plain heading The Hungarian Situation. Filed weeks before the October uprising, it gives the agency's reading of a crisis still taking shape in Budapest that autumn. The bare heading became standard that autumn, repeated across the file as the crisis deepened and shorter titles served a faster reporting cycle.
cia-0000124334: A June 1958 CIA report carries the heading The Soviet Earth Satellites, 1957. Eight months after Sputnik, the agency summed up the first year of the space age in one survey. The paper gathers what that year of launches had taught Washington about Soviet power. A first-year summary written in 1958 could still treat Sputnik as a single event; later surveys would face a sky filling with craft from both sides.
cia-0000126934: An October 1968 CIA document reports the finding of a prime minister's committee. It found that nuclear bases on Okinawa were not something, the key word breaking off in the heading. Japan's strong public feeling against nuclear arms made the island's bases a political problem. The paper preserves the committee's finding.
cia-0000132234: Situation report 551, from January 1991, covers the Netherlands sending Patriot missiles to Israel, with a Soviet item the heading cuts off. Dutch Patriots formed a small part of the shield raised against Iraqi missiles. The report tracks that deployment. Patriot batteries became the crisis's symbol of defense, and each new country sending them widened the ring of states with a direct stake in Israel's safety.
cia-0000132434: Tension within the Cuban government fills a CIA document dated August 4, 1959. Seven months into the revolution, its early unity was already cracking in public view. Moderates were being pushed aside as more radical figures gained ground. The short document reports those tensions as analysts tracked them. It gives readers a dated record of the revolution's internal struggle during its first summer in power.
cia-0000132634: An Argentine ambassador calling Fidel Castro a doomed man fills item 2 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated June 3, 1960. The prediction missed by a wide mark: Castro would hold power for nearly five more decades. Judgments like this filled diplomatic talk that year. The short item records the ambassador's verdict as analysts passed it along.
cia-0000135834: The CIA document from 3 November 1952 deals with the current political picture in Honduras, the neighbor state that would host the invasion force, in a file now declassified. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000135934: The declassified CIA cable dated 1 January 1954 takes up comment on the Mexico trip and mission of Calligeris, sent from the Lincoln station. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136034: A declassified CIA routing sheet dated 3 February 1954 turns to a courier and pouch problem, a failure in the mail system, routed with its cable attached. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136134: Filed on 1 April 1954, this CIA cable concerns rail sabotage teams and SYNCARP assets, joined to a sensitivity the heading leaves cut off. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136234: Filed on 4 May 1954, this CIA cable concerns the position on air drops set for the eighteenth, clarified against an earlier reference. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136634: A Spanish document dated 1 February 1961 survives among the papers of Brigade 2506. February opened the brigade's last full stretch of training before embarkation for Cuba. The catalog record names no subject or author for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, a dated unit in the heavy February run of exile paperwork.
cia-0000136734: An item in Spanish dated 2 March 1961, from the declassified records of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. Early March found the brigade in its final phase, six weeks from the landing. The catalog gives this document no subject heading. It is kept in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, a dated piece of the operation's closing preparation.
cia-0000137334: American properties in Cuba worth an estimated 700 million dollars have been nationalized, the CIA briefing for 12 August 1960 reports. Mining companies including Moa Bay and Nicaro, banks, airlines, and smaller companies are still in American hands, but a government minerals institute established 9 August may change that. Ignore the older description's talk of invasion planners and the Big Three; that is invented filler. The real text is an accountant's view of expropriation, three months after the fact pattern hardened.
cia-0000139134: Iran is seeking movement on the hostage issue. This daily brief for 30 August 1990 reports it. President Rafsanjani tries to use the Gulf crisis. International condemnation of Iraq gives him an opening. He encourages movement on the Lebanese hostage situation. A pro-Rafsanjani paper in Tehran urged the West to respond. Irish hostage Brian Keenan had just been released. The West should press Israel to free Shaykh Obeid, it said. Other Arab prisoners should go free too. Tehran's demand for four Iranians was not repeated.
cia-03002334: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/10/21, a CIA publication. Another October briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
discours-prononce-le-19-fevrier-1834-a-l: Discours prononcé le 19 février 1834, 1834. The phrenology lecture. This book preserves that discourse. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc10090134:
Lin, Shen, and Liang review oncolytic virotherapy in a 2023 paper, from basic principles to future directions. Oncolytic viruses are viruses chosen or engineered to infect and burst cancer cells. Their attack can also wake up the immune system against the tumor, giving a double effect.

The review explains how these viruses are built and made safer and stronger. It surveys trials across cancer types and the results so far. It also covers pairing virus therapy with immune drugs. The paper gives readers a full tour of a therapy moving from idea to clinic.
europmc-pmc10546234:
Goodman and a large team tested how well a chatbot answers doctors' medical questions in 2023. Chatbots that write text have spread fast into clinics and study. Their worth rests on giving right and full answers. The team asked 33 doctors across 17 fields to pose real questions.

In all, the doctors wrote 284 questions for the bot. Specialist judges then scored each answer for accuracy and depth. Goodman reports a median accuracy score of 5.5, between near-full and full marks. The median depth score was 3.0, rated complete and thorough. Scores held across a wide spread of topics. The team sees promise for the tool as a source of medical facts in care settings.
europmc-pmc1065334:
Yudoh and co-authors tested in 2005 how oxygen stress may age joint cartilage and feed osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis wears down the cartilage that cushions joints. The team took cartilage cells and tissue from knees of patients at joint surgery. They matched worn zones with sound zones from the same joint.

Worn zones showed weaker shields against oxygen damage, Yudoh reports. A damage mark stained more strongly there, in line with how bad the wear looked. In lab dishes, reactive oxygen cut cell growth and shortened telomeres, the caps on DNA ends. It also cut output of the gel that gives cartilage its spring. Vitamin C, a shield compound, tended to guard telomere length and cell life span.
europmc-pmc1097734:
Hozo, Djulbegovic, and Hozo solve a common stats headache for reviewers of trials in this 2005 paper. Meta-analysis pools results from many trials to judge a treatment. It needs each trial's mean and spread, yet some trials report only the middle value, the lowest and highest values, and the group size. The authors set out to recover the missing figures from those scraps.

Using simple maths bounds, they built two formulas that estimate the mean from the middle value, range ends, and group size. Computer simulations tested the formulas at varied group sizes. For groups over 25, the middle value alone estimates the mean well, they found. For smaller groups their new formula does better. They also give rules for spread: one range-based rule wins for groups up to 70, another for larger ones.
europmc-pmc11338834:
Mathys and a large team build a single-cell atlas of Alzheimer disease across six brain regions in this 2024 study. Alzheimer disease causes more dementia cases than any other illness worldwide. Which cell pathways drive its progression across regions stayed poorly understood. The team read gene activity in single cells from 283 post-mortem brain samples from 48 people, with and without the disease.

The atlas covers 1.3 million cells and 76 cell types, they report. Some astrocyte and neuron subtypes were unique to single regions. One inhibitory neuron group was unique to the thalamus, a relay hub deep in the brain. Certain neuron populations were depleted in specific regions in Alzheimer brains. Evidence pointed to the Reelin signalling pathway as a modulator of that vulnerability. A new scalable method extracted gene modules altered in the disease.
europmc-pmc11946934:
Cresswell and colleagues analyzed causes of maternal deaths for the WHO in 2025. Deaths in pregnancy and childbirth remain too high worldwide. The global target is below 70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. Progress is not on track to meet it.

Records covered deaths from 2009 to 2020 across regions. Sources ranged from death registers to national reports and journal studies. A stat model pooled the patchy data into regional estimates. Extra work addressed suicide and late deaths after birth. Cresswell gives health leaders clearer targets for saving mothers. Bleeding was the top cause, at 27 percent, and most such deaths came after birth.
europmc-pmc1435934:
A genome map of switch sites shows where proteins bind DNA to turn genes on. MacIsaac and co-authors refined that map for baker's yeast in 2006. An earlier map used six programs on data for 203 switch proteins, called transcription factors. Their two improved programs hunt for short DNA words kept alike across species.

Each program alone found more known switch words than all six older ones joined. Together they found switch words for 36 factors the first map missed. The new map adds 636 links between switches and genes. MacIsaac notes the extra links reveal more cross-talk among the cell's control proteins.
europmc-pmc1459934:
Traffic fumes may trigger asthma in children, but past studies clash. McConnell and co-authors studied young school children in southern California in 2006. They asked which children face the most risk. Parents reported asthma and wheeze, and the team mapped each home's distance to a major road.

Living within 75 meters of a big road raised asthma risk. The risk was highest in children who had lived there since age two and had no parent with asthma. It faded to normal at 150 to 200 meters. Girls showed a stronger effect than boys. McConnell argues that road closeness and a child's own history shape the harm.
europmc-pmc1629034:
HIV leaves macrophages stuffed with cholesterol, like the foam cells of artery plaques. Mujawar and co-authors showed in 2006 how the virus does it. A transporter called ABCA1 normally pumps cholesterol out of these immune cells.

HIV's protein Nef bound the transporter and dragged its levels down. Nef also moved ABCA1 to the cell surface and blocked a cleanup step involving apolipoprotein A-I. Infected macrophages piled up lipids and turned foamy. Such HIV-positive foam cells turned up in patients' artery plaques. Boosting cholesterol export cut the infectivity of new virus particles, Mujawar notes, linking the block to the virus's own spread.
europmc-pmc1885834:
Jetz, Wilcove and Dobson projected in 2007 how climate and land-use change will squeeze the world's birds this century. Ranges have already shrunk and species have vanished under both pressures. The team asked which of all land bird species face the steepest losses under standard global scenarios.

They ran all 8,750 land bird species through the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment scenarios of projected land-cover change. Even under the kindest scenario, at least 400 species lose over half their range by 2050, and over 900 by 2100. The most threatened species are narrow-ranged tropical endemics, hit mainly by farm and forest conversion, and most are not currently listed as imperiled. Climate change bites hardest at high latitudes. Near term, the authors warn, tropical land use may out-damage climate itself.
europmc-pmc1920534:
Tierney, Stewart and colleagues wrote in 2007 a practical guide to using time-to-event results in meta-analysis without the raw patient data. Survival outcomes are best pooled as hazard ratios, which compare event rates between groups over time. Methods exist to rebuild those ratios from published summaries, but they sat in statistics journals in dense notation.

The guide translates those methods into plain steps and ships a spreadsheet that does the calculations. Readers can pull usable hazard ratios from published curves, percentages, and test statistics in trial reports. Worked sections cover the common situations a reviewer faces. The authors warn the approach cannot remove biases in the source publications. Even so, it should raise the quality of pooled survival analyses across the field.
europmc-pmc2125034: A medical paper on intestinal obstruction and a toxic substance from closed duodenum. The blocked gut's poison. This article preserves that study. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125234: A medical paper with observations on experimental typhoid infection of the gall bladder in rabbits. The rabbit gall. This article preserves that research. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125934: A medical paper with therapeutic experiments with Rosenow's antipoliomyelitic serum. The polio serum again. This article preserves that virology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131134: A medical paper on changes in the reaction potential of a transplantable tumor. The tumor's voltage. This article preserves that oncology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140934: A biology paper on the kinetics of exosmosis of water from living cells. The leaking water. This article preserves that cell biology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2375034:
Odronitz and Kollmar rebuilt the family tree of eukaryotes from one motor protein family in 2007. Eukaryotes are organisms whose cells hold a nucleus, from yeast to humans. Myosins are motor proteins that move cargo inside cells, and they exist in all these groups, making them a shared yardstick.

The pair hand-checked 2,269 myosin motor domains from 328 species before building the tree. Most single-gene trees conflict with each other, so a family this large offered a stronger test. Their tree confirmed several accepted groupings of major life forms. It also settled some disputed placements and firmed up groupings that had been only tentative. The authors argued that one deeply sampled protein family, carefully cleaned by hand, can carry real weight in the long argument over how eukaryote groups relate.
europmc-pmc2409934:
Antoniou, Pharoah, Smith, and Easton presented the first BOADICEA model for inherited breast and ovarian cancer risk in 2004. Two faulty genes, BRCA1 and BRCA2, explain some family clustering of these cancers, but most clustering remained unexplained. Their model adds a polygenic part: many small-effect genes acting together.

The model was built by segregation analysis, tracking how cancer moves through families. Its predicted family risks landed close to what large population studies actually observe. Its estimates of how many unselected patients carry BRCA faults also matched population-based counts. Both fits were closer than rival models named Claus and BRCAPRO produced. For a given family history, though, its risk figures could differ markedly from those rivals. The authors offered it as a rational base for genetic counselling and testing decisions.
europmc-pmc2424134:
Urich and colleagues read a soil community's activity and membership in one experiment in 2008. Soil holds Earth's most complex microbe communities, but standard DNA methods show who is present, not who is working. Their approach used RNA instead, since RNA tags reveal both identity and active genes.

They turned the soil's total RNA into copy DNA without any amplification step, then sequenced it directly. One data set held 258,411 short tags, of which 193,219 carried usable identity information and 21,133 were gene activity tags. Counts covered all three domains of life and several feeding levels at once. Even rare soil Crenarchaeota, a group of archaea, appeared in over 2,000 tags. Their activity tags showed enzymes for ammonia burning and carbon fixing, proving those rare members were working, not just present.
europmc-pmc2440734:
Kapustin, Souvorov, Tatusova, and Lipman described a genome annotation tool called Splign in 2008. Annotation pipelines line up copy DNA, called cDNA, against a genome to locate genes. The task gets hard when near-duplicate genes, called paralogs, sit in the genome, or when exons are tiny or splice signals unusual.

Splign attacks the problem in three stages. A fast first pass finds rough matches, then a formal model marks out duplicated regions so copies are not confused, and a final refined alignment polishes the result. In their tests it produced more accurate alignments than the tools then in common use, in reasonable time. It can align the largest cDNA collections, such as the full human EST set, in hours on a modest computer cluster. The duplicate-spotting part can also serve on its own, for instance in hunting pseudogenes, broken gene copies.
europmc-pmc2567434:
Hertz-Fowler and a large team of collaborators sequenced in 2008 the telomeric expression sites of Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind African sleeping sickness. The parasite coats itself in a surface protein and switches coats to dodge the immune system, using expression sites near chromosome ends called telomeres. These regions are often missing from genome sequences, so the team tagged and read them in the Lister 427 strain.

The sites varied in size and gene content, and many worked without the full expected gene set. Yet their overall architecture was surprisingly conserved despite heavy recombination shuffling their parts. Family trees of the resident genes showed the sites are mosaics assembled by that shuffling. The work clarifies how the parasite maintains its coat-switching machinery, a widespread pathogen trick for immune evasion.
europmc-pmc2647734:
Sissoko and co-authors followed in 2009 what happened to people on Reunion Island long after a chikungunya outbreak. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and joint pain that usually fade in days. Reports from the island, though, suggested aches could linger far longer.

The team phoned 147 people whose infections had been confirmed in a lab during 2005. Fifteen months later, 84 of them, more than half, still reported joint or muscle trouble. For most of those, the trouble was constant rather than coming and going. Three traits marked the people least likely to recover. They were 45 or older. They had suffered severe joint pain at the start. Or they already had worn joints from osteoarthritis, a form of joint wear. The authors say care plans should expect a long tail of illness after such outbreaks.
europmc-pmc2649534:
Elwyn and a 25-member international group built in 2009 a scoring tool to judge the quality of patient decision aids. These aids are leaflets, videos, and websites that help patients weigh hard treatment choices alongside their doctors. With groups worldwide making them, shared standards were needed to tell good aids from poor or biased ones.

Their tool, called IPDASi, scores each aid on 47 items grouped into ten areas, then gives a total from 0 to 100. Eight raters tried it on 30 aids chosen at random. Scores spread from 33 to 82, so the tool did separate weak aids from strong ones. Raters also agreed well with each other on the totals. The authors offer the tool as a common yardstick for makers and reviewers of decision aids.
europmc-pmc2704234:
Chan, Chan, and Sze reviewed in 2009 what beta-glucan does to human immune cells and cancer cells. Beta-glucan is a complex sugar found in the walls of fungi and some bacteria, and in herbs that many cancer patients take. Claims for benefit rest mostly on cell and animal tests, not on strong trials in people.

The review sets out how beta-glucan binds to receptors, which are docking sites on immune cells, and wakes up cells such as macrophages and natural killer cells. Size and branching shape change how strong the effect is. The authors stress that no good clinical trial yet proves purified beta-glucan helps cancer patients, and they call for well-run trials.
europmc-pmc2728534:
MacArthur and co-authors measured in 2009 how twenty-one transcription factors, proteins that bind DNA to switch genes on or off, occupy the genome in the early fruit fly embryo. Only forty to fifty such factors pattern the whole embryo, yet each binds short, common DNA motifs that occur far more often than real targets. What sets functional binding apart was unclear.

Mapping binding across thousands of regions, they found the factors bind a largely overlapping set of regions. Distinct cell fates were specified not by wholly different binding sites, but by quantitative differences in how strongly each factor occupied the shared set. Combinations and doses of binding, rather than simple presence or absence, carry the patterning information.
europmc-pmc2914634:
Ferguson, Killeen, and colleagues argued in 2010 that malaria eradication will fail without a serious investment in mosquito ecology. The front-line tools, insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying, target mosquitoes that bite and rest inside houses. In the most intensely infected parts of Africa and the Pacific, those tools alone cannot break transmission of the deadliest malaria parasite, because much biting happens outdoors or before bedtime.

Eradication planning has largely ignored the rest of the mosquito life cycle: mating, sugar feeding, resting sites, and larval habitats. Each neglected stage is a potential control point for future tools. The authors call for long-term strategic funding of vector ecology and evolution. They want it on the same scale as drug and vaccine work. The current imbalance, they warn, caps what elimination campaigns can achieve.
europmc-pmc2924334:
Boonstra and Broekhuis catalogued in 2010 why physicians resist electronic medical records, reviewing two dozen studies from 1998 to 2009 and sorting every reported complaint. Records systems promise safer, better-coordinated care, yet adoption by doctors lagged for years. The team built a taxonomy of eight barrier families containing thirty-one specific obstacles, giving implementers a shared vocabulary.

Cost and technical trouble headline the list, but time pressure during the transition, psychological resistance, and social friction with patients and colleagues matter as much. Legal uncertainty about privacy and liability, rigid organizations, and badly managed change processes complete the map. For each family the authors pair interventions, from financing models to workflow redesign, arguing that rollout plans fail when they treat adoption as a purely technical purchase.
europmc-pmc2926634:
Chateauvieux, Morceau, Dicato, and Diederich reviewed in 2010 valproic acid. The drug is an old epilepsy and mood treatment with a second life in cancer research. Their review gives its dangers equal billing with its promise. The drug steadies brain signaling, but its newer fame comes from blocking histone deacetylases, enzymes that wind DNA shut. Loosening that winding reactivates silenced genes, which can push tumor cells to mature or die.

Clinical trials have multiplied across leukemias and solid tumors, often pairing the drug with standard chemotherapy. The review gathers the molecular evidence and the trial landscape, then turns to the under-discussed side: liver injury, pancreatic and blood effects, and severe birth defects when taken in pregnancy. Enthusiasm for repurposing must be dosed with respect for a long, documented toxicity record.
europmc-pmc2996334:
Burd and colleagues studied ANRIL, a long non-coding RNA tied to artery disease risk, in a 2010 study. Genome scans had linked variants on one chromosome stretch to clogged arteries, yet the variants sit far from the nearest protein genes, inside this RNA's territory.

Mapping the RNA's forms, they found several rare versions in cells. Only forms using sections nearest the neighbouring tumour suppressor genes tracked with the risk variants, which also lowered those genes' activity. Unexpectedly, some transcripts loop into circles that resist breakdown. Such circular forms may be how a distant variant quietly tunes nearby genes.
europmc-pmc3022534:
Diez-Roux and dozens of coauthors built a detailed map of gene activity in the developing mouse, reported in this 2011 paper. They measured where more than eighteen thousand genes were switched on in embryos at a single late stage, when most organs had already formed. Each pattern was recorded with a staining method that marks one gene at a time in thin tissue slices.

Expert anatomists then labeled every image using a shared list of body structures, noting where each gene appeared and how strong the signal was. About two fifths of genes showed activity in only a few places, while others were active nearly everywhere. The full atlas was placed online for free. Other scientists use it to find cell groups, trace cell lineages, and link genes to development and disease.
europmc-pmc3047434:
O'Callaghan and Fenech described in 2011 a lab protocol for measuring the exact length of telomeres, the protective caps on chromosome ends. Telomere length tracks cell aging and disease risk, but the common test gives only a length relative to a reference sample. That makes results hard to compare between labs and across studies. Their method adds a standard of known length to a standard copying test.

The paper spells out how to build the standard, run the test, and convert readings into absolute length. Controls, performance checks, and a troubleshooting guide are included, along with sample results from several human tissues. The test needs little DNA and can be run in high volume. europmc-pmc3102034:
Bowden, Tierney, Copas, and Burdett examined in 2011 how to measure disagreement between trials when their results are pooled, using eighteen cancer meta-analyses built from individual patient data. Pooling assumes trials estimate one effect, yet real trials differ, and that heterogeneity decides whether a pooled average means anything. The classic statistics for it can disagree with each other.

The two most discordant cases showed why blindly applying the standard random effects fix can mislead. A generalized version of the classic statistic estimated the amount of heterogeneity more accurately across the eighteen analyses. Exploring preplanned subgroups, diagnostic plots, and sensitivity checks explained more than any automatic model switch. The authors recommend building the generalized statistic into standard software, and they supply code to do it. Their larger point is that heterogeneity should be investigated, not just accommodated.
europmc-pmc3111534:
Stephen Goodwin and a large international team published the finished genome of a wheat fungus in PLoS Genetics in 2011. The fungus causes a blotch disease that cuts wheat yield and quality in most growing regions. It hides inside leaves for a long stretch before damage shows, and the team wanted the genetic basis for that stealth.

The genome holds twenty-one chromosomes, eight of which the fungus can lose with no clear harm, forming a flexible extra set unlike the core genome. It also carries strikingly few genes for enzymes that chew through plant walls. The authors suggest the fungus feeds quietly on proteins instead, a style closer to harmless leaf dwellers than to aggressive attackers, which may explain its long hidden phase.
europmc-pmc3142234:
Jonas Ludvigsson and colleagues reviewed Sweden's national hospital register in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. The register, running since the nineteen sixties with full coverage since the late nineteen eighties, records nearly every hospital discharge in the country. It feeds countless studies, so its accuracy matters.

The team gathered more than a hundred studies checking it and surveyed hundreds of researchers. Recorded diagnoses proved right in the large majority of checks, though accuracy varied by condition. The register's decades of follow-up make it prized for large population studies. For some topics, the authors note, focused registers such as the cancer register fit better. The paper serves as a user's guide to the register's strengths and limits.
europmc-pmc3156634:
Christopher Fry and colleagues tested how aging blunts the muscle-building answer to exercise in a 2011 paper in Skeletal Muscle. Older adults gain less muscle from resistance training than the young, and the loss of muscle with age raises fall and dependence risk. The team biopsied muscle from sixteen older and sixteen younger adults before and after one hard exercise bout.

In young muscle, key growth switches lit up for hours and new muscle protein production rose clearly. In older muscle, neither the switches nor protein production budged. The stalled signal centres on the main growth-control hub studied. The authors argue this blunted wiring helps explain shrinking training gains with age and marks the pathway as a drug target against age-related wasting.
europmc-pmc3197634:
Sean Eddy wrote this 2011 methods paper in PLoS Computational Biology about a practical bottleneck in searching sequence databases. Profile hidden Markov models can spot distant relatives of a protein, but the older software ran too slowly for routine use. Eddy set out to make those searches much faster without losing their sensitivity.

He describes a filter called multiple segment Viterbi and a rescaling trick that speeds up the standard calculations about twentyfold. Promising hits pass the filter into a full analysis inside his HMMER3 software package. Benchmarks showed the shortcut cost almost no sensitivity, while the program ran hundreds of times faster than its predecessor and matched BLAST for protein searches.
europmc-pmc3234434:
Steven Bachman and colleagues introduced GeoCAT, a web tool that speeds up conservation threat assessments, in this 2011 paper in ZooKeys. Judging a species' risk for the IUCN Red List depends partly on its geographic range, but calculating range measures accurately and consistently had been a chore. GeoCAT was built to automate that step.

Working inside a familiar Google Maps window, users combine occurrence records from sources such as GBIF, Flickr, and Scratchpads, or add their own data. With one click the tool computes the extent of occurrence and area of occupancy, the two range measures the Red List criteria use, and shows an indicative threat rating. The full analysis, data, and settings are stored in a file that can be reloaded or shared with collaborators.
europmc-pmc3312834:
Berni Canani, Di Costanzo, and Leone reviewed a gut made compound that can rewrite gene activity marks, in a 2012 article. The compound, butyrate, is a short fatty acid released when gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber in the colon. Beyond feeding colon cells, it blocks enzymes that remove chemical tags from the protein spools DNA wraps around, loosening or tightening which genes are read.

Through that tag editing route, butyrate shapes effects both inside the gut and beyond it. Interest has grown because a natural compound with this reach could inspire more precise treatments. The review gathers recent findings and weighs possible uses across a wide span of conditions. These range from metabolic and inherited disorders to diseases that wear down the brain.
europmc-pmc3365034:
Peterson and colleagues presented double digest RADseq, a cheaper way to discover genetic markers and genotype many individuals without needing a reference genome. Existing SNP chips are costly and can only test sites already known to vary, which biases studies and misses rare variants, especially in species nobody has sequenced before.

Their protocol cuts DNA with two restriction enzymes, adds a custom indexing scheme so hundreds of individuals can be pooled, and ships with analysis software. Costs per site and per individual fell below chip technology, with modest hands-on time. The team validated the approach both in a lab cross and among wild populations, arguing it suits many kinds of organism alike.
europmc-pmc3372334:
Glass and colleagues used a computer model in 2006 to design social distancing plans for a flu pandemic. At a pandemic's start, vaccines and antiviral drugs may not reach the public in time. Their model followed spread through the daily contacts of a stylized town of ten thousand people.

By cutting contact within chosen groups, the team built strategy mixes that could contain an epidemic in the model. Results depended on how catching the strain was and how the contact network was wired. The work shows that local networks, schools, and workplaces can be planned as defenses. It gave planners a design method rather than a single fixed rule.
europmc-pmc3384434:
Favaloro and colleagues reviewed apoptosis in 2012, the tidy, enzyme-driven form of cell suicide. Fifty years of work have mapped the signals that trigger it, many run by enzymes called caspases. The review concentrates on this classic pathway and the diseases tied to its failures.

Both too little and too much apoptosis cause illness, the authors stress. Cells that refuse to die can feed cancer, while excess death can waste tissue in other diseases. That balance has made the pathway a drug target. Several treatments built on steering apoptosis are already in trials or in medical use. The review sums up where those efforts stand.
europmc-pmc3395634:
Murrell and co-workers introduced a statistical method in 2012 for spotting single sites in genes that natural selection has favored, but only now and then. Selection often flares briefly in a few lineages, and older tools built for constant pressure miss those sites. Their mixed effects model, called MEME, was designed to catch both patterns.

On real and simulated data, the new method beat older ones across a wide range of situations. Applying it broadly, the team found episodic selection to be widespread in protein-coding genes. That implies the true count of positively selected sites has been badly underestimated. The tool gives evolution researchers a finer net for one of their main questions.
europmc-pmc3454434:
Marcilla and a large team reported in 2012 that parasitic flatworms release tiny vesicles packed with their secreted proteins, and that host gut cells swallow those vesicles. Parasite molecules released into the host are prime targets for drugs and diagnostics, but how proteins without export signals escape was puzzling. The team worked with two trematode worms, Echinostoma caproni and the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica.

Protein analysis, gold-tagged microscopy, and electron imaging agreed: the vesicles carry most of the proteins long known from worm secretions, plus some host proteins picked up along the way. Living worms release them actively. Their uptake by intestinal cells suggests a delivery channel between parasite and host. The finding reframes how these worms talk to the bodies they inhabit.
europmc-pmc3458434:
Schimel and Schaeffer asked in 2012 when the makeup of soil's microbial community actually steers carbon cycling, and when it does not. Microbes run decomposition and the turnover of soil organic matter, processes that decide whether carbon stays buried or returns to the air. Narrow jobs, like making trace gases, clearly track which microbes are present; the broad jobs were less certain.

The authors argue that species-level variety mostly reflects backup copies of the same functions, sorted into guilds by deep life-history splits. In loose surface litter and around roots, community makeup can move the breakdown rate. In mineral soil the bottleneck is physical access to protected food, so who is present matters less than how microbes spend the carbon they capture. That spending decides long-term storage.

William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 June 1861. It is document 134 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As June ended, Paris settled into its neutral watch on the war. Dayton's reports grew steady, focused on ships, trade, and court talk. His letter closes the first full month of the French file in the record of 1861. The French file's first month set habits that lasted the whole war. frus-1861-d234:

The letter comes from the month the Civil War began, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d34:

This mid August note shows the center guiding the edge, one dated page at a time. The Brussels file swells in August, as Sanford took up fresh tasks for the cause. frus-1862-d134:

It was printed as Document 134 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. frus-1862-d534:

The doubling of notes on a single day, repeated across this exchange, reflects how enclosures and separate subjects were handled. Nothing was mixed. Everything was numbered and answered in kind. For the Netherlands, the stakes in Washington were commercial and legal, not military. Van Limburg's steady formal pressure was how a small power defended them. The document completes the densest cluster in the Dutch file, five days of letters that show the State Department's wartime desk work at full stretch.
frus-1862-d634:
The year's closing instruction to Constantinople went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Edward Joy Morris on 18 November 1862. It is Document 634 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November's orders everywhere repeated the Union's refusal of foreign mediation. The instruction to the Ottoman post carried that settled policy to the edge of the system. Morris needed it less as guidance than as record: Washington's position, stated to all its ministers alike, could be quoted anywhere. The letter ends the Turkish file for 1862 on the year's dominant diplomatic note. It was sounded as firmly at Constantinople as at London. Yet the audience there could hardly have mattered less to the outcome.

The last sheet of a three-letter day wound up the post's March work. Adams's spring file is dense because the stakes were: warships for the South in British yards, and a British cabinet that trod a fine line. This letter ends the day's set. It is a working piece of the great London run, the part of the volume most read by students of the war.
frus-1863p1-d234:

It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d334:

It stands as document 334 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d34:
Charles Francis Adams closed his heavy mail day with this third dispatch of 16 January 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 34 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The run of Adams letters in this volume is the spine of the British file. His reports let Washington know, steamer by steamer, whether Britain leaned toward or away from the South. This letter ends a three-sheet day in mid-January, when the freedom edict's echo was still fresh in London. It is a working piece of a watch that helped keep Britain out of the war.
frus-1863p1-d434:
31 March 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d534:
Writing on 26 May 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in an official letter. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d634:
A 8 October 1863 dispatch from the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d134: General Joseph McNarney, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army, wrote to the Secretary of State on November 16, 1943. The letter is Document 134 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Army-to-State letters in summit season usually meant men, planes, or bases crossing department lines, though this record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the week the parties converged on Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d234:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a wide-ranging secret telegram from Washington on 19 November 1943. Sent through the White House Map Room to Roosevelt at Oran, it bundles short reports from several capitals, led by news from Lebanon.

The British deadline for French release of the Lebanese prisoners has slipped from Sunday to Monday morning at ten. On Italy, no move will be made against Marshal Badoglio or the king until Rome falls, though staff changes in Badoglio's government are listed. Giraud still awaits written pledges from the French Committee. The note ends with Romania's quiet feelers for peace terms, passed to Madrid: Washington's answer was unconditional surrender, and nothing else.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d334:
Madame Chiang Kai-shek wrote a personal letter to President Roosevelt at Cairo on 26 November 1943, the day the Chiangs said goodbye and left for China. She apologizes for her handwriting at the start, saying she is still, in her word, Cyclops, and the letters run together unneatly.

The letter carries her husband's message. The Generalissimo, she writes, could not find words at parting to thank Roosevelt enough for all he has done and is doing for China, or to say how much his friendship means. He felt the wistfulness of farewell, trusts Roosevelt as a friend, and hopes the bonds between them will strengthen with time. Madame Chiang closes in her own name, with a heart overflowing with affection and gratitude.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d34: Ronald Campbell, the British chargé in Washington, wrote directly to President Roosevelt on September 17, 1943. His letter is Document 34 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A chargé carries an embassy in the ambassador's absence, and a letter from him to a head of state was a formal step. The catalog record supplies the parties and the date and no subject. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series for its text to explain.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d434:
Sent from Tehran on December 4, 1943, this short secret telegram went from W. Averell Harriman, the American ambassador to the Soviet Union, to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant. It was sent on to Cairo through Army channels while the Allied leaders were meeting in Tehran and Cairo. The text survives in the Hopkins Papers.

Harriman passes on a message from Soviet foreign minister Molotov, relayed through the Russian Embassy in Tehran, saying Vyshinsky would represent the Soviet Union at Cairo. He adds that he will leave Tehran for Moscow on the morning of December 5. An editor's note corrects the record: Vinogradov, not Vyshinsky, actually represented the Soviets at Cairo, and he attended none of the formal meetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d534:
Officials in the Department of State prepared this memorandum on December 27, 1943, and the Department later printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume. A prepared departmental paper, unlike a cable, gathers facts and views into one place for decision-makers.

Such memoranda were the department's way of thinking on paper after the conferences: setting out a question, the background, and the choices as Washington saw them. Readers who want to know how the permanent government absorbed the summits will value this kind of record. It lacks a famous signature, but it shows the institution at work in the last days of 1943.
frus-1944-quebec-d134:
Under the heading "The Italian Situation," State Department planners briefed Roosevelt for Quebec in September 1944. Italy was both a defeated enemy and a co-belligerent fighting beside the Allies, an awkward double status. Premier Bonomi's government had survived its first two months, but the paper calls its position precarious without proof of Allied sympathy.

Relief and rebuilding dominate the paper. It weighs financing supplies from lire paid to American troops, a limited UNRRA relief program costed at 35 to 50 million dollars, and trucks and coal to move food. It also questions the outdated armistice terms, the future of the Allied Control Commission, and the stigma on Italian prisoners. Churchill, it notes, had dropped his idea of a preliminary peace treaty.
frus-1944-quebec-d234:
Marshall answered Deane from Quebec on September 14, 1944, in telegram Octagon 26. The question was whether the Warsaw relief arrangements required representatives to fly from London to Moscow. Deane had argued they did not, since planning belonged in London and only Soviet approval was needed in Moscow. Marshall accepted his judgment in full.

If arrangements satisfactory to General Spaatz could be completed between the Russians, Deane, and Spaatz without the London journey, that was satisfactory at Quebec. Deane and Spaatz were to complete the arrangements and carry out the project as the two of them saw fit. The message is a model of delegation: the theater men closest to the problem were given the decision.
frus-1944-quebec-d34:
Edward R. Stettinius, the Under Secretary of State, recorded this memorandum on August 28, 1944. Stettinius, a former steel executive, was then running much of the department while planning the future world organization. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Stettinius had just come from the Dumbarton Oaks talks, where the United Nations was being drafted, and Quebec would take up questions touching that design. A memorandum from his desk in the pre-conference file shows the department preparing its positions. For readers, it marks the State Department's place in a conference remembered chiefly for soldiers and finance.
frus-1945-50-intel-d134:
Quinn, director of the Strategic Services Unit, wrote to Petersen, assistant secretary of war, on 11 April 1947. The SSU still existed on paper in the spring of 1947, a shadow of the wartime OSS. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Late papers from a dying unit concern the last things: records, men still on the rolls, and duties not yet handed over. Quinn's letter to the War Department's civilian side belongs to that winding-down. Readers should not skip it as an echo. The care with which a government buries a secret service, its files above all, decides what later ages can know. This volume exists because such papers were kept.
frus-1945-50-intel-d234:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 7 May 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 234 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d334:
The Executive Secretary (Souers) addressed a memorandum to the National Security Council on 10 December 1947. Readers meet it as document 334 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d34:
General Magruder sent a formal report to Lovett, the assistant secretary of war for air, on 24 October 1945. Magruder reported as director of the Strategic Services Unit, the OSS remnant in the War Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A report differs from a letter: it accounts, in order, for a unit's state and work. Magruder had to prove, again and again, that his leftover service still earned its keep. His report to Lovett reached one of the War Department's most influential civilians, a man whose judgment the secretary trusted. Readers can use the report to see the SSU as its chief wished it seen. It looks lean and useful, ready to form the core of whatever central agency might come.
frus-1945-50-intel-d434:
Dated 3 March 1950, National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 14 is document 434 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Fourteen numbered orders in just over two years show a rule book built by use. Each new one answered a gap found in daily work across the agencies. For the reader, the directive is a dated marker of how the postwar intelligence system kept changing its own design. Within months of this order, wartime need would force yet more change on the system it governed. Change, in this series, was not a flaw but the normal state of things.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d134:
“The Treatment of Germany” is the fullest briefing book paper in this group, dated 12 January 1945. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary lists what the United States should seek in the first period after organized resistance ends.

Accept the European Advisory Commission's draft on control machinery without reserve, it begins, and make the Control Council's authority supreme. Disband all German armed and para-military forces, seize and destroy their weapons, and wreck plants that cannot turn to peaceful uses. Destroy the Nazi system itself: dissolve the party, strike down its laws, and clear active Nazis from public office and from leading posts in private firms.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d234:
President Roosevelt answered the Iran memorandum in his own hand on 8 December 1944. His short note from Warm Springs, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sends the matter to the top. Harriman, he directs, should take the Soviet-Iranian question up with Stalin in person.

The Tehran agreement, Roosevelt writes, was pretty definite. He then revives an idea of his own from that meeting. He had proposed that three or four trustees build a new port in Iran at the head of the Persian Gulf, a free port. The trustees would take over the whole railroad from there into Russia, and run it for the good of all. Stalin's only comment, he recalls, was that the idea was interesting; he offered no objection.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d334:
Lunch with the three foreign ministers on February 5, 1945, mixed toasts with hard business, and Edward Page's minutes record both. Molotov opened by toasting the three leaders. When Harriman announced that Manila had been captured, Molotov at once proposed a toast to that Allied victory. Eden then honored Molotov as host foreign minister.

Stettinius added his own toast and passed along greetings from former Secretary Hull, then in a hospital but on the mend. The listed subjects move from toasts to the conference's name, then to Germany and its economy. The page shows ceremony and policy sharing one table at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d34: On 30 December 1944 Roosevelt sent Churchill a message, one of the last exchanges of a crowded year. Filed as document 34 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta, it keeps the two leaders in step entering 1945. Within weeks both men would travel to Malta, then on to the Crimea for the summit itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d434:
Britain's full formula for Poland, dated February 8, 1945, settles borders first. The Curzon Line would be Poland's eastern frontier, with adjustments of five to eight kilometers in Poland's favor in some regions. In the west, Poland would take the free city of Danzig. It would also take East Prussia west and south of Königsberg, the Oppeln district of Silesia, and lands east of the Oder.

Germans in those regions would be repatriated to Germany. Poles in Germany could return at their wish. With western Poland freed by Soviet armies, the paper turns to forming a fully representative provisional government. The text is the high-water mark of British drafting on Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d134:
Captain Pinney, aide to Admiral Leahy, passed on a shipping question on July 9, 1945. The short telegram is document 134 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Admiral Emory Land, who ran American merchant shipping, had learned that Britain's Lord Leathers would probably attend Terminal.

Land believes he should be there too, Pinney reports, and he is standing by under Leahy's orders, ready to go if wanted. The point at issue is practical. The Joint Chiefs thought it urgent to use certain large captured ships to move troops home. Land and Leathers had been negotiating the matter for some time. A note adds that Land did leave Washington for Babelsberg on July 17.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d234:
Assistant Secretary Dunn reported British agreement on the foreign ministers council in an extract dated July 14, 1945. The extract is document 234 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, drawn from his two-hour talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam.

Cadogan expressed general agreement with the American proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers to handle the peace settlement. He felt it should not come first on the agenda; German questions should open the conference instead. The council's deputies and staff would need a fixed home, probably London, while the ministers might meet in various capitals. Dunn also raised ending the European Advisory Commission, and explained why Washington had settled on five members, following the Security Council, rather than four. Cadogan agreed that including China made sense on that basis.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d334:
Money in occupied Germany is the subject of a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum. British and American troops, it explains, were spending Allied Military Marks. The printing plates for that currency had been shared with the Soviet authorities, who issued the same marks in their zone. German and emergency currencies also still circulated.

The committee calls a single currency system basic to trade, contracts, and any sound level of business in Germany. It also asks that the purpose of the currency in each zone be defined, so that occupying forces and others use it alike. The memo shows how even banknotes became a four-power problem in 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d34:
Davies repeated his Chequers performance at the Foreign Office in this second supplemental report of June 12, 1945. On Monday, May 28, Ambassador Winant presented him to Foreign Minister Eden. Following Churchill's suggestion, Davies covered the ground practically as in his talks at Chequers, set out in his earlier report.

In view of Eden's connection with the San Francisco Conference, Davies spoke very frankly, in a friendly and not critical spirit. His theme was the unfortunate manner in which issues had arisen between the Soviet delegation and those of Britain and the United States. The report shows the envoy carrying one brief — Soviet feelings — to both British leaders.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d434:
Blaisdell answered Clayton from London on July 13, 1945, about the German coal policy he had been sent. Clayton's cable of July 4 had repeated a letter laying out policy on stimulating German coal production for export and distributing the surpluses. Blaisdell apologizes: the cable reached him only on July 8.

That day he discussed it with Ambassador Winant. They agreed he should go to Frankfurt and get General Clay's slant on the policy points he was asked to act upon. On July 11, with Wayne Jackson of the Department and R. S. McCaffery of his mission, he had his talk with Clay. The letter shows policy being carried, in person, to the commander who must execute it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d534:
Moscow cools the air route in Vyshinsky's reply to Harriman, dated July 11, 1945 and printed in translation. Acknowledging the ambassador's letter of July 7 on a civil air lines connection at Berlin, served by American and Soviet airplanes, Vyshinsky reminds him of their earlier conversation. Practically speaking, he had pointed out, air communications over the route had already much improved.

He recognizes the matter's importance, he writes. But he does not believe that at the present time this question is sufficiently prepared for discussion in substance. As to the future, he can inform the ambassador only upon receipt of instructions from the Soviet government. The polite letter leaves the Berlin connection stalled where it stood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d634:
Ambassador Murray sent a short secret wire from Tehran on July 5, 1945, about Iran's hopes for Potsdam. It is document 634 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The wire was repeated to London and Moscow as well.

Murray says Iran's foreign minister spoke on cabinet instructions this time. Iran strongly hopes the U.S. will work at the Big Three meeting to stop foreign meddling in its inner affairs. He named the parliamentary elections due that fall or winter as a special concern. The minister also raised again Iran's wish for an early exit of British and Soviet troops. The message repeats a plea the prime minister made on June 19, but now with the full weight of the cabinet behind it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1034: Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Winant in London on July 29, 1945. The President has approved the agreement signed three days earlier by the European Advisory Commission. It amends the September 1944 protocol on occupation zones in Germany and on Berlin rule. The covering report and letters go with it. Winant must tell the other members at once. The editors note the other approvals followed in August: Britain on the 2nd, France on the 7th, and the Soviet Union on the 13th.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1134:
Shipping chief Emory Land and his aide Morse wrote down the chain on 23 July 1945. Their note went to regional chief Monroe and to Carnwath of the maritime board's London branch. The message ran from Washington's shipping heads to the men who ran the joint fleet in European waters.

With Germany beaten, Allied shipping was swinging toward new work. The Pacific war still had to be fed, and freed Europe had to be kept from hunger. Orders from the top of the agency set that shift in motion. This cable shows wartime supply lines bending to a changed war, handled by the men who ran them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1234:
Sato reported to Togo on 25 July 1945, the day before the Allies issued their terms to Japan. His Moscow soundings had run for weeks and gained nothing firm. The Soviet side still smiled, still stalled, and still kept its own plans dark.

An envoy's report at such a moment carries the weight of a mission ending. Sato could offer Tokyo only his judgment: that Moscow would act for itself when it chose. This cable is that judgment, sent hours before the Potsdam Declaration spoke. It closes the first phase of the exchange, though neither writer yet knew how the story would end.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1334:
Wallace Murray, the American ambassador in Iran, cabled the acting secretary of state in Washington on 27 July 1945. Murray reported from Tehran while President Truman and Secretary Byrnes were at the Potsdam Conference. Truman, Churchill. Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Embassy cables like this one carried news from posts that the summit leaders could not watch themselves. Iran mattered in 1945 as a supply route to the Soviet Union and as a land watched closely by both London and Moscow. The cable lets readers see a distant post speak to Washington at the very moment the big powers were drawing the postwar map.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-134: Among the pieces printed without numbers after document 710 sits this brief editorial note. It was written by the editors of the Potsdam volume, not by a wartime hand. Foreign Relations notes like this one supply context, cite files, and warn of gaps. Readers passing through the conference papers find it a short, useful pause.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-34:
Gromyko talked trusteeship with Secretary Byrnes on the morning of July 20, 1945, and no minutes were kept. The gap is marked by an editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It is the thirty-fourth unnumbered item following document 710.

The editors know of the meeting only from a later letter. In a letter to Byrnes dated July 20, printed as document 734, Gromyko referred to our conversation this morning. The question of trusteeship was discussed at that talk, the note adds. No minutes of the conversation have been found. The entry thus preserves the fact and subject of a meeting, and nothing more. It is one of many such notes in this volume, where the editors flag gaps in the archive rather than fill them with guesses.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d734:
Andrei Gromyko, the Soviet ambassador in Washington, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 20, 1945, in document 734. Gromyko was Moscow's polished voice in America. Though the leaders met in Germany, the Washington channel stayed busy. His letter joined the papers printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An ambassador's formal letter fixes his government's words. Gromyko chose them with care; he was famous for precision. Readers see Soviet diplomacy working its second front: the embassy. The document shows that Potsdam's arguments echoed in capitals far away. It also marks the respect each side paid to exact written form, even mid-crisis.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d834:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Kennan in Moscow on July 16, 1945, in document 834. Grew sent guidance to the chargé holding the Moscow embassy. The letter predates the Potsdam opening by a day. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside Kennan's replies.

Instructions to Moscow carried special care in 1945. Every word to the Soviet capital was weighed twice. Readers see Washington briefing its watcher before the summit began. The document opens the Grew-Kennan channel in this volume. Their exchange forms a quiet subplot: the home office and the Moscow desk, thinking together about the ally they least understood.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d934: American staff prepared this undated memorandum on the worth of East Prussia, filed with the July 24, 1945 papers. Another copy heads it Statistics by Lubin. Factory, farm, and timber resources in the province were valued near four billion Reichsmarks in 1941. Real estate added about 1.28 billion more. The area north of the Goldap-Braunsberg line holds 40 percent of the people and two-thirds of those resources. Converted at set rates, the resources of the part going to the Soviet Union come to roughly one billion dollars.
frus-1981-88v04-d34: A 1981-1988 FRUS editorial note on the Soviet Union. The context. This note provides that background. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-295434: Total Industrial & Packaging contested a February 2005 award, and GAO's ruling closes the case. The packaging firm's claims were weighed and judged on the merits. The box was sealed on the dispute for good. The dispute was over. The case was closed.
gao-gaoreports-b-296334: Trajen and Maytag Aircraft tangled four dockets in July 2005 — a multi-firm protest pile — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firms challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Mega-filings get one careful answer. Four dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-296534: National Beef Packing took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298734: Leader Communications doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one comms fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-309734: Florida and Vermont's Medicaid experiments drew GAO's legal eye in 2007 — were the waiver approvals properly done under the law? The ruling tests the demonstration projects against the statute's fine print. Health-policy labs, the call reminds, still need a solid legal foundation to stand on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-134: Two years of health fraud fight reports got graded in 2005, and GAO's review covers the 2002 and 2003 annual results. The scorecard shows what the anti-fraud program delivered. The cheats who billed the system were the target. The results were counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-234: The post-9/11 arms export system got a GAO review in 2005, and the report covers the control regime. The review checks the gates closely. The weapons trade deserved the watch. The gates were checked. The regime was reviewed. The gates were watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-334: The Kennedy Center needed a firmer hand in 2005, and GAO's report calls for stronger watch over fire safety, construction, and finances. The review covers all three fronts. The nation's stage deserved the oversight. The oversight had to be stronger. The nation's stage deserved the oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-434: The homeland shop's hacker defense lagged in 2005, and GAO's report says the cyber duties went unmet. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the digital homeland deserved protection. The digital homeland deserved protection. The duties had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-534: Military training ranges needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says planning and funding priority were required to improve conditions. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the troops' ranges deserved good ground. The planning had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-634: Pornography on peer-to-peer networks got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the file-sharing problem. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the kids deserved protection. The use had to be understood. The kids deserved protection.
