gao-gaoreports-gao-06-134: Enlisted recruitment needed an action plan in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed a plan to address the challenges. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the ranks deserved filling. The plan had to be made. The ranks deserved filling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-434: Credit card minimum-payment disclosures needed customizing in 2006, and GAO's report says tailored disclosures would inform consumers more. The findings prescribe the fix. The report warns that the plastic's fine print needed clarity. The disclosures had to be customized. The fine print needed clarity.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-634: The Webb telescope needed a smarter buying approach in 2006, and GAO's report says a knowledge-based acquisition method was key to the program's challenges. The findings prescribe the discipline. The report warns that the billion-dollar eye needed building right. The approach had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-834: Disaster relief billions needed tracking in 2006, and GAO's report says a governmentwide framework was required to collect and report the spending. The findings demand the system. The report warns that the relief dollars should not vanish into fog. The framework had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-934: New Orleans' levees needed more than patches in 2006, and GAO's report says strategic planning was required beyond the interim repairs. The findings demand the long view. The report warns that the city's walls needed a real future. The planning had to be strategic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1034: The world's anti-slavery projects were flying half-blind in 2007 — GAO's report says U.S.-backed trafficking programs lacked solid tracking, though experts saw fixes. The findings pair a measurement gap with a reform sketch. Good intentions, the report argues, need good yardsticks to free anyone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-134: The SEC's books got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the commission's financial statements for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the market cop's own ledger got checked. The regulator's books had to balance. The market cop's ledger got its audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-234: The Pentagon's supply chain was slowly improving in 2007, and GAO's report says progress had been made on the high-risk fixes, though the full gains were unclear. The findings balance credit and doubt. The report warns that the war machine's shelves had to stay stocked. The chain had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-634: Airport screening rules were finally getting risk-based in 2007 — GAO's report says threat levels, hard experience, and passenger gripes drove the changes. The findings grade the new approach. The report's balance: safer skies without treating every grandma like a suspect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-734: Ultrasound billing needed a second opinion in 2007 — GAO's report weighs payment reforms and tech-qualification rules for the scans. The findings probe whether Medicare paid right for the pictures. The report's question is dollars and sense: fair price, qualified hands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-134: The Government Accountability Office dug into chemical Demilitarization: Additional Management Actions Needed to Meet Key Performance Goals of DOD's Chemical Demilitarization Program in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-34: GAO's 2007 report looks at a bold fix for clumsy agencies: put a top boss in charge of just running the shop. The chief operating officer idea splits policy from plumbing, giving one leader the job of making the agency work. The report tracks how agencies tried the role — and whether the new bosses truly changed how business got done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-634: The Government Accountability Office dug into prison Construction: Clear Communication on the Accuracy of Cost Estimates and Project Changes is Needed in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
hercules-piochymicus-1634: Hercules piochymicus, 1634. The pious chemical Hercules. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
hippolytus-apostolic-tradition-easton-19:
Hippolytus of Rome wrote the Apostolic Tradition around A.D. 215, and Burton Scott Easton translated it into English in 1934 with an introduction and notes. The work is the earliest surviving church order, a rule book for how a Christian community should run its shared life.

Inside, Hippolytus spells out how bishops, priests, and deacons were chosen and prayed over. He describes baptism step by step, along with fasting, daily prayer, and the shared meal of the Eucharist. Because so little else survives from that early, the text is a key witness to how worship took shape in the third century.
howe-mormonism-unvailed-1834:
Eber Dudley Howe was an Ohio newspaper editor who published Mormonism Unvailed in 1834, the first book-length attack on the new faith. Joseph Smith had published the Book of Mormon only four years earlier, and converts were gathering fast. Howe set out to stop the movement with print.

The book gathers sworn statements from Smith's neighbors calling him a fraud and a money-digger. Its famous claim, the Spalding theory, holds that the Book of Mormon was copied from a lost novel by Solomon Spalding. Howe's attack set the terms of anti-Mormon writing for the rest of the century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messing-10734:
Messing was a Prussian family whose members settled in the United States during the nineteenth century, profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Cyrus Adler and Isidore Singer. The entry centers on Joseph Messing, a Talmudist and rabbi born at Argenau in 1812, and on the sons and grandson who followed him into the rabbinate.

Joseph held pulpits at Gostyn and Witkowo and wrote commentaries on Megillah, the tractate Abot, and the Haggadah before his death in London in 1880. Three of his sons became American rabbis, serving in New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Indianapolis, and St. Louis. The youngest figure, Abraham Joseph Messing, graduated from Hebrew Union College in 1897 and took a pulpit in Montgomery, Alabama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milhaud-latin-a:
Milhaud is a village in the French department of Gard whose medieval Jewish community left almost no documents behind. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The writers warn against confusing it with Millau in Aveyron, where Jews probably never lived at all. What is known can be told quickly.

The Jews of Milhaud were expelled in 1306 and found refuge in the Comtat-Venaissin, above all at Carpentras, where their descendants still lived four centuries later. The surname Milhaud, in its several spellings, stayed common among southern French Jews. The entry closes with a roll of the village's scholars, several of them physicians and translators of medical works, who carried its name abroad.
laennec-auscultation-forbes-1834:
Rene Laennec invented the stethoscope and described its use in his French treatise of 1819. John Forbes translated that work into English, and the edition here dates to 1834. Laennec called his method mediate auscultation, meaning listening through an instrument. The stethoscope let doctors hear the chest with new precision.

Laennec links each sound in the chest to a state of the lungs or heart. Breathing, voice, and cough all become signs a doctor can read. His system founded modern diagnosis of chest disease. English speaking medicine learned the method largely from Forbes's version. The book changed what a doctor does at a bedside. Its plates and terms shaped practice.
landor-citation-shakspeare-1834:
Landor invented a legal scene for young William Shakspeare in this playful work of 1834. In his telling, the future playwright stands before Sir Thomas Lucy in September 1582, charged with stealing deer from the knight's park. Witnesses named Euseby Treen, Joseph Carnaby, and Silas Gough support the case, by the title page.

Shakspeare defends himself in dialogue with wit, while the magistrate blusters at him. The piece gives the old Stratford deer-stealing legend a full hearing it never had in real life. Added at the end is a talk between Edmund Spenser and the Earl of Essex on the state of Ireland in 1595.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-3:
Planetary motions and lunar theory fill books six and seven of Laplace's Mecanique Celeste. Nathaniel Bowditch published his translation of that third volume in 1834. The Moon's path posed some of the hardest problems in all astronomy. Sailors and navies needed exact lunar tables for finding position at sea.

Laplace attacks the Moon's many small wobbles with powerful analysis. Bowditch adds commentary and tables that make the work usable. The volume stands third in his four volume English set. It shows theory serving a plain practical need. Few books join deep math to sea travel so directly. Its tables guided real ships.
lectures-on-phrenology-delivered-before-: Lectures on Phrenology, 1834. The young men's lectures. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
lettres-a-camille-sur-la-physiologie-de-: Lettres à Camille sur la physiologie de l'homme, 1834. The Camille letters. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
marcus-aurelius-meditations-casaubon-163:
Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations in Greek, and Meric Casaubon made the first English version in 1634. Casaubon gave England the Roman emperor's notebook, not meant for any eyes but his own. He wrote on campaign along the Danube, in Greek, amid war and plague years there.

The notes urge calm, duty, and scorn for fame, wealth, and the fear of death. All is flux, he reminds himself, and the mind can stay free in any fort. He thanks gods and kin, and checks his temper toward fools and flatterers at court. Stoic counsel here is plain, brief, and meant for daily use in hard times. Casaubon's version made the book a fixture of English moral reading for centuries.
milton-comus-1634:
John Milton's masque Comus was first performed in 1634 at Ludlow Castle. This volume joins it with L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas. Together they form the classic set of Milton's essential early poems in English and Latin.

Comus, a tempter with a magic cup, traps a lost Lady in his wood. Her brothers and a guardian spirit free her through chastity's strength. L'Allegro praises mirth, and Il Penseroso praises sober thought and study. Lycidas mourns a drowned friend in some of the finest pastoral verse in English. The set shows a young poet of rare range and control.
openalex-w2159284134: Agitation — restlessness, aggression, distress — is common in dementia and other brain disorders, yet doctors have never agreed on what exactly counts as agitation. This 2014 paper from the International Psychogeriatric Association offers a provisional consensus definition for both clinics and research. A shared definition matters because agitation drives disability, nursing-home placement, and suffering for patients and caregivers alike.
openalex-w2768742734: Lakes and reservoirs bury organic carbon faster than the oceans do — yet their role in the carbon cycle is underappreciated. This 2017 Nature Communications paper quantifies organic carbon burial in global inland waters. The numbers show these water bodies punch above their weight in locking carbon away from the atmosphere.
openalex-w2891785734: As groundwater extraction soared over sixty years, engineers learned to put water back — managed aquifer recharge. This 2018 Hydrogeology Journal paper offers the first global review of six decades of progress, from new water-treatment technologies to intentional replenishment. The history charts how societies learned to bank water underground.
openalex-w2966305634: The bandgap — the energy leap electrons must make — defines every semiconductor, yet measuring it has been inconsistent for two centuries. This 2019 Scientific Reports paper revisits the optical bandgap's determination and proposes a unified methodology. The standardization brings order to one of materials science's most basic measurements.
openalex-w2966591034: Add fresh organic matter to soil and microbes may devour old carbon too — the 'priming effect,' with big implications for carbon cycling. This 2019 Nature Communications paper surveys 86 sites worldwide to find the global ecological predictors of priming. The drivers identified help models predict how soils will respond to change.
openalex-w3003604034: Tumors co-opt both inflammation and blood-vessel growth to thrive. This 2019 Frontiers in Oncology paper reviews how angiogenesis contributes to inflammation and cancer — from initiation through progression. The intertwined processes offer combined therapeutic targets.
openalex-w4380871934: This 2023 Intensive Care Medicine paper presents ESICM guidelines on acute respiratory distress syndrome — updating the 2017 guidance on definition, phenotyping, and respiratory support strategies. Limited to adult non-pharmacological support, the guidelines standardize care for a lethal syndrome.
openalex-w4412648834: Light can be guided along protected paths that ignore defects. This paper reviews the team's work on topological edge modes for mid-infrared light: designing, building, and testing photonic crystals. The authors verified the modes with reflection spectroscopy. An optics review of light that refuses to scatter.
openalex-w4413733734: A crystal's defects can flip its thermoelectric sign. This theory paper explains how misplaced atoms in Fe2VAl reverse the Seebeck coefficient, the voltage from a temperature difference. The authors built a model with random-defect effects. A materials-theory study of disorder as a design knob.
openalex-w4414920434: PrSb2 hides a weird electric signal inside its magnetic state. This lab paper reports voltage tests revealing a twist-based Hall effect, a sign of knotted magnetic patterns, in its ordered phase. The team tied it to the crystal's charge waves. A study of math-like twists showing up in a real crystal.
openalex-w7129071434: Surgeons sometimes nick the gallbladder during keyhole removal, but does it matter to patients? This study tracked pain and daily life after such accidental tears. The team filled a gap in what we know. A surgery study of a common slip and its aftermath.
openalex-w7165044234: College students need someone to talk to. This study tracked use of counseling rooms at two Juntendo University campuses, which serve over 3,000 students. The team mapped who sought help and why. A campus mind-health study of demand meeting supply.
openalex-w7204540334: Trajan was Rome's first emperor born outside Italy, in the province of Hispania. This history article studies how that province's ties with Rome set the stage for his rise at the end of the first century AD. The authors trace the politics of integration and power that made a provincial the most powerful man in the world. Ancient history with a modern echo about outsiders reaching the top.
openalex-w7204657734: A cat arrived at the clinic with a suspicious lump, and tests pointed to fibrosarcoma, a tumor of connective tissue. This case report walks through how the vets diagnosed it and chose treatment, noting that the tumor's location did not match the usual vaccine-linked pattern. The authors share the case to help other vets recognize similar ones. Short, clinical, and useful at the exam table.
openalex-w7206159834: The city of Bayeux in Paraiba got its name from the French town freed by the Allies in World War II. This study reconstructs the city's political history and identity through the pages of the Paraiba newspaper A Uniao in 1944. The author shows how wartime news shaped local memory. A fine piece of press-based history, reading a city's story in the ink of its time.
outlines-of-phrenology-1834: Outlines of Phrenology, 1834. Another outlines. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
pare-workes-1634:
Ambroise Paré was a French barber-surgeon who treated wounded soldiers on sixteenth-century battlefields. He wrote his surgical works in French from hard experience rather than university training. Thomas Johnson translated the full set into English, and the combined volume appeared in London in 1634.

Paré explains how to treat gunshot wounds with gentle dressings instead of boiling oil. He also describes tying off arteries during amputation, making artificial limbs and eyes, and helping women in childbirth. His clear, case-based writing helped turn surgery into a respected craft. The book is a landmark in the birth of modern surgery.
pare-workes-johnson-1634:
Ambroise Paré was the leading French surgeon of the sixteenth century, famed for gentle methods and sharp observation. Thomas Johnson Englished his Workes in 1634, a huge folio of surgical knowledge. Among its books stands the celebrated treatise Of Monsters and Prodigies.

Paré tries to explain nature's errors with a surgeon's care. He lists causes of monsters, from God's will to defects of seed and womb. His woodcuts show conjoined twins, sea monsters, and strange beasts. The treatise founded the study of birth defects, called teratology. It also preserves what a great medical mind of 1600 could believe about the strange.
phrenology-in-connection-with-the-study-: Phrenology, in Connection with the Study of Physiognomy, 1834. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
plos-pbio-0020234:
Rick S. Mitchell, Brett F. Beitzel, Astrid R. W. Schröder, and co-workers compared where retroviruses insert their DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. Retroviruses copy their genes into the host's genome. The team tracked insertion sites for three of them: ASLV, a bird virus; HIV; and MLV, a mouse virus.

Each virus favors different kinds of spots. HIV leans toward active genes, while the others show their own patterns. Those choices affect both harm and use. An insertion inside a vital gene can cause cancer, a known risk in gene therapy with such viruses. Knowing each virus's taste helps predict that risk and pick safer vectors for treatment.
plos-pbio-0020334:
Amit Dutt, Stefano Canevascini, Erika Fröhli, and their team traced a growth signal in the worm C. elegans in PLOS Biology in 2004. EGF signals help shape the worm's egg-laying organ, the vulva, during development. A protein called ROM-1, from the rhomboid family, helps pass that signal along.

Rhomboid proteins cut other proteins inside cell membranes, freeing signal pieces to act. Showing that ROM-1 shapes EGF spread in a living animal gave the family a clear job in development. That matters beyond worms. Human rhomboids and EGF signals are both tied to cancer and to diseases of the skin and gut, so the worm work offers clean leads.
plos-pone-0000034:
Karl Maurer, John Cooper, Marcelo Caraballo, and co-authors built a tool for printing DNA in a 2006 methods paper. DNA microarrays, chips spotted with thousands of DNA samples, are made by building each spot in place. One route uses acid to unblock growing DNA strands, but the acid must stay exactly where it is put.

The team generated the acid electrochemically, with electric current, and contained it to reaction areas just 100 microns across, about the width of a human hair. Neat containment means denser, cleaner chips. Microarrays were then a workhorse of genetics, used to read gene activity in cancer and many other fields, so better printing meant better data everywhere.
plos-pone-0000134:
Jaime H. Reina, Teldja N. Azzouz, and Nouria Hernandez published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It introduces Maf1 as a player in the control of human RNA polymerase III. That enzyme copies a small but vital set of genes, including ones for transfer RNA, the adapters used to build proteins.

Cells must tune this copying to their growth state, making more building blocks when times are good. The authors show Maf1 helps regulate that process in human cells. The work connects a conserved control protein to basic cell growth, with relevance for understanding diseases where growth control fails.
plos-pone-0000234:
Seiya Tsujiuchi, Elena Sivan-Loukianova, Daniel F. Eberl, and colleagues published this hearing study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honey bees communicate with waggle dance sounds, vibrations made by dancing bees that tell hive mates where food is. The authors examine how the bee auditory system handles these sounds. They focus on dynamic range compression, the squeezing of loud and quiet into a range the ear can manage.

Bees must hear faint dance sounds amid a noisy hive. Compression helps an ear stay sensitive without being overwhelmed. The paper details how the bee's auditory system achieves it. That adds to the science of hearing in insects and to the study of the waggle dance itself.
plos-pone-0000334:
Jonathan H. Fox, Jibrin A. Kama, Gregory Lieberman, and colleagues published this Huntington's disease paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Copper ions interact with the huntingtin protein whose mutant form causes the disease. The authors study the mechanisms by which copper drives the progression of Huntington's disease.

Metals like copper can push toxic proteins to clump or damage cells. Tracing copper's role suggests ways to slow the disease by managing metal chemistry in the brain. The paper joins a line of research treating Huntington's partly as a problem of protein-metal interaction.
plos-pone-0000434:
Kunihiko Kaneko modeled how gene networks stay steady in a noisy world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Cells must keep their gene expression stable even though molecules collide at random and mutations keep arising. Kaneko studied the evolution of robustness to both noise and mutation in the dynamics of gene expression.

Robustness is itself a trait that evolution can build. Simulations of this kind test whether networks that survive random jolts also, as a side effect, survive genetic change, and vice versa. That question sits at the heart of evolutionary theory. It may explain why living systems are stable day to day. It may also explain how they still evolve over generations.
plos-pone-0000534:
Ping-Ping Chen and colleagues measured three related genes across lung cancer patients, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes, Cyr61, CTGF, and WISP-1, belong to one family involved in growth and tissue repair. Their expression correlated with clinical features of lung cancer, the measurable traits of each patient's disease.

A gene whose activity tracks stage or outcome can serve as a biomarker, helping doctors judge how a tumor will behave. Three family members measured together give a stronger signal than any one alone. Studies like this screen the genome's output for clinically useful patterns in the world's deadliest cancer.
plos-pone-0000634:
Michael A. Brockhurst asked whether population bottlenecks keep cooperation alive in bacterial biofilms, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. A bottleneck is a crash that leaves few survivors to restart a population. Theory assumes such crashes help social traits persist in microbes. Events like colonizing a new site, or a disturbance, can cause them.

A bottleneck raises relatedness among survivors, since offspring descend from a handful of cells. Relatives gain more from each other's cooperation, so cooperative traits can pay. Brockhurst's title gives his answer: bottlenecks do promote cooperation in biofilms, the layered communities bacteria build on surfaces. The result informs debates about how social life evolves in microbes.
plos-pone-0000734:
Jonatan Blais, Ciro Rico, Cock van Oosterhout and colleagues compared immune genes in cichlid fish from Africa's great lakes. The haplochromine cichlids of Lakes Malawi and Victoria are among the most important study systems in evolutionary biology, famous for rapid speciation. Identifying adaptive divergence between closely related species may reveal the processes that built that diversity.

The team focused on MHC genes, which present invader fragments to the immune system and vary hugely between individuals. Their title reports adaptive divergence in MHC between closely related species living in the same waters. Diverging immune genes in side-by-side species suggests parasites and disease help drive cichlid splitting.
plos-pone-0000834:
Leeanne McGurk, Harris Morrison, Liam P. Keegan and colleagues found a way to see inside an intact adult fruit fly, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The major hindrance is the dark exoskeleton: the fly's cuticle blocks imaging of internal organs. The team beat that obstacle. They describe a method to image the internal organs of adult Drosophila in three dimensions. It works by bleaching and clearing the tissue.

Drosophila is genetics' most powerful insect model, yet adult anatomy was largely read from dissections. Whole-body 3D imaging preserves the spatial relations dissection destroys. Screens for internal defects, in guts, brains, or reproductive organs, become feasible at a scale matching the fly's genetic tools.
plos-pone-0000934:
Ethan Decker, Andrew Kerkhoff and Melanie Moses charted how city sizes are spread across the globe, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cities draw in huge flows of energy and materials. Knowing whether a country has many mid sized cities or one giant one shapes how growth can be managed.

The authors look for the fundamental drivers behind those size patterns. Regular patterns across very different countries hint at shared rules of growth. Finding the rules would help planners predict where pressure will build next. It would also help weigh the costs that giant cities place on the wider environment. The study treats cities as a global system, not isolated cases.
plos-pone-0001034:
Edna Caceda and Tadeusz Kochel compared a modified culture method for catching arboviruses in patient samples, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Arboviruses spread by insects, and patient blood often carries too few virus particles to isolate easily. The pair tested a modified shell vial culture procedure against standard detection.

Their panel covered dengue, yellow fever, Saint Louis encephalitis, West Nile, Ilheus, group C viruses, Oropouche, Mayaro and Venezuelan equine encephalitis. A bench method that catches more of these viruses helps clinics in the Americas name infections that look alike. Naming matters, since these diseases differ in risk and in the response they demand.
plos-pone-0001134:
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an inherited disease that affects muscle and many other systems. Esther Llagostera and co-authors studied one of its common features, insulin resistance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The disease is caused by an expanded repeat in the DMPK gene, which codes for a protein kinase.

The team examined what DMPK itself does in glucose balance and in how muscle responds to insulin. Separating the kinase's normal job from the damage caused by the repeat helps explain why patients handle sugar poorly. The work points to where in this chain a treatment might intervene.
plos-pone-0001234:
Schizophrenia has a strong genetic component, and one suspect region is 22q11.2, a chromosome segment tied to susceptibility. Ruby Hsu and colleagues examined a candidate gene there, RTN4R, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The gene codes for the Nogo receptor 1, which regulates axon growth and limits regrowth after injury.

Using both human and mouse genetic approaches, the authors evaluate evidence for association between common variants in the gene and schizophrenia. A gene that controls wiring in the brain, sitting in a known risk region, is a strong functional and positional candidate. Their analysis weighs whether it truly contributes to the disease.
plos-pone-0001334:
The C/EBP family of transcription factors includes five genes, two of which are essential for ovarian granulosa cell function. A-Mei Huang and colleagues explored a third family member, Cebpd, in the mouse ovary, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cebpd is switched on by luteinizing hormone in theca and interstitial cells of the ovary.

By expression and functional analysis, the authors conclude that Cebpd, while induced by the hormone, is not essential for mouse ovary function. Genes can be hormone-responsive yet dispensable, because relatives compensate. Sorting essential from incidental family members is basic groundwork for reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0001434:
Guillaume Pézeron and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on embryo growth in zebrafish. A growth factor helper plays a key role in forming the germ layers of the embryo. Its loss causes a one eyed mutant form in fish. The team asked which other genes tune that helper's effect.

They found that lowering a gene called rasl11b eased the one eyed trait. In other words, the second gene acts as a brake on the same path. Pairs like this help map the web that guides early growth. They also show how one fault can be softened by a second change nearby.
plos-pone-0001534:
Ralf Engbert and Antje Nuthmann wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eye jumps during reading. As we read, our eyes jump to land each word near the center of view. Faults in that system spread landing spots wide, with overlap between words. That spread made it hard to tell which word a gaze was truly on.

The pair offer a self consistent way to gauge missed landings from the data itself. A sound gauge cleans up decades of reading data. It lets labs test models of eye control with less noise. Reading science gains a sharper tool for a core measure.
plos-pone-0001634:
Yasuhiro Takeuchi and co-authors studied how a virus gene mixes and matches its parts over time, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The gene is cap, from adeno-associated virus, a small virus often used as a carrier in gene therapy. When two versions of a virus infect the same cell, their genes can swap pieces, a process called recombination, which creates mosaic genes.

The authors looked for signs of such swaps across virus samples and asked what the mosaics mean for the virus. The full text gives the sequence comparisons, the swap points they found, and their view of how common this mixing is. The work matters for gene therapy because the cap gene builds the shell that decides which cells the carrier virus can enter.
plos-pone-0001734:
Nelson K. F. Chen, Jen San Wong, Irene H. C. Kee, and their co-authors corrected diabetes in a large animal model with modified liver cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gene and cell therapies face limits that block wide clinical use. Using diabetes as the test case, the team sought to get around those limits.

They took primary liver cells from the animals themselves, added a nonviral insulin expression vector by electrotransfer outside the body, and returned the cells. The treated cells corrected diabetes and prevented target organ injury, per the paper's title. The full text gives the model, the cell handling, and the glucose results. Avoiding viruses as carriers removes a major safety worry for gene therapy.
plos-pone-0001834:
Létitia Jean and co-authors used an enzyme as a model for amyloid formation in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clumping into amyloid fibrils is a crucial step in brain diseases such as Alzheimer's. How amyloid builds is set by the chain's own traits and specific side chain contacts, since fibrils from unlike proteins share a like shape.

Their cholinesterase model system probes which parts govern the birth of amyloid. The full text gives the fibril tests and the part contrasts. A tractable model enzyme lets labs test anti amyloid ideas quickly, before moving to the disease proteins.
plos-pone-0001934:
Clara Menendez and co-authors ran a trial on malaria care in pregnancy in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In Africa, pregnant women are urged to sleep under insecticide-treated nets and to take preventive doses of malaria drugs at clinic visits. Whether the two work safely together had not been tested.

The team ran a randomized, placebo-controlled trial with one thousand thirty pregnant women in Mozambique. All got nets through the antenatal clinic; some also got the preventive drug doses, and some got a placebo. The design checks whether the drug adds gain on top of nets without adding harm. Proof here guides care for millions of women.
plos-pone-0002034:
Kurt Reed and co-authors modeled where a dangerous fungus lives in Wisconsin, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Blastomycosis is a lung illness that can kill, caught by breathing in spores of the fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis from the environment. Where that fungus lives was poorly known, in part because its niches are hard to find by sampling.

The team used ecological niche modeling, which maps the conditions at known case sites and projects them across the state. A map of likely habitat guides doctors to suspect the illness sooner and guides field teams to the soils where the fungus hides.
plos-pone-0002134:
Ping Kei Chan and co-authors tested a boundary piece of DNA in the beta-globin gene region, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Beta-globin genes make part of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. A control region switches these genes on at the right times. One site in it, called 5'HS5, was thought to act as a border between active and quiet DNA.

The team removed that site and watched the shape of the gene region using a method that captures how DNA folds in the cell. The active hub of the locus still formed without it. The result narrows down which parts of the control region truly run the show.
plos-pone-0002234:
Jeongheon Yoon and co-authors followed two gene-silencing proteins through the making of eggs in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Germline stem cells in the fly ovary divide unevenly, keeping one stem cell and producing a cystoblast that goes on to form eggs. They are, in effect, immortal stem cells.

The team shows that two enzymes that tag histones, dSETDB1 and SU(VAR)3-9, act one after the other as these cells differentiate. Orderly tagging of the genome's packing helps switch gene sets as a stem cell becomes a gamete. The sequence adds detail to how stem cells hand their potential down one path only.
plos-pone-0002334:
Anuradha Ratnaparkhi, George Lawless, Felix Schweizer, and co-authors built a fruit fly model of an inherited form of ALS, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. ALS8 is a type of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis caused by a dominant mutation in the protein VAPB, which helps membranes meet inside cells. The gene is conserved across evolution, which makes the fly a fair test bed.

The team put the corresponding mutation into the fly version, dVAP33A, and examined the effects. Their results suggest the mutant protein acts through a dominant negative mechanism, poisoning the normal copy's work. A fly model lets researchers screen genes and drugs for this disease quickly and cheaply.
plos-pone-0002434:
A research team led by Edelweiss reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Evelina Edelweiss, Taras G. Balandin, Julia L. Ivanova, and others. Its subject is barnase as a New Therapeutic Agent Triggering Apoptosis in Human Cancer Cells. RNases are currently studied as non-mutagenic alternatives to the harmful DNA-damaging anticancer drugs commonly used in clinical practice.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002534:
Work from Martí and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Daniel Martí, Gustavo Deco, Maurizio Mattia, and others. Its subject is a Fluctuation-Driven Mechanism for Slow Decision Processes in Reverberant Networks. The spike activity of cells in some cortical areas has been found to be correlated with reaction times.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002634:
Luisa Cironi led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was IGF1 is a common target gene of ewing's sarcoma fusion proteins in mesenchymal progenitor cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Luisa Cironi, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The EWS-FLI-1 fusion protein is associated with 85–90% of Ewing's sarcoma family tumors (ESFT). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002734:
Claudia Wellbrock led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with oncogenic BRAF regulates melanoma proliferation through the lineage specific factor MITF. The catalog record names Claudia Wellbrock first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is an important regulator of cell-type specific functions in melanocytic cells. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002834:
Bekim Sadikovic led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was in vitro analysis of integrated global High-Resolution DNA methylation profiling with genomic imbalance and gene expression in osteosarcoma. Authorship is credited in the record to Bekim Sadikovic and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Genetic and epigenetic changes contribute to deregulation of gene expression and development of human cancer. The summary also notes a further point. Changes in DNA methylation are key epigenetic factors regulating gene expression and genomic stability. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002934:
Giselle Chamberlain, Karina Wright, Antal Rot and co-authors compared chemokine receptors on mouse and human stem cells in 2008. Mesenchymal stem cells are marrow stromal cells that can become bone, cartilage, and other tissues. They are rare in marrow but grow well in culture while keeping their range.

Chemokine receptors guide where such cells travel in the body. The PLOS ONE study found the mouse cells carry a restricted set of working receptors, and compared that set with human cells. The contrast warns against assuming mouse results will match patients in stem cell therapy trials.
plos-pone-0003034:
Thomas Burgold, Fabio Spreafico, Francesca De Santa and co-authors studied the histone demethylase Jmjd3 in 2008. Methyl marks at lysine 4 and 27 of histone H3 track with gene activity and repression. Those patterns are set during development and are thought to lock in lineage-specific gene programs.

Jmjd3 removes the repressive mark at lysine 27. The title reports it is required for neural commitment, the step where stem cells commit to becoming nerve tissue. Published in PLOS ONE, the enzyme is a gatekeeper for one major cell fate decision. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003134:
Lu-Ning Liu, Abdalmohsen T. Elmalk, Thijs J. Aartsma and colleagues study how red algae shed excess light energy in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants and algae that use sunlight have built many ways to avoid damage under bright light. Red algae and cyanobacteria use large antenna complexes called phycobilisomes to harvest light. Some cyanobacteria use an orange protein in this process as well.

Working at the single molecule level, the team describe light-induced energetic decoupling as a route for energy loss tied to phycobilisomes. Readers see protection from bright light at the scale of single complexes. The work adds detail to how algae keep photosynthesis safe.
plos-pone-0003234:
Antonina Y. Alexandrova, Katya Arnold, Sébastien Schaub and colleagues compare cell flow and adhesions in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The dynamic actin network at the leading edge of the cell is linked to the matrix outside through focal adhesions. At the same time, it undergoes retrograde flow. The flow has different dynamics in two distinct zones. Those zones are the lamellipodium, a fast flow zone, and the area behind it.

The title reports that formation of nascent adhesions triggers the transition from fast to slow flow. Readers see adhesion birth and actin flow as coupled events. Cell migration underlies wound healing and cancer spread, so its mechanics matter widely.
plos-pone-0003334:
Thomas R. Welch and Lisa W. Blystone study complement and kidney disease in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The role of circulating complement in host defence and immune disease is well established. Although a number of cells and tissues are capable of synthesizing complement components locally, the importance of such local synthesis in immune disease has been difficult to establish.

The authors report immune complex glomerulonephritis following bone marrow transplantation in C3 deficient mice. Readers see a test that separates blood complement from locally made complement. That distinction matters because blocking complement only in one place might treat disease with fewer risks.
plos-pone-0003434:
Nicholas Juleff and colleagues found a hiding place for a livestock virus in this 2008 paper. Foot-and-mouth disease virus spreads fast among farm animals. It is the top barrier to world trade in animals and meat. Two basic puzzles about it still block better control.

The virus was found lingering in the light zone of germinal centres. Those are training sites inside lymph nodes where immune cells mature. A refuge there could shield the virus from full clearance. Knowing the hiding place helps explain lasting infection in herds. Foot-and-mouth outbreaks close borders to livestock trade within days of first detection.
plos-pone-0003534:
Douglas B. Stairs and co-authors studied a lining change that precedes cancer in this 2008 paper. In Barrett's esophagus, the normal flat lining of the food pipe changes type. It becomes a simple columnar lining, more like the small intestine. That switch is a premalignant step toward cancer.

Two genes, Cdx1 and c-Myc, fostered the start of that change. Their activity helps drive the transdifferentiation program. Naming the initiators shows where the identity switch begins. Blocking that start might halt the march toward cancer. Acid reflux is the usual driver behind this lining change over years.
plos-pone-0003634:
Thomas Widmann, Urban Sester, Barbara C. Gärtner, and colleagues published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cytomegalovirus, or CMV, is the most common viral problem after stem cell transplants from donors. The team tracked the T cells that target CMV in patients after transplant.

Levels of these CMV-specific CD4 T cells rose and fell over time in each patient. Their levels tracked closely with how much virus was active in the blood. The pattern suggests that watching these cells could help doctors judge a patient's risk and time treatment against the virus.
plos-pone-0003734:
Yusuke T. Maeda, Junya Inose, Miki Y. Matsuo, and colleagues published this cell movement study in PLOS ONE in 2008. With no signal to follow, most moving cells still crawl by coordinating their own shape changes with their motion. How cells run that coordination on their own was little known.

The authors measured cell shape during spontaneous migration and found ordered patterns. A cell's deformation and its direction of travel stayed correlated in set ways. The study reveals an inner choreography behind the seemingly aimless crawl of cells left to themselves.
plos-pone-0003834:
Neelam Engineer, Keelin O'Donoghue, Ruwan C. Wimalasundera, and colleagues published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In monochorionic twin pregnancies, too much amniotic fluid, called polyhydramnios, can complicate care. A short cervix raises the risk of early birth. The team tested how the two problems relate.

In a controlled intervention study of forty women, they tracked cervical length as fluid volume was normalized. Their hypothesis was that shortening reflects the degree of excess fluid. The results clarify when extra fluid truly threatens preterm birth in these complicated twin pregnancies.
plos-pone-0003934:
Kleber S. Vieira, Cristina Arzabe, Malva I. M. Hernández, and co-authors measured body variation in a Brazilian toad in 2008. The toad Proceratophrys cristiceps lives only in South America. It inhabits the dry Caatinga region of northeastern Brazil. Little detailed measurement of its body form had been published.

Their PLOS ONE article examines how size and shape vary within one population. Such data show how much a species can differ across a harsh, dry home. The measures help separate this species from close relatives. They also give a base for tracking change as the Caatinga climate shifts.
plos-pone-0004034:
Xiangyang Xue, Jun Sun, Qingfeng Zhang, and co-authors found new microRNAs in a parasitic worm in 2008. Schistosomiasis japonica remains a major public health problem in China. Its worm, Schistosoma japonicum, has a complex life cycle. Genes switch on and off across its life stages.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies and describes novel microRNAs from the worm. MicroRNAs are small regulators that tune gene activity. Stage-specific regulators are promising targets for control. Cataloguing them is a first step toward drugs or vaccines. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004134:
Chihiro Kakiuchi and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Valproate is a standard drug for bipolar disorder and a first-line mood stabiliser, yet how it works in the brain is still unclear. One clue is that it changes gene activity. It also switches on proteins that help cells handle stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, a cell compartment where proteins are folded.

The team reports that valproate raises production of WFS1, a gene also known from a rare form of diabetes. They also show it changes how WFS1 interacts with GRP94, a protein tied to that same stress system. The findings offer one concrete path by which the drug may calm mood swings.
plos-pone-0004234:
Yujun Liang, Shicui Zhang, and Zhiping Wang published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most invertebrates fertilise their eggs externally, so their embryos develop in water full of microbes, many of them dangerous. How those embryos defend themselves was an open question.

Working with amphioxus, a small fish-like animal, the team studied the fluid inside its eggs. They found alternative complement activity there, a part of the innate immune system, and present evidence for a defence role of maternal complement components. In short, the mother loads the egg with weapons before it ever hatches.
plos-pone-0004334:
Ana Mingorance-Le Meur, Alma Mohebiany, and Timothy O'Connor published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The rat PC12 cell line is a traditional model for neurite outgrowth and growth cone behaviour, used because its cells grow neuron-like fibres. To clarify how far PC12 neurite terminals can be compared with real neuronal growth cones, the team analysed their morphology and protein distribution.

They describe two kinds of terminals: varicones and growth cones. Distinguishing them matters, because experiments using this classic cell line may be reading two different structures as one. PC12 cells come from a rat adrenal tumour, called a pheochromocytoma.
plos-pone-0004434:
Adult neural stem cells taken from the brain's smell center may carry a hidden risk, warn Patrizia Casalbore, Manuela Budoni, Lucia Ricci-Vitiani, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. These stem cells, found in the olfactory bulb, can copy themselves and make new nerve cells. Reports had said they can be grown for long periods without turning dangerous.

The team grew human stem cells from this region and watched the switches inside them. They report that the cells' power to form tumors goes together with two genes being switched on: TERT and NOTCH1. That link is a caution for any plan to use such cells in therapy. It also helps explain how quiet stem cells can cross the line into cancer.
plos-pone-0004534:
A stand-in for the amino acid proline disrupts the parasite that causes Chagas disease, report Anahi Magdaleno, Il-Young Ahn, Lisvane Silva Paes, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite is Trypanosoma cruzi. Proline plays several roles in its life: it feeds energy metabolism, helps the parasite change form, and helps it resist osmotic stress, the strain of shifting water balance.

The team tested a proline analogue called L-thiazolidine-4-carboxylic acid, shortened to T4C. A look-alike molecule can slip into the machinery that uses proline and jam it. Studying what T4C does to the parasite shows which proline jobs it cannot live without. Those jobs are candidate targets for new Chagas drugs, in a field where current treatments are old and harsh.
plos-pone-0004634:
A family of signaling brakes is switched on by the fusion protein that drives Ewing tumors, report Yoshitaka Miyagawa, Hajime Okita, Mitsuko Itagaki, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brakes are the Dickkopf family, regulators of Wnt and beta-catenin signaling. That signaling has a crucial role in development, and the Dickkopf family had recently been implicated in tumor formation.

Ewing family tumors are aggressive cancers of bone and soft tissue, mostly in the young. They are driven by fusion proteins such as EWS/ETS, made when two genes wrongly join. The team shows EWS/ETS regulates expression of the Dickkopf family in these tumor cells. The link may explain part of how the fusion drives growth, and offers markers for these rare tumors.
plos-pone-0004734:
Benjamin Uzan and colleagues traced how a growth factor drives pancreas duct cell growth and change, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor, called KGF, acts with high focus on surface lining cells. It helps keep lining growth and balance in many organs, the pancreas among them.

The team mapped the inner signals KGF triggers in duct cells of the pancreas. They asked which paths push cells to divide and which push them to mature. Clear maps may help heal pancreas injury one day. They also inform work on growth gone wrong in tumors. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004834:
Jérôme Rambert and colleagues showed that molecular blocking of CD23 supports its role in arthritis pathogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. CD23 is an activation antigen expressed by various hematopoietic and epithelial cells and detected in soluble forms in fluids. Initially known as the low affinity receptor for immunoglobulin E, CD23 displays various other physiological functions in immunity, allergy, and inflammatory joint disease studied.

Blocking CD23 altered disease relevant pathways in models. That supports causality, not mere association. CD23 becomes a candidate drug target. Arthritis affects millions with unmet needs. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004934:
Telomeres are protective caps on the ends of chromosomes. They shorten as cells divide. Organs that renew often, like skin, depend on telomere upkeep. Ignacio Flores and Maria Blasco studied mice born with short telomeres. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

Those mice stay small. Their skin stem cells lose function early. The results include hair loss, graying and slow wound healing. The study shows the protein p53 drives much of this decline. It does so by limiting stem cell activity. The work links the cell's ageing clock to ageing of the whole body.
plos-pone-0005034:
BRCA1 is famous for breast cancer risk. It also works with a helper protein called Cobra1. Cobra1 is part of a complex that pauses gene copying. Asma Amleh and colleagues tested its role in mouse embryos. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They removed the mouse Cobra1 gene.

Embryos without Cobra1 could not develop past the earliest stages. The helper is required for early embryogenesis. Biochemical studies had shown its role in pausing polymerase in dishes. The mouse work proves it matters in a living animal. The finding reveals a developmental job for the BRCA1 partner team. It also shows how transcription control shapes the first days of life.
plos-pone-0005134:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs progressively. It does not respond to current therapy and often kills. Yet patients decline at very different rates. Kathy Boon and colleagues compared their gene profiles in PLOS ONE in 2009. They contrasted relatively stable patients with progressive ones. The hypothesis was that molecular patterns separate the two.

The gene expression profiles did distinguish the groups. Molecular phenotypes mark whose disease will advance. Those signatures could predict a patient's course. They could also guide the timing of transplants and trials. A disease with no good treatment needs such foresight. The study gives clinicians a possible early warning system. It may also reveal what drives progression itself.
plos-pone-0005234:
Chronic granulomatous disease is an inherited immune failure. Faults in the NADPH oxidase complex stop white blood cells from making the burst of chemicals that kills germs. Van den Berg and colleagues gathered the European experience with this rare disease in PLOS ONE in 2009.

A Europe-wide picture can show patterns that no single clinic sees enough cases to spot. The report covers the gene faults, infections, and outcomes of patients across the continent. For families and doctors facing a rare disease, shared data of this kind directly improves care.
plos-pone-0005334:
Borderline personality disorder is a severe condition that clearly runs in families. Family and twin studies put the genetic share of its variance at roughly a third to just under half. Distel and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether that resemblance is genetic or cultural.

Families share homes and habits as well as genes, so resemblance alone cannot separate the two. Their analysis teases apart genetic transmission from cultural transmission of borderline features. The answer shapes how prevention and family support should be designed. If much of the link is learned at home, then help for young kin of patients may cut risk in the next group. A hope that pure gene views would not have raised at all.
plos-pone-0005434:
Yoshimi Kanie and colleagues studied sugar chains on a fly protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many proteins carry sugar chains that help them fold, stick, and send signals. Cells build those chains step by step without a fixed template, so the same protein can carry many forms.

The team used a method that weighs tiny bits of matter to read the sugar chains on chaoptin, a protein from the fruit fly eye. They looked at how the cell controls which forms get made. The work helps explain how cells keep sugar building in order despite having no template.
plos-pone-0005534:
Liisa Ukkola and co-authors linked musical talent to a gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Making, improvising, and arranging music are complex creative acts. Practising music is also a form of social contact, which may be why the trait has value in evolution.

The team tested whether forms of a gene called AVPR1A, known for roles in social behaviour, track with musical aptitude. They found a link between certain forms of the gene and test scores for hearing and structuring music. The work adds a biological thread to the study of musical talent.
plos-pone-0005634:
Sidney Omelon and co-authors studied how vertebrate skeletons harden in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Vertebrate bones and teeth are made of a calcium phosphate mineral laid into a protein frame. Many simpler animals build shells from other minerals instead.

The team examined compounds called polyphosphates for a role in controlling where the mineral forms. Their evidence places these compounds in the process that guides hardening. Control over mineral placement is what lets skeletons grow in precise shapes rather than as shapeless crusts. How mineral starts, rather than how much forms, may be the key step this work brings into view.
plos-pone-0005734:
George Dyer and co-authors traced how engineered genes move through Mexico's maize seed trade in 2009. Mexico is the birthplace of maize, so stray engineered traits there carry weight. Most models of gene flow focus on pollen, but seed moves genes too, in farmers' hands.

The team used antibody tests to screen seeds moving through local systems. They charted where engineered traits show up and how seed sharing spreads them. Their work says seed networks must be part of any plan to guard native maize. It gives Mexico hard data for a charged debate.
plos-pone-0005834:
Sandra Macedo-Ribeiro and co-authors followed a disease protein as it moves in and out of the cell nucleus in 2009. Ataxin-3, when expanded by a repeated gene segment, causes Machado-Joseph disease, an inherited movement disorder. The protein tends to clump, often inside the nucleus.

The team characterized how ataxin-3 shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm. Where it gathers may decide how toxic it becomes. That movement is a possible drug lever: keep the protein out of the nucleus and harm may fall. The study gives the shuttling signals and rates needed to test that idea.
plos-pone-0005934:
People who had the BCG shot as children may need a boost against tuberculosis later. Kathryn Whelan, Ansar Pathan, Clare Sander and colleagues tested one option in a 2009 PLOS ONE trial. Healthy adults who had BCG before got a fresh BCG dose in the skin, and the team checked safety and immune response.

The results were then set beside an earlier trial that boosted the same kind of volunteers with MVA85A, a newer TB vaccine. A head-to-head look of this kind helps planners judge whether the old vaccine still earns its place. The study gives booster policy a firmer base than guesswork about how long BCG lasts.
plos-pone-0006034:
Genes that set blood pressure have been hard to pin down. Siim Sõber, Elin Org, Katrin Kepp and colleagues took a focused approach in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper targets one hundred sixty candidate genes for blood pressure control, using genotyping array data from a cohort of more than sixteen hundred people in southern Germany.

Genome-wide scans had lately passed the old candidate genes by, so a direct test was overdue. Checking known suspects with wide data settles which of them still deserve trust. The study serves hypertension genetics at a turning point, when the field was learning to weigh careful candidate work against the flood of whole-genome results.
plos-pone-0006134:
Pregnancy reshapes a woman's arteries, and doctors lacked normal ranges to judge that change. Asma Khalil, Eric Jauniaux, Derek Cooper and colleagues measured the change across a full pregnancy in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper is a prospective longitudinal study of pulse wave analysis, a method that reads arterial stiffness and is prized in hypertension care outside pregnancy.

Stiffness is already known to rise once pre-eclampsia is established, but the normal course was unmapped. A baseline lets clinicians spot the turn toward disease rather than the disease itself. The study follows the same women over time, which makes its ranges a true record of change, not a guess stitched from strangers.
plos-pone-0006234:
Dying cells dismantle their nucleus in an orderly set of steps. Lisa Trisciuoglio and Marco Bianchi examined those steps in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on apoptosis, the cell's programmed death. The steps include DNA chopped into a ladder pattern, breakdown of the nuclear shell, and marks on packaging proteins.

Several of the events depend on the executioner enzyme caspase-3 being switched on. Yet they do not form one single common pathway, the authors show. Shared triggers can still branch into separate routes. That distinction shapes how scientists interpret death signals and how drugs might steer them.
plos-pone-0006334:
A tiny peptide made in mitochondria may link brain protection to whole-body insulin action. Radhika Muzumdar and colleagues studied humanin in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Declining insulin action is a feature of ageing and feeds type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease; humanin was known to protect neurons against Alzheimer's-related harm.

Humanin acts as a central regulator of peripheral insulin action, the title reports. A brain signal adjusting body-wide insulin sensitivity is a new lever. It connects two age-related diseases through one small molecule. The work suggests shared treatments might be possible.
plos-pone-0006434:
Iris Eke and colleagues tested a drug against head and neck cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells that resist radiation and drug treatment limit patient survival, so new targets are needed. One candidate target is integrin-linked kinase, a protein many see as druggable. The team studied a small molecule blocker of it called QLT0267.

Their title reports that QLT0267 makes squamous cell carcinoma cells of the head and neck more sensitive to radiation. A drug that primes tumor cells could let radiation work harder at the same dose. The study builds on the group's earlier findings. It points toward combined treatments for hard-to-treat cancers.
plos-pone-0006534:
Nalini Vudattu and co-authors profiled immune cells in autoimmune disease for PLOS ONE in 2009. High content immune profiling in peripheral blood may reflect immune aberrations associated with inflammation in multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases. The team counted IL-7 receptor molecules on a specific T cell subset. They report increased numbers of these receptors on CD4 positive, CD25 negative, CD107a positive T cells in patients.

More receptors could make those cells respond more strongly to IL-7 signals. A blood marker like this might track disease activity. It also points to IL-7 pathways as possible treatment targets. The study shows the value of detailed cell-by-cell profiling.
plos-pone-0006634:
Beatriz Santamaría and co-authors built a nano-sized inhibitor to protect tissue lining cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inflammation may lead to tissue injury. The team studied modulation of inflammatory milieu-induced tissue injury, as exemplified by the mesothelium, the lining of body cavities. Peritoneal dialysis is one setting where this lining suffers.

Their nanoconjugate carries an Apaf-1 inhibitor, blocking a step in programmed cell death. The title reports it protects mesothelial cells from cytokine-induced injury. Targeted nano-delivery can concentrate protection where it is needed. The approach may help dialysis patients keep their membrane working longer.
plos-pone-0006734:
Takahiko Ishikawa and colleagues studied how cholera bacteria coordinate a secretion system in PLOS ONE in 2009. Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium behind cholera. It carries a type six secretion system, a molecular syringe. One core part of that system is the protein Hcp. The bacterium holds two copies of the hcp gene.

The authors examined how quorum sensing regulates both hcp copies. Quorum sensing lets bacteria act together once enough cells gather. They worked in O1 strains, the group behind most epidemics. Coordinated control links cell density to secretion weapon use. Understanding that link may reveal ways to weaken cholera bacteria during infection.
plos-pone-0006834:
Philippe C. Morand and his team watched how a meningitis germ steers the cells it lands on in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ is Neisseria meningitidis, and it lives just in man. It can sit in the throat with no harm, then turn deadly with no warning. To invade, it must cross the walls of the throat or of blood tubes. Fine hairs on the germ, called type IV pili, do much of that work.

Two parts of those hairs, PilC1 and PilC2, steered host cells in unlike ways. The team split what each part does to cell motion. Fine control like that may help the germ spread or pry walls open. The work adds fine print to how this feared illness starts.
plos-pone-0006934:
Toshie Sakuma, Akira Sakurai, and Jiro Yasuda studied an antiviral protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is tetherin, also known as BST2 or CD317. It had recently been reported to inhibit a wide range of viruses. How it did so was still unknown. Both ends of the molecule attach to the cell membrane, and it can pair with itself.

The team tested whether that pairing, called dimerization, is required for its antiviral effect. They used the Lassa and Marburg viruses as test cases. Their results showed the pairing is not essential. That narrows the search for how tetherin blocks dangerous viruses.
plos-pone-0007034:
Guojiang Chen, Gencheng Han, Jiannan Feng, and colleagues grew regulatory T cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Therapies based on these cells are a hopeful route against autoimmune diabetes. Success may depend on which antigen pieces stimulate the cells. The team used pieces derived from glutamic acid decarboxylase, a target of the disease.

They found that epitopes with specific domains expand CD4 and CD25 regulatory T cells. Growing the right regulators outside the body is a step toward cell therapy. Such cells could calm the immune attack on the pancreas without shutting down immunity as a whole.
plos-pone-0007134:
Jose Morales-Corraliza, Matthew Mazzella, Jason Berger, and colleagues measured protein turnover in mouse brains in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease centers on two proteins, tau and the amyloid precursor protein APP. The team measured how fast these proteins and their products turn over in living brains. They used cycloheximide to block new protein synthesis, then watched levels fall.

They compared normal mice with Tg2576 mice, which deposit amyloid. A secreted APP fragment, sAPP, proved more stable in the depositing mice. Stability differences may help explain why deposits form. They also hint at treatment points in the amyloid pathway.
plos-pone-0007234:
Elena Tassi, Marco Braga, Renato Longhi, and colleagues studied immune responses in pancreatic cancer patients in 2009. Pancreatic cancer is aggressive and has a poor prognosis. Its tumors sit in dense fibrotic tissue that helps the cancer progress quickly and resist treatment in many patients.

The team had earlier found a selective Th2 skew in these patients' immune responses. Th2 cells are one class of helper T cells. The authors test whether the signals IL-12 and IL-27 can shift that polarization. They study T cells specific to a tumor antigen from patients.
plos-pone-0007334:
Geoffrey W. Stone, Suzanne Barzee, Victoria Snarsky, and colleagues tested a nanoparticle cancer vaccine against melanoma in 2009. Stimulating CD40 or Toll-like receptors can power tumor immunotherapy. Combining both stimulations can be synergistic, producing stronger dendritic cell and killer T cell responses against tumors in animal models.

The authors deliver DNA encoding a multimeric soluble CD40 ligand by nanoparticles. They combine it with Toll-like receptor agonists. They test the treatment on established B16F10 melanoma tumors in mice. Their PLOS ONE approach aims to turn tumor immune stimulation into a practical delivered therapy.
plos-pone-0007434:
Matthew Feldhammer, Stéphanie Durand, and Alexey Pshezhetsky published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Sanfilippo syndrome type C, a severe inherited disorder. Children with the condition lose mental abilities as they grow. The cause is a faulty lysosomal enzyme called HGSNAT, which healthy cells need to break down complex sugars. The team asked why the enzyme fails.

They found that the problem begins with the protein's shape. Mutant HGSNAT folds incorrectly, and the cell's quality control system destroys it before it can do its job. So the enzyme is not merely weak; it never reaches working form. That reframing matters for treatment. Drugs that help the protein fold correctly might rescue it, opening a route that replacement strategies cannot offer.
plos-pone-0007534:
Stéphanie Le Hellard and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the genetics of memory and thinking ability. Both traits run in families and vary widely between people. A brain growth factor, BDNF, plays a known role in forming memories. The team looked at genes switched on by BDNF. One, called DCLK1, became their focus for variant testing in human subjects.

Variants in DCLK1 were associated with differences in memory and general cognitive ability. People carrying certain versions scored differently on the tests. That connects a molecular growth signal to everyday mental differences. The gene's name reflects its kinship to proteins that guide brain development. Finding its fingerprints on adult cognition strengthens the BDNF pathway's importance. It also adds a piece to the puzzle of why minds differ.
plos-pone-0007634:
Jeremiah Roeth and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how embryonic tissue holds together while it changes shape. Cells in the fruit fly's outer layer must keep stable adhesion even as they move and reshape. One way to manage that is regulated trafficking: shipping junction proteins where they are needed. The team explored the trafficking protein Rab11 in the developing ectoderm. They tracked its care of the adhesion system.

Rab11 helps maintain the Crumbs protein at the cell's top surface and keeps adherens junctions intact. Without that delivery service, the tissue's seams weaken. Building an embryo needs seams that can flex without tearing. Rab11 supplies the recycling that makes such seams possible. The finding reveals the logistics behind stable-yet-plastic tissue. Development is as much shipping as it is signaling.
plos-pone-0007734:
Nicolae Adrian Leu and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines an enzyme called arginyltransferase, which tags proteins with an extra building block. The tagging, done by the gene Ate1, is essential for heart and blood vessel development. It also helps cells move and keep their inner scaffolding.

The team deleted Ate1 in the mouse germ line, using a switch active in reproductive tissue. The loss caused defects in sperm and egg formation. Embryos also died early. The study shows this single protein tag matters from the first steps of life.
plos-pone-0007834:
Brian Russ and Yale Cohen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how much rhesus monkeys value hearing the calls of their own kind. Adaptive behavior blends current and past information into choices. Calls from fellow monkeys are one important signal type.

The authors gave monkeys a free-choice task. Monkeys could pay a small cost, or pass up a reward, to hear vocalizations. Their choices revealed the value they place on social sounds. Measuring that value in the lab is tricky but revealing. It shows how the brain prices social information when it decides what to do.
plos-pone-0007934:
Andrew Pogozelski and colleagues pinned down a switch for muscle fuel use in PLOS ONE in 2009. The switch is an enzyme called p38 gamma, part of a family that relays signals in cells. Training for endurance reshapes muscle, and the team asked how this enzyme helps.

In mice, the enzyme proved central to how skeletal muscle adapts its fuel burn. Without its normal action, the usual gains from an active life did not fully take shape. Naming this switch helps explain, at the level of molecules, why steady training makes muscle work better and may guard against metabolic disease.
plos-pone-0008034:
Sotaro Shimada asked what happens in the brain of a fan watching baseball, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Watching others act wakes the viewer's own movement areas, a system tied to grasping what others feel and intend. A game adds stakes: each play helps or hurts one side.

Brain measures shifted with how the play turned out for the player being watched. Movement areas did not merely mirror the action; they weighed its outcome. The result helps explain the pull of sport watching, where the body seems to play along from the stands.
plos-pone-0008134:
Sulagna Das and colleagues found that a brain virus can wake immune skills in brain stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neural stem and progenitor cells are prized for transplant work partly because they barely stir the immune system. In inflamed tissue, that quiet manner can change.

After Japanese encephalitis virus infection, the cells began showing the tags and helper molecules of immune-active cells. A graft placed in an infected or inflamed brain may thus behave unlike the same graft in a calm brain. Transplant planners need that warning when picking where and when to place cells.
plos-pone-0008234:
Tarik Attout and colleagues studied the human onchocerca nodule in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Onchocerciasis is caused by the parasitic worm Onchocerca volvulus. It leads to severe skin disease and blindness. The disease carries heavy social and economic costs in affected regions. Its damage is thought to follow long-standing infection in the body.

The team examined lymphatic vessels and Lyve-1 positive macrophages within nodules. Nodules are the lumps where adult worms live under the skin. Their findings show how local vessels and immune cells shape the nodule. That adds to knowledge of how river blindness develops.
plos-pone-0008334:
Xiao-Feng Li and colleagues studied reproductive signals in rats in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Kisspeptin and its receptor GPR54 are essential for activating the reproductive hormone axis. In rats, kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus help drive hormone secretion. Another group sits in a nearby hypothalamic region. The arcuate group was suspected to control pulse timing.

The team showed kisspeptin signalling there regulates the GnRH pulse generator frequency. GnRH pulses drive the release of reproductive hormones. Setting their rhythm is central to fertility. The study pins down a control point in that system.
plos-pone-0008434:
Jedidah Mwacharo and co-authors report a 2009 PLOS ONE study of Kenyan children given a trial malaria shot. T cells play a key role in control of malaria. That holds after natural infection and after a shot. But T cell responses vary a lot from child to child. Both the type of response and its balance seem to matter.

The team use a test called quantitative PCR to measure cell responses. They check how strong the responses are and what kinds appear. The method lets them judge the shot in fine detail. Such checks help show if a trial shot works as hoped.
plos-pone-0008534:
Katherine Clark-Knowles and co-authors engineer ovarian tumors in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Epithelial ovarian cancer is thought to arise partly from the ovarian surface. The molecular events behind that transformation are poorly understood. Inherited mutations in BRCA1 greatly raise ovarian cancer risk. The team inactivate three tumor suppressors together in mouse ovaries. Those genes are Brca1, p53, and Rb.

Combined inactivation leads to development of leiomyosarcomas in the ovaries. Leiomyosarcomas are cancers of smooth muscle tissue. The result was unexpected for a model aimed at epithelial cancer. It reveals how suppressor loss can divert tumor type in the ovary.
plos-pone-0008634:
Vikrant Sahasrabuddhe and co-authors measure cervical precancer in HIV-infected women in India in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, or CIN, is a precancerous change in the cervix. Prior prevalence estimates in this group rested on cytology, or Pap tests. Cytology may have underestimated the true disease burden. The team use colposcopy and histopathology to confirm CIN directly. They also evaluate risk factors in their cohort.

They establish firmer prevalence estimates for confirmed CIN in those women. Certain factors predict which women carry precancerous lesions. HIV care in India should include cervical screening with confirmatory testing. Early detection prevents progression to invasive cervical cancer.
plos-pone-0008734:
Giorgio Fedele, Fabiana Spensieri, Raffaella Palazzo, and colleagues studied how whooping cough steers immunity. Their article appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ Bordetella pertussis harms airways with several weapons. One weapon is a toxin that floods cells with a messenger chemical. Dendritic cells, which brief T cells, are key targets of that steering.

Exposed human dendritic cells pushed T cells toward Th1 and Th17 modes. Those modes favor germ-killing and inflammation. A signaling route inside the cells carried part of the effect. Knowing how the germ biases defense helps improve whooping cough vaccines.
plos-pone-0008834:
Mahesh Gokara, Babu Sudhamalla, Damu Amooru, and colleagues measured how a plant flavone grips the blood's main carrier protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human serum albumin hauls many compounds through the blood. Trimethoxy flavone comes from a medicinal plant used against diabetes. How tightly it binds albumin affects how long it stays active. Binding also decides how much free compound reaches tissues.

Spectroscopic tests located the flavone's grip on the protein. They measured the strength and style of the bond. Such data predict how the compound would travel in patients. Albumin binding is a standard early check in drug development.
plos-pone-0008934:
Ralph Pethica and co-authors built TreeVector, a web tool for drawing family trees of species, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Evolutionary trees show how species relate, but big ones are hard to read. Older software drew them as fixed pictures that could not be explored. Growing DNA databases were making the trees far larger.

TreeVector draws trees inside a web browser and lets users zoom and pan. It can handle large trees without special software on the user's computer. Because it runs online, researchers can share a living, clickable tree instead of a flat image. The tool suits both research teams and students learning how evolution branches.
plos-pone-0009034:
Marcus Drotz, Tomas Brodin, and Anders Nilsson sorted out a puzzling pattern on diving beetle wing cases, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Agabus bipustulatus is one of Europe's most common diving beetles. Its wing cases carry a net-like surface pattern, called reticulation. The pattern's depth varies a lot between places and altitudes.
