The team tested whether the pattern forms arose once or many times. Evidence pointed to multiple separate origins within the species complex. Similar living conditions likely sculpted similar patterns again and again. The case warns taxonomists that look-alike traits may not mark close kinship.
plos-pone-0009134:
Mika Gustafsson and Michael Hörnquist described the method that won a gene prediction contest, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predicting gene activity helps reveal which genes work together. It also forecasts how drugs will ripple through a cell. The DREAM3 challenge scored rival methods on hidden data.

Their approach, soft integration with the elastic net, took best performance. It blended several data sources gently instead of trusting one fully. The elastic net kept the model lean by shrinking weak links. Contest wins like this set the practical standard for systems biology.
plos-pone-0009234:
Diane Latawiec and co-authors published this Parkinson's study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A protein called alpha-synuclein clumps inside brain cells in Parkinson's disease. The brain chemical dopamine may influence that clumping. Dopamine and its breakdown products can bind the protein loosely and slow its clumping in test tubes.

Building on that effect, the team tested dopamine-like compounds as clumping blockers. They measured how each analog changed the way alpha-synuclein gathered into aggregates. Compounds that keep the protein apart could, in principle, slow the disease process. The study maps which chemical features help, giving drug designers a starting point.
plos-pone-0009334:
Jorge Tavel published this HIV trial report in PLOS ONE in 2010. Interleukin-2 is a signal that tells immune cells to multiply. Doctors hoped bursts of it could rebuild CD4 counts in people with early HIV. The STALWART study tested that hope head-on.

Participants not on steady antiretroviral therapy received intermittent IL-2, with or without drug therapy around each cycle. The comparison group received no therapy. The question was whether IL-2 raised CD4 counts enough to matter. Trials like this shaped whether IL-2 earned a place in HIV care beyond the standard drugs.
plos-pone-0009434:
Ingeborg Brouwer, Anne Wanders, and Martijn Katan reviewed human studies on trans fats in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trans fats come from two sources. Factories make some when they harden plant oils. Cows and sheep make others in their stomachs, so they occur in meat and milk. Both types had been linked to heart risk.

The review pooled results from many trials to compare the two sources side by side. It looked at their effects on good and bad cholesterol in the blood. The findings help sort out whether farm made trans fats act the same as factory made ones. That matters for food rules and for advice on what to eat.
plos-pone-0009534:
Allison Leidner, Nick Haddad, and Thomas Lovejoy asked what forest cutting does to butterflies over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breaking a forest into fragments is a main cause of species loss. Species react in opposite ways: some gain, some lose. Those mixed reactions could make counts swing more from year to year. The team tracked butterfly communities in tropical forest fragments.

They tested whether groups in fragments varied more over the long term than groups in whole forest. Swings in numbers matter because deep dips raise the odds of local extinction. The study adds a time dimension to fragmentation research. It asks not just how many species remain, but how steady their hold is.
plos-pone-0009634:
Jin Hee Hong and co-authors reported a measurement pitfall in brain clock research in PLOS ONE in 2010. The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the brain's master clock. Its neurons fire in daily rhythms, and calcium inside them rises and falls too. Researchers read that calcium with dyes built on a chemical called BAPTA. The team found that those dyes can themselves provoke sharp calcium spikes in the clock neurons.

A tool that changes what it measures is a serious concern. Spikes once read as natural clock behavior may in part be dye artifacts. The finding does not undo the field, but it demands care. Future work must separate the clock's true signals from the probe's side effects.
plos-pone-0009834:
Muscles burn long-chain fatty acids for energy, and the burn leaves chemical traces. Erin Seifert and colleagues linked the burn rate to those traces in muscle mitochondria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Mitochondria are the cell's power stations, where fuel becomes usable energy. Metabolites are the small molecules left by chemical reactions in cells. Each combustion rate came with a unique metabolite profile, a fingerprint of small molecules. Profiles like these can reveal how hard mitochondria are working. They may also help track muscle metabolism in health and disease.
plos-pone-0009934:
Tamoxifen is a breast cancer drug best known for blocking estrogen signals. Rongmin Zhao and colleagues found a second action for it on a protein-folding machine. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug has been in use for decades.

The machine is Hsp90, a molecular chaperone that helps other proteins fold correctly. Tamoxifen enhanced the chaperone's ATPase activity, the energy-spending step of its cycle. Many cancer proteins depend on Hsp90 to stay working. A familiar drug with a hidden action could inspire new uses. Chaperones are the cell's folding helpers.
plos-pone-0010034:
The authors were Laure Diancourt, Virginie Passet, Alexandr Nemec, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped the family tree of Acinetobacter baumannii. Drug-resistant forms of this hospital germ cause outbreaks worldwide. Yet little was known about its overall diversity and how outbreak strains spread between places.

The team found that today's resistant clones grew out of an older, drug-sensitive pool. In other words, resistance spread by expanding a few successful lines. Tracking those lines can help hospitals spot outbreaks early and understand how resistance travels. That family history is the core evidence in the paper.
plos-pone-0010134:
Robert Lim, Lester Kobzik, and Morten Dahl combined past studies on asthma inheritance in 2010. Many studies found that a mother's asthma raises a child's asthma risk more than a father's does. A few studies, though, found the opposite pattern. Their PLOS ONE meta-analysis pooled the evidence to judge which claim holds and by how much.

Meta-analysis weighs many studies together, smoothing out the noise of single samples. Sorting out parent-of-origin effects matters for counseling families about asthma risk. It may also hint at biology, such as effects during pregnancy, that shape a child's airways.
plos-pone-0010234:
The authors were Zhiqian Tong, Wenhong Luo, Yanqing Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study probed why cancers in bone hurt so much. Bone cancer pain is severe and hard to treat, and its molecular causes were under study. Blood and urine formaldehyde runs high in many cancer patients. The cancers involved, including breast and prostate tumors, often spread to bone.

The team found that formaldehyde from tumor tissue and the acidic tumor setting act together. In synergy, they induce bone cancer pain in their model. That pairing points to new targets for easing one of cancer's worst symptoms.
plos-pone-0010334:
Pontus Skoglund and Jacob Höglund compared two willow grouse populations in a 2010 PLOS ONE genetics study. Birds in Scotland and birds in Scandinavia wear different winter feathers. Both males and females show the contrast clearly. Seasonal color change is well known, but population-level differences like this are rare in birds. The gene basis behind the difference was mostly unknown.

The authors read DNA in candidate genes, ones already suspected in feather color. They looked for sequence differences that matched the two winter looks. Such work can show whether a visible trait traces to a few genes or many. It also links field biology, what birds look like in snow, to changes at the level of code. Evolution here can be checked base by base.
plos-pone-0010434:
Maciej Boni and colleagues set out rules for spotting gene swapping in flu viruses. They published the guidelines in PLOS ONE in 2010. Influenza changes fast, mostly by small copying errors. It can also change by reassortment, trading whole gene segments. A rarer route, recombination within a segment, is often claimed but hard to prove. False claims can mislead outbreak tracking.

Their guidelines tell researchers what proof a recombination claim needs. Clear rules help journals and labs separate real events from analysis errors. Flu surveillance feeds vaccine choices each year, so accuracy has public stakes. A shared standard makes reports from different countries comparable. This methods paper aims to clean up a noisy corner of flu science.
plos-pone-0010534:
Mark Handley and colleagues studied a faulty calcium sensor protein found in a person with autism in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, NCS-1, senses calcium inside neurons and adjusts their development and signaling. It acts through several partner proteins. A changed version turned up in a case of autistic spectrum disorder. The team compared the mutant's structure and function with the normal protein.

The mutant showed clear structural and functional deficits in tests. A single calcium sensor's failure rippling into brain development is a plausible disease path. Such case-based finds rarely prove cause alone, but they open precise hypotheses. Autism genetics needs these mechanistic footholds. This study supplies one, tied to a named protein and patient.
plos-pone-0010634:
Sherilyn Goldstone and colleagues studied how chromosomes move during cell division in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fission yeast pulls its chromosomes to opposite ends along tracks called microtubules. A protein named Tip1 rides to the growing ends of those tracks.

When Tip1 was missing or faulty, chromosomes moved toward the poles unevenly. Some lagged or stalled before reaching their end. The protein seems to keep the pulling machinery attached and steady. Faulty chromosome movement causes lost or extra chromosomes in other organisms, so this basic yeast work speaks to cancer and birth defects too.
plos-pone-0010734:
Bryndís Ragnarsdóttir and colleagues studied gene variants that may soften severe urinary infections, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The sensor TLR4 gives the body early warning of many bacteria. Faults in the sensor itself are rare, since it is so vital. The team looked instead at the promoter, the dimmer switch that sets how much sensor gets made.

Common promoter variants changed how strongly TLR4 was expressed. Carriers of some variants were less prone to severe urinary tract infection. A quieter alarm can paradoxically protect, by limiting tissue damage from the response itself. The finding shows protection can come from tuning a response, not just strengthening it.
plos-pone-0010834:
Silke Langenheder, Mark Bulling, Martin Solan and co-authors reported this ecology experiment in PLOS ONE in 2010. Scientists worry that losing species weakens how ecosystems work, but the setting may change that effect. The team asked whether a richer, more complex environment strengthens the link between bacterial diversity and ecosystem function.

They built communities from six bacterial species in every possible mix, and fed them different numbers of food substrates to vary environmental complexity. Richer settings gave diverse communities more room to divide resources and help each other, shaping how the diversity effect played out over time. Langenheder and colleagues show that context matters: the payoff from biodiversity is not fixed. That lesson guides how lab results on species loss should be read for the real, messy natural world.
plos-pone-0010934:
Giordano Mancini, Ilda D'Annessa, Andrea Coletta and co-authors published this cancer drug simulation in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human topoisomerase I loosens DNA coils so the cell can copy and read its genes. The camptothecin drug family, including topotecan used against lung and ovarian cancers, works by trapping this enzyme mid-cut on the DNA.

The team ran long computer simulations of the enzyme bound to DNA, with and without topotecan attached, and compared how each complex moved. The drug narrowed the range of shapes the complex could adopt, freezing it in its trapped state. When a copying fork later crashes into that stalled complex, the DNA breaks lethally for the cancer cell. Mancini and colleagues show, motion by motion, how a successful drug turns an essential enzyme into a roadblock.
plos-pone-0011034:
Camille Lepoittevin, Jean-Marc Frigerio, Pauline Garnier-Géré and co-authors published this tree genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breeders want DNA markers called SNPs to map traits in maritime pine, a conifer with a huge genome. Markers can come from two routes. One reads genes directly. The other mines expressed gene collections by computer. The authors compared which route yields markers that actually work.

They built a genotyping array holding several hundred SNPs from both sources and scored how many produced usable results. About two-thirds of the assays succeeded overall, and the comparison revealed systematic quality differences between the sources. Lepoittevin and colleagues give forest geneticists practical guidance for a non-model species: where marker candidates come from predicts how many will survive contact with a real genotyping platform.
plos-pone-0011134:
Paige, Osugi, Afanasiev and colleagues grew stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human embryonic stem cells can become heart cells, but only if the right signals arrive. The team asked whether a signal made by the cells themselves, from the Wnt family, was truly needed for that step.

They showed heart formation failed without that internal signal and its partner protein in the cell. That makes the pathway a required checkpoint in early heart growth. Labs growing heart tissue for research or repair must respect that timing. Getting the signal right early may improve efforts to make working heart cells in a dish.
plos-pone-0011234:
Agnarsson, Kuntner and Blackledge described record breaking silk in PLOS ONE in 2010. A giant river orb spider spins webs across streams in Madagascar. In this prospecting study, the team characterized the silk of that spider and measured its strength and stretch.

The silk proved to be among the toughest biological materials known. It absorbs more energy before breaking than man made fibers like Kevlar. Such a fiber could inspire new materials for medicine and engineering. The study also rewards looking to remote species for solutions that industry has not matched.
plos-pone-0011334:
Kyong-Su Park and colleagues investigated in 2010 how a common gut germ can trigger a body-wide crisis. Sepsis, a severe reaction to infection, kills many people each year, and germs with an outer coat are a frequent cause. The team focused on tiny bubbles that Escherichia coli sheds from its outer surface as it grows.

They showed that these shed bubbles alone can set off the full pattern of harmful inflammation seen in sepsis. The bubbles carry germ material deep into the body, where immune cells react as if a major infection were present. Naming the bubbles as a direct trigger sharpens the search for treatments. Blocking the bubbles, or the alarm they raise, could one day help doctors calm sepsis before it damages organs.
plos-pone-0011434:
Lyle McKinnon and co-authors studied in 2010 which starting conditions predict immune recovery in Kenyan women beginning HIV treatment. Antiretroviral therapy rebuilds the infection-fighting CD4 cells that HIV destroys, but recovery varies widely from patient to patient. Clinics with limited staff need to know who will recover well and who needs closer watching.

The team related recovery after treatment began to the women's starting state, including viral load, CD4 count, and stage of disease. Those baselines carried real information about the road ahead. With that knowledge, clinics can set honest expectations with patients and direct scarce follow-up visits where they matter most. The study grounds its advice in the population it serves, Kenyan women, rather than borrowing predictions from trials run on other continents and other patients.
plos-pone-0011534:
Bredford Kerr and co-authors found in 2010 that an enriched environment changes gene activity in the Rett syndrome brain in an unexpected way. Toys, tunnels, exercise, and company ease symptoms in mouse models of Rett syndrome, and enrichment normally leaves a characteristic pattern of gene activity in the brain. The team read that pattern in their Rett model mice after enrichment.

The transcriptional response proved unconventional, departing from the pattern seen in typical brains rather than simply being weaker. Enrichment thus seems to rewire the Rett brain through unexpected routes, not by replaying the normal program at low volume. That surprise matters for therapy: treatments borrowed from typical brains may miss the pathways this brain actually uses. It also gives researchers a distinctive signature to aim at when testing drugs meant to mimic enrichment's benefits.
plos-pone-0011634:
Christy Ventura and co-authors hunted for new toxins made by Staphylococcus aureus germs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This germ is a top cause of infection in hospitals and in the wider public, and tough drug-proof strains such as USA300 often sicken healthy people. Some of its weapons are two-part toxins that kill white blood cells.

The team scanned the proteins displayed on the germ's outer surface and found a two-part toxin no one had described before. The find adds to the known set of tools the germ uses to beat immune defences. Each new toxin is also a fresh target for drugs that aim to disarm the germ.
plos-pone-0011734:
Isabelle Chantret and co-authors studied trimming enzymes in human liver cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. As proteins are coated with sugars during N-glycosylation, about a fifth of the sugar chains end up released as free fragments. What the enzymes that handle those fragments actually do in the process was unclear.

Working in HepG2 liver cells, the team identified roles for two enzymes, peptide N-glycanase and Engase1p, during sugar coating. Their step-by-step roles reveal a quality-control system inside the cell's coating line. Understanding it matters for diseases where sugar coating goes wrong.
plos-pone-0011834:
Masakazu Kamata and co-workers reported in 2010 on a way to watch human stem cells being made and guided, live, inside the dish. Their cells are induced pluripotent stem cells, adult cells coaxed back into a flexible state that can form many tissue types. For medical use, researchers must confirm the change worked and see when new cell types appear.

The group built a lentiviral reporter that lights up according to the cells' own microRNAs, tiny RNA pieces whose levels rise and fall as cell identity changes. Because the signal comes from living cells, the same culture can be followed day after day without being destroyed. That kind of live check could make stem cell production safer and easier to control.
plos-pone-0011934:
Xuting Wang and colleagues studied in 2010 the airway lining of smokers who face a high risk of lung cancer. Earlier studies had shown that gene activity in bronchial airway cells reflects smoking exposure and might serve as an early warning sign of cancer. The team asked how a person's own genetic variation shapes that response.

They focused on antioxidant response genes, the defenses airway cells raise against smoke chemicals. Differences in how strongly those defenses switch on may help explain why only some heavy smokers develop cancer. Airway cells can be collected without surgery, so a reliable defense signature could one day sort smokers by risk for closer watching.
plos-pone-0012034:
Eric Brunskill and Steven Potter mapped in 2010 the gene programs of the cells lining kidney blood vessels. Endothelial cells differ remarkably between organs in form and function, and they help build every organ system. Their failure also contributes to diseases such as diabetic nephropathy, a leading cause of kidney failure.

By profiling endothelial cells from the developing and diseased mouse kidney, the team charted which genes define this population at each stage. A program-level map shows what kidney vessel cells need to form properly and what changes when disease begins. That gives kidney researchers specific genes to test rather than treating endothelium as generic plumbing.
plos-pone-0012134:
Mathieu Coureuil, Nicolas Ugolin, Marie Tavernier, and co-authors studied radiation damage in mouse testes for PLOS ONE in 2010. The stem and progenitor cells that start sperm production are killed by radiation through a controlled cell-death program watched over by a guard protein. Which executioner pathways carry out that death, though, was still poorly mapped.

The team showed that two different death pathways split the work between distinct groups of these early cells. One works from inside the cell, the other takes signals from outside. Sorting out which cells die by which route matters for protecting fertility during cancer treatment, and for understanding how the testis recovers after injury.
plos-pone-0012234:
Hideyuki Tanabe, Issei Takayama, Takashi Nishiyama, and co-authors studied a scaffolding protein in mouse cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Periostin normally works outside cells, helping them grip their surroundings. The Notch1 protein, by contrast, is a signal receiver whose level decides many cell fates, and cells guard its supply, especially under stress.

Unexpectedly, the team found periostin working inside the cell, physically holding the young Notch1 protein and keeping its level up under stress conditions. An outside protein with a hidden inside job redraws its job description. Since Notch signaling drives several cancers and developmental disorders, a partner that sustains it is a new place to intervene.
plos-pone-0012334:
Carmen Marsit, Andres Houseman, Brock Christensen, and co-authors searched silenced genes for marks of aggressive bladder cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Half a million Americans diagnosed with bladder cancer need repeated scope examinations for life, because the cancer so often returns or advances, at a cost of billions each year. A urine or tissue test that flags dangerous tumors could relieve much of that burden.

The team identified genes whose methylation silencing pattern matches aggressive disease. Silencing marks are stable and detectable, which makes them practical test material. If validated, such a panel could tell which patients need the closest surveillance and which can safely be scoped less often.
plos-pone-0012434:
Carole Fureix, Hervé Menguy and Martine Hausberger studied aggression in horses with chronic pain, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Sudden pain is known to raise aggression in people and animals, but most past work looked at brief pain or lab settings. The authors asked whether long-lasting pain turns horses sour-tempered, and whether such partners should be avoided or treated.

Horses with chronic pain conditions showed more aggression toward people than pain-free herd mates. The link argues for curing rather than rejecting: a bad temper may be a pain signal. Vets and owners who read aggression as a health clue can catch hidden suffering earlier and keep handlers safer.
plos-pone-0012534:
Mohammed Al Gadban, Kent Smith, Farzan Soodavar and colleagues tracked two forms of bad cholesterol inside macrophages, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Oxidized LDL cholesterol and its immune complexes both stuff macrophages into foam cells, the fatty cells that seed artery plaques. The two forms were known to enter cells by different routes, and routes shape the stress that follows.

The team compared trafficking of each form and its effect on oxidative stress in the cells. The forms diverged in handling and stress output, which may explain their different roles in plaque growth. Heart disease prevention may benefit from targeting the more harmful route specifically.
plos-pone-0012634:
Ali, Al-Olayan, Lewis and co-authors looked for triggers that make malaria parasites kill themselves. Some single-celled parasites show a death process much like the programmed cell death of larger organisms. In the rodent malaria parasite, this happens in the ookinete stage, which grows inside the mosquito gut.

Their 2010 study searched for natural signals that set off that death. If parasites can be pushed to destroy themselves, the mosquito stage could become a drug target. Blocking malaria inside the mosquito would stop spread before the parasite ever reaches a person.
plos-pone-0012734:
Wang, Chen, Liu and co-authors engineered a longer-lasting version of a diabetes hormone. GLP-1 lowers blood sugar in several helpful ways, but the natural hormone breaks down in under two minutes. Their 2010 paper fused GLP-1 to other protein parts, building a chimera meant to survive in the body.

The fused protein kept strong action on the GLP-1 receptor while lasting far longer. Long action means fewer injections and steadier sugar control for patients. Their design adds one more entry to the race for weekly diabetes drugs.  Sugar control was checked in diabetic animal models too.
plos-pone-0323234:
Boniphace Marwa and colleagues price a program that made births safer in Tanzania. This cost study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The program, a bundle of safer-birth measures for labor wards, joined staff training with better tools. It ran in thirty health facilities from 2021 to 2023. Deaths of mothers and newborns fell while it ran.

The team counted what the program cost. They then set that cost against the lives saved. Each life saved cost under five thousand dollars. Each year of life gained cost far less. Every dollar spent returned many times its value in benefits. Numbers like these decide whether a health ministry expands a pilot. Here the case for growth is strong.
plos-pone-0328334:
Nyagwaswa Michael and colleagues gather views on stroke care in 2026. They spoke with survivors, caregivers, and health workers in Tanzania. Late arrival and weak referrals cost lives there. High personal costs and few stroke ready sites add harm. Rehab services are also thin on the ground. Talks were held at a national referral hospital.

Six linked themes came out of the talks. Raise public awareness of stroke risks and care. Build up resources at primary care sites. Widen health financing and insurance cover. Join up health information systems for stroke. Train mixed teams in stroke care and clear talk. Smooth care delivery across the whole path. Patient steps and system steps must move together.
plos-pone-0328634:
Qiang Yin builds a system for predicting how high school students will perform, and for explaining its guesses, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Schools want early warning of struggling students, but many prediction models are black boxes and falter on modest datasets. Yin pairs a newer model called TabPFN, designed to learn from prior data patterns, with SHAP, a method that credits each input for its share of a prediction.

On records of four thousand Spanish high school students, the paired system beat seven rival models on accuracy. It also held up when the training data shrank: with only five hundred students it matched what older models needed thousands to achieve. The explanation step pointed to study habits, above all weekly study hours, attendance, and tutoring. Teachers get both a forecast and a reason they can act on.
plos-pone-0329934:
Pegah Safari and Mehrnoush Shamsfard build a system that pulls a person's basic profile, such as age, job, and hobbies, out of chat text in Persian. Such profiles power suggestions and personal assistants, but big language models handle Persian poorly. Their 2026 study tests many models and finds them tripped up by scarce training material and the language's complex structure.

The team's hybrid method mixes slot filling, learning from examples in the prompt, and reasoning over a knowledge map. It beat famous large models by wide margins, even versions fine-tuned for the task. It was also far better at catching clashes in what a user claimed. The work shows smaller, well-guided tools can outdo giants in less-served languages.
plos-pone-0330134:
Msuya and colleagues, in a 2026 study, map the reach of Tanzania's 2024 measles-rubella vaccination campaign for young children. Measles still kills children worldwide, and rubella causes severe birth defects, so campaign coverage decides real outcomes. A survey after the February campaign covered more than sixteen thousand children aged nine months to just under five years.

About four in five children received the vaccine. Coverage swung widely by region: two regions reached nearly every child, while two others barely passed three in five. Statistical mapping showed real clustering, pockets of high coverage beside pockets of low. A child's chances rose with household wealth, living in town, and having an older, married, more educated caregiver. The authors say national averages hide the map that matters; campaign teams should hunt the cold spots their analysis names.
plos-pone-0333334:
María Magdalena Vaccarezza, Verónica Laura Sanguine, and Giselle Balaciano present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of ketogenic diet therapies for epilepsy that does not respond to drugs. The reviewers searched four databases and kept seventeen randomized trials covering children, adolescents, and adults, with follow-up from six months to two years. These high-fat, low-carbohydrate diets come in several forms, all included here.

In children, about thirty-seven in a hundred may at least halve their seizures on the diet, on moderate-certainty evidence. Adults and adolescents also gained, with roughly sixteen more people per hundred reaching that mark than with usual care. Evidence on deep seizure control, quality of life, and thinking was thin and uncertain, and sticking to the diet was slightly harder than usual care. The authors present the diets as a real option with honest caveats.
plos-pone-0334734:
Djamayl Engelen and co-authors tested whether routine gene sequencing could track drug-resistant gut bacteria across a whole region. The germ, a form of Enterococcus that resists the antibiotic vancomycin, spreads quietly in hospitals. Five Dutch hospitals sent their isolates to one lab for a year of shared surveillance, and the lab read each germ's full genetic code.

Sequencing grouped most isolates with at least one match, and patient movement records showed nearly all spread happened inside a single hospital, with a few jumps between hospitals. The shared system exposed one outbreak spanning centers and two local ones. The authors argue that pooled sequencing gives infection teams a clearer map of how resistance travels.
plos-pone-0339634:
Grace Ellen Brannon led a team of six authors on this 2026 interview study of Spanish-language COVID-19 vaccination videos made for Hispanic audiences in the United States. Forty-nine people in a southern suburban county watched four television messages built from earlier local research and shared their reactions.

Warm, human-centered messages that framed vaccination as a gain landed well, while pushier suggestions risked resistance. Participants wanted quality Spanish-language health information in Spanish news outlets they already trust. Brannon argues gentle, gain-framed messaging earns credibility and attention in communities facing health gaps.
plos-pone-0343134:
Agustín Blanco-Echevarría and a large team asked what drives the dangerous blood fats seen in fatty liver disease: the inflammation of active disease, or the scarring of advanced disease. Forty-nine patients with suspected fatty liver gave biopsies during surgery, and their blood was profiled with standard tests plus advanced methods that separate fat particles by size and type.

Only activity mattered. Patients whose livers showed active disease carried higher levels of the particles most tied to artery damage, including the cholesterol cargo protein and triglyceride-rich particles. Scarring showed no link with any fat measure. The authors call this an atherogenic momentum set by disease activity, suggesting that calming the active phase, not just staging scars, should guide heart-risk treatment in these patients.
plos-pone-0344934:
Md Ismail Hossain and Azizur Rahman led a study of child deaths in Bangladesh. They tracked deaths before age five in all eight regions. The span ran from 1990 to 2022. They then forecast the path to 2030. The data came from a big national survey. Birth records for near sixty-five thousand children fed the work.

Gaps between regions were weak across the whole span. But they flared in the early nineties and late twenty-tens. Sylhet kept the worst rates and Khulna the best. Sylhet and Rangpur also improved at a slow pace. Forecasts show gains that flatten with time. The team says the last pockets of high deaths need focused aid.
plos-pone-0345134:
Bassani and colleagues, in a 2026 driving simulator study, ask whether the sulphites in wine affect driving beyond the alcohol itself. Sulphites preserve wine and stop spoilage, and drinkers often blame them for feeling off. Thirty-two volunteers each drove the simulator three times: sober, and after red wine with low or high sulphite content, both times at about Italy's legal alcohol limit.

On easy rural roads, only alcohol mattered, making drivers wander more within their lane on curves; sulphite level changed nothing. In a busy town scene the picture split. With high-sulphite wine, drivers were more careful when pedestrians stepped out at crossings. Yet in a follow-the-car task, the same drivers kept higher speeds and shorter gaps than when sober. The authors call the effect context-dependent: the same glass can steady a driver in one scene and embolden them in another.
plos-pone-0345434:
Jillian H Hurst leads a team of eight predicting which toddlers will keep getting ear infections, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Recurrent ear infection, three episodes in six months or four in a year, drives antibiotic use and surgery referrals. The team used electronic health records for more than sixty-five hundred children born at one health system between 2014 and 2022. All had at least one ear infection. The model asked who progressed to the recurrent pattern.

A quarter of the children did. A model using only first visit data already discriminated moderately well between future recurrent and one off cases. Three features stood out: the child's age, prior antibiotic courses, and a diagnosis of acid reflux. The authors offer the model as a triage aid. Flag the risky quarter early and watch them closely. The rest may be spared unnecessary intervention.
plos-pone-0346234:
Daisy Fancourt and Feifei Bu analyze a 2025 national survey of social prescribing link workers in England, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Link workers connect patients to community help such as exercise groups or debt advice, and national rules say they should track outcomes, though nobody knew how consistently they do.

Among four hundred nine workers with caseloads, only a little over half often recorded individual patient outcomes, and fewer still tracked service-level results. Under half used standard quantitative measures. The authors link the patchiness to workload and systems rather than unwillingness, and suggest simpler tools and clearer expectations if social prescribing is to prove its value.
plos-pone-0346434:
Safia Arbab and colleagues tested retail meat sold in Sindh, Pakistan, for bacteria that resist antibiotics. They examined one hundred twenty-three samples, including ground meat, beef burgers, frozen chicken, and swabs from chicken carcasses. Every sample grew Gram-negative bacteria, a broad class that includes several gut germs.

E. coli was the most common find, followed by Klebsiella and Salmonella. Many isolates resisted widely used antibiotics, including several penicillin and cephalosporin drugs. Resistant bacteria on meat can reach kitchens and, from there, people. The findings support tighter hygiene in meat handling and more care in how antibiotics are used in food animals.
plos-pone-0347134:
Hao Wang, Hongquan Liu, Fengze Sun, and Jitao Wu went hunting for genes that might connect bisphenol A, a common plastics chemical, to bladder cancer. Their 2026 study is computational, merging gene activity data from large cancer databases with toxicology records and a set of genes tied to a recently described cell process called lactylation. Machine learning filters then narrowed the field.

Four genes survived every filter and were linked to metabolism, immunity, and gene-control features of tumours. Computer checks suggested the chemical could plausibly bind the proteins involved. The authors present the four genes as candidates for laboratory follow-up, offering a map of how an everyday chemical might nudge bladder cells toward cancer.
plos-pone-0347234:
Jingming Gai and Wei Li pressed porous red sandstone under high pressure. Deep oil and gas work needs such tests. Pressure came from all sides at once. A custom rig held the load. Ball indenters then pressed into the rock. Simulations helped explain the dent response. Failure modes were tracked as pressure rose.

Three failure modes appeared in turn. Shear came first. Spreading cracks came next. Crushing flow came last. Dent stiffness dropped near one switch point. That drop defies the usual rising trend. Leftover stress drove long side cracks. Drill designers must respect that dip. Bit force maths can fail in deep wells without it.
plos-pone-0347334:
Andrea Martínez-Ballesté and colleagues studied the useful wild plants, called ethnofloras, kept by twenty-two ethnic groups across Mexico. Published in PLOS One in 2026, their study drew on earlier field reports covering nearly three thousand plant species. It asked why groups living in the same country end up using such different sets of plants.

Each group used a very large number of species, yet few plants were shared between groups, so variety turned over sharply from place to place. Distance mattered most, because far-apart regions grow different wild plants. Groups whose languages were close tended to use more similar plants, while shared Spanish and everyday contact seemed to blur differences in how plants get used.
plos-pone-0347734:
Osita Sunday Nnyigide, Haewon Byeon, and Uchenna Esther Okpete simulated how two common detergents unfold a tiny model protein in 2026. The protein, Trp-cage, folds into a neat cage shape, making it a handy test of what helps or breaks protein structure.

In pure water the protein stayed compact when cool and loosened when hot. The negatively charged detergent invaded its oily core and spread it into many shapes, while the positive one partly shielded it from heat at higher strength. The contrast comes down to electric attraction and oily contact, lessons for handling proteins in labs and products.
plos-pone-0348234:
Rebecka Mac and colleagues studied the rollout of Braining, a twelve-week structured exercise program offered inside Swedish outpatient psychiatry. Exercise helps mental health, yet patients often need organized support to keep going. Earlier hints suggested patients benefited, but nobody had asked the staff whether the program fits real clinic life. Workers from substance-use psychiatry units answered surveys and joined focus groups over a year.

Staff rated the program's acceptability, fit, and practicality at one, four, and twelve months, and team members discussed what helped or hindered delivery. Implementation studies like this matter because a good intervention that clinics cannot sustain helps no one. The findings guide how Braining, and similar exercise offers, can spread to more units.
plos-pone-0348934:
Temitope Osifeso and colleagues interviewed fifteen clinicians who treat firefighters with work-related shoulder disorders, the third most common muscle and joint problem in the profession. Firefighting loads shoulders through lifting, hauling, and overhead work, but clinicians' views on causes and best care had not been gathered in depth. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed for recurring themes.

Eight themes emerged, covering how the job's nature worsens shoulder damage, how slips and falls cause sudden injuries, and how injury patterns differ by sex and experience. Clinicians also flagged a lack of targeted training exercises for shoulders. Their frontline perspective can shape prevention programs and return-to-work plans that fit the realities of the fire service rather than generic shoulder care.
plos-pone-0349034:
Questionnaires about life quality in multiple sclerosis were mostly written by clinicians, not patients. Ambra Mara Giovannetti and colleagues reviewed existing tools, then sat patients and health professionals in focus groups to rebuild the domain list together, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Four meetings mixed people with the disease across severity levels and regions with the professionals who treat them. Their categories were compared systematically against the literature's domains. Some patient priorities, around identity, fatigue's social cost, and planning around uncertainty, were thin or missing in older tools. The revised map will guide an adaptive questionnaire that asks each patient the questions that measure them best.
plos-pone-0349134:
Hirokazu Doi and colleagues mapped how pressure spreads under the feet of healthy Japanese adults walking at their own pace, hunting for precise differences between men and women. Ninety-two volunteers crossed a pressure-sensing plate while the team recorded step timing, force, and contact patterns. Then they used a statistical method that pinpoints exactly where and when the sexes diverge across the whole step.

Women took quicker, shorter steps and pressed harder, relative to body weight, through most of the step. The clearest gaps sat under the heel and under the second toe bone. The authors link these localised patterns to why some foot injuries strike one sex more than the other. They also report a previously unseen difference in how total force rises and falls across the step.
plos-pone-0349234:
Filip Viskupič and colleagues surveyed South Dakota beef producers on whether their personal COVID-19 vaccine choices spilled over into how they vaccinate their cattle. Experts had worried that pandemic vaccine conflict would sour attitudes toward vaccines generally. Three hundred thirty-nine producers answered in October 2024 about their herds' routine shots, their openness to a future bird flu vaccine for cattle, and their own COVID vaccination.

Nearly all producers used established cattle vaccines, and over forty-four percent had never taken a COVID shot themselves. Yet the statistical analysis found no association between the personal decision and cattle practices. A quarter would consider the bird flu vaccine for their herds. Producers, it seems, judge animal vaccines on animal terms, a reassuring result for livestock health programs.
plos-pone-0349934:
Haoxiong Sun and co-authors reanalysed a workplace walking contest in 2026, asking whether people who feel in control of their lives walk more. Modern office work leans on self direction, so such traits may decide who health programs actually reach.

Four hundred twenty-six Melbourne office workers took part in a four month team pedometer challenge in 2008, aiming at ten thousand steps a day. Sense of control was measured at the start and twice later. Workers with a stronger internal sense of control at baseline performed better in the program. Programs that build confidence alongside steps may hold the less self directed workers they usually lose.
plos-pone-0350034:
Tropical farmers need to know where soil holds water. Widodo and colleagues mapped underground moisture in West Java, Indonesia. They studied three contrasting landscapes. One was a coastal plain. One was an upland area. One was a set of terraced hills. Their method sent electric signals into the ground.

One technique imaged slices down to five meters deep. Another swept sideways at fixed depths. Coastal soil read wet and salty. Its water table sat shallow. Upland sands read dry and free-draining. Terraced fields stored moisture deep in clay layers. A dry topsoil covered that store. Slope, grain, and drainage together explained the patterns.
plos-pone-0350134:
Juan Zhu and Yao Wang stress tested how city polycentricity, having several centres rather than one, is measured in Chinese cities in 2026. Studies disagree wildly because each picks its own centre rules and yardsticks, making comparisons shaky.

Hangzhou, Wuhan, and Nanning were each measured with four centre finding methods and five indicators, covering shape based and function based versions. Shape based results barely cared which centre method was used. Function based results swung with method, and method and indicator interacted. The warning is practical: anyone ranking cities by polycentricity must declare and defend the recipe, or the ranking means little.
plos-pone-0350334:
Shuai Liang and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study linking oxidative stress, the damage caused by reactive oxygen inside cells, to prostate cancer outcomes. Drawing on public cancer databases, the team searched genes related to oxidative stress and built a risk score from four of them. They then focused on one gene, MINK1, and tested it in laboratory prostate cancer cells.

Patients with high risk scores had worse survival, and their tumors also showed more immune cell activity and responded better to one immunotherapy in the data. MINK1 was abundant in two aggressive cell lines, and switching it off slowed the cells' growth, movement, and invasion while stalling their division cycle. The authors propose MINK1 as a candidate marker and treatment target worth further study.
plos-pone-0350434:
Tri Nugraha Susilawati and colleagues analysed malaria cases in Sorong City, Papua, Indonesia, using 2024 health reports, in work published in 2026. Papua carries much of the country's malaria burden, and routine data can show where care works and where it strains.

Nearly four thousand confirmed cases were reviewed. Most patients were males aged fifteen or older, many were students, and most lived where malaria is common. Community health centres reported most cases, microscopes were the main test, and one parasite species caused about two thirds of illness. The breakdown helps local services plan testing, drugs, and hospital referral where need is greatest.
plos-pone-0350734:
Ibtisam Khalifa Al-Maskari and co-authors reviewed hospitalized dengue cases in Muscat, Oman, across 2022 and 2023 to chart who got sick, where, and when. Dengue has been establishing itself locally in the sultanate, and planners need its seasonal rhythm. Their 2026 study used national surveillance records for three hundred forty-five confirmed patients admitted to two major hospitals.

Nearly all infections were caught locally, and cases clustered in one district, Seeb, which supplied about seven in ten patients. Admissions peaked in April and May in both years, though more arrived across the dry season overall. Most patients showed warning signs, about fifteen percent turned severe, and nearly all recovered. The authors note that wet-season patterns in testing and referral may explain some timing effects better than transmission alone.
plos-pone-0350834:
Shu Hui Huang and Kerri Kobryn tinkered with a bacterial enzyme to find the smallest change that flips its job entirely. The enzyme normally finishes off the ends of linear chromosomes by sealing them into hairpin loops. Close relatives instead shuffle DNA segments around. Earlier work needed a pile of mutations to convert one job into the other, including deleting a whole restraining section.

Changing just two acidic building blocks in the enzyme proved enough to make the switch. With that pair altered, the enzyme stopped resolving chromosome ends and started performing the recombination reaction typical of its shuffling relatives, producing the crossed intermediate those enzymes are known for. The authors show how little separates these two molecular trades, a clue to how such enzymes evolved and how they might be re-engineered.
plos-pone-0351134:
Ayaz Ahmad and colleagues turned okra slime, the thick juice from okra pods, into small sugar chains by fermenting it with a yeast. Plant based options draw interest as safer routes for swelling and high blood sugar. Lab tests checked whether the new chains could calm swelling and lower sugar, with follow up tests in mice.

One batch stood out. It protected blood cell walls almost as well as a standard drug, and in mice it cut paw swelling sharply. The same batch lowered blood sugar strongly in diabetic mice and improved blood fat measures. Early results look promising, yet dose, safety, and human benefit all still need careful study.
plos-pone-0351534:
Meng Liu and four colleagues published an education study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They used results from PISA 2022, a global test of school students, and looked at science scores across nine school systems. Their question was which factors best explain strong or weak science results in each place.

Liu's team found some patterns that repeat across systems, and others that belong to one system alone. That mix is useful: shared patterns hint at lessons that travel, while local patterns warn against copying another country whole. For education leaders, the study works as a diagnostic tool, showing where their own system's science teaching is held back and where it is strong.
plos-pone-0351734:
Sanogo and colleagues tested sea mammals along United States coasts for signs of the pandemic coronavirus in a 2026 study. Many sea mammal species were predicted to be vulnerable from their cell receptors. Samples gathered from 2020 to 2025 covered more than eighteen hundred swabs and hundreds of blood samples across twenty-one species.

All swabs were negative, showing no active infection. A small share of seals and sea lions carried neutralizing antibodies, the first such evidence in these animals. Past exposure without illness suggests limited spread at sea. Watching wildlife for human viruses guards both animal health and early warning of new spillovers.
plos-pone-0351834:
Isabel Restrepo-Carvajal, Nicola Clerici, and Swanni Alvarado map how seed-carrying mammals move through Colombia's Coffee Region. Their 2026 study works in a transformed Andean landscape. Forest survives on less than a fifth of its original extent, in scattered fragments. Four mammal species that disperse seeds were modelled. Resistance maps, graph mathematics, and sensitivity tests measured how well patches connect for each animal. Protection coverage was checked too.

Connectivity came out low for every species. Patterns tracked the elevations each animal tolerates, not how far it roams at home. Narrow-elevation specialists were the most cut off. Generalists kept more routes open. A few habitat patches mattered disproportionately as stepping stones. Many sat outside the current protected network. Because mammals carry seeds, their isolation slows forest recovery itself. The prioritisation framework, which admits its own uncertainty, tells conservation planners exactly which patches to defend or reconnect first.
plos-pone-0352334:
Kazuaki Okamura and six colleagues model heatstroke damage to the brain's protective barrier in this 2026 laboratory study. Heatstroke is the deadliest heat illness, and brain dysfunction is its hallmark. The blood-brain barrier normally seals the brain off from the bloodstream. The team grew a barrier model from vessel-lining cells and support cells. Three hours at high heat, mimicking heatstroke, injured it badly.

Left alone, the barrier failed to recover over the next day. Its electrical tightness collapsed, and leak tests confirmed the breach. Then the researchers added dexamethasone, a common anti-inflammatory steroid, after the heat insult. Treated barriers regained tightness during recovery. A key sealing protein increased, and permeability fell. The work is confined to a dish, not patients. Still, it nominates a familiar, cheap drug as a candidate for protecting the brain when heatstroke strikes.
plos-pone-0352434:
Yunyun Zhao and four colleagues test mindfulness training for liver cancer patients around a targeted procedure. Their 2026 retrospective study covers advanced cases treated with chemoembolization, which blocks the tumour's blood supply. One group received standard perioperative care alone. The other added mindfulness-based stress reduction, a structured meditation programme. Outcomes included pain scores, anxiety and depression scales, and confidence in self-care.

The mindfulness group fared better across the board. Their pain ratings were lower at every check after the procedure. They also needed less pain medication, with fewer dose escalations. Anxiety and depression scores dropped further than in standard care. Self-care confidence rose significantly higher. Post-embolization syndrome, a common flu-like reaction, struck less often, and hospital stays shortened. Because the study looked backwards at records, it cannot fully prove cause. The pattern still supports offering mindfulness support alongside this demanding treatment.
plos-pone-0353234:
Grinschgl, Kohlmeier, and Neubauer asked who would accept methods that claim to boost thinking in a 2026 study. Brain stimulation, pills, and training games promise sharper minds, yet proof of broad benefit stays shaky. Two registered lab studies measured willingness to try such methods and the reasons behind it.

More than two hundred people took part in the first study alone. Motives ranged from curiosity and self-improvement to worry about side effects and fairness. Knowing who is drawn to enhancement, and why, helps regulators and schools prepare as these products spread. Acceptance research matters most before a market matures, not after habits harden.
plos-pone-0353834:
Lianne Davis and seven colleagues probe how an approved drug for a rare childhood disease actually works inside cells, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Niemann-Pick disease type C jams the cell's recycling centres, the lysosomes. The drug, an altered amino acid, is the only approved single therapy. Working in human cells, including a disease model, the team watched its effect on TFEB, the master switch for lysosome genes.

In healthy cells the drug switched TFEB on; in diseased cells, where the switch was stuck on from stress, it dialled the switch back toward normal. Only one mirror-image form of the molecule worked — the other cancelled it out. The two-way normalising action may explain the drug's benefit.
plos-pone-0353934:
Habtemichael and colleagues, in a 2026 study, map mineral-rich rock in the Asmara Belt of Eritrea using satellite images and field geology. The area is known for deposits formed by ancient underwater hot springs, which carry copper, zinc, and other metals. Ground exploration there is costly, slow, and hard in remote terrain.

The team used images from the Sentinel-2 satellite, sharpened with ratio tricks that highlight rusty surface stains left by altered rock. Several classification methods sorted the land into rock types, and field samples with known deposit sites trained and checked the maps. The altered zones tied to deposits stood out from common iron-rich soils that can fool the eye. The final maps matched existing geological maps well and pointed to known deposit sites. The authors say the low-cost approach can guide drilling and fieldwork across the wider region, where similar ancient rocks stretch across national borders.
plos-pone-0354034:
Shibeshi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine when women in Lesotho first marry, and what pushes that age up or down. Early marriage can cut schooling and strain health, and it persists in Lesotho despite laws against it. The team used the country's latest national health survey, covering more than six thousand women aged fifteen to forty-nine.

The middle age at first marriage was twenty-four. Working women married later, as did women in middle-wealth households, in less poor communities, and in towns. Women whose schooling stopped at primary level married earlier, a pattern that fits the wider story of schooling delaying marriage. The model separates personal, household, and community forces, giving program designers a clearer view of where pressure for change might work.
plos-pone-0354134:
Felix Briem and colleagues report in 2026 several years of automatic trap records for a fruit fly that invades soft fruit crops worldwide. Custom traps at four sites in southwest Germany emptied every few hours across three seasons, paired with detailed weather records. Lab studies had described daily rhythms, but long field records were rare.

Activity was low in winter, rose through late spring and summer, then fell in autumn. On busy days flies clustered in daylight, often with morning and late afternoon peaks, while quiet periods showed no clear daily pattern. Rain cut catches in every season. Growers should read trap counts with season and weather in mind, the authors say.
plos-pone-0354234:
Peter Wang and colleagues run a deep one-person study, named DELTA, that aims to make the body tougher with age. Lands are ageing fast, while grave ills strike the young more and more. That widens the gap between years lived and years lived in good health. Their 2026 plan tracks one healthy man through set tests and dense body checks.

The plan mixes time-boxed eating, strength and cardio work, a diet in the style of the Mediterranean, and supplements. Fasting tests probe how well the man's body bends and bounces back. The team pledges strict, open reports so others can copy the design. They frame DELTA as a model for rich, personal health research.
plos-pone-0354334:
Md Ramjan Sheikh and seven colleagues profile a cell-surface protein called mesothelin across many cancers in this 2026 study, with special attention to pancreatic cancer. The protein appears at high levels in several tumors but barely in most healthy tissue, which makes it attractive both for diagnosis and as a drug target. Using large public cancer datasets, the team mapped where it is switched on and what that means for patients.

Mesothelin ran high in pancreatic, ovarian, and mesothelioma tumors, and it distinguished pancreatic cancer from healthy tissue with high accuracy. Its value for predicting survival depended on the cancer type, and few tumors carried mutations in the gene itself. Computer modeling of candidate drugs singled out a plant-derived compound that bound the protein stably, though the authors caution that its predicted safety profile needs work before any real treatment use.
plos-pone-0354634:
Fereshteh Esmaeilzadeh, Davoud Koolivand, and Abozar Ghorbani sequenced the complete genomes of two Iranian isolates of a virus that blights tea plantations. The virus causes necrotic ring blotches. Their 2026 study used high-throughput sequencing on samples from Iran, where the virus arrived in 2021. It assembled all four genome segments. It profiled which viral genes switch on hardest. It also catalogued the small mutations circulating within the viral population.

One gene, P22, was by far the most strongly expressed, though its job remains unknown. Ninety-three single-letter variants peppered the genome, concentrated in two segments. Family trees placed the Iranian isolates closest to Chinese ones. The first complete Iranian sequences give plant health officials reference material for tracking the virus's spread through tea regions.
plos-pone-0354734:
Geraldine Vitry and co-authors explore in 2026 whether a simple skin swab can reveal how much radiation a body has received. Quick, non invasive checks are needed after medical, work, or space exposure. Lab grown human skin and mice were exposed to set doses, and swabs were profiled for small chemicals, fats, and microbes together.

Two chemical panels emerged: one separated exposed from unexposed skin, and another separated dose levels. Some markers were shared across models, while others tied to skin barrier health. Shifts in protective microbes supported a repair response. Human testing is still needed before real world use, the authors note.
plos-pone-0354834:
Abdoul Malik and Selim Aras published this 2026 study of a lean artificial intelligence system that reads electrocardiograms, the heart's electrical traces. Expert reading is scarce in many clinics, and heavy models are impractical there. Their design combines a small neural network on the raw trace with a frequency analysis branch, and checks whether its confidence scores can be trusted.

Validated patient by patient on a public data set, the tiny model stayed accurate and its probabilities were well calibrated, meaning its confidence matched reality. Malik and Aras target dependable heart screening on modest equipment.
plos-pone-0355234:
Yanlong Gao and five colleagues published this 2026 paper on shrinking satellite images with deep learning. Satellites send down far more picture data than ground links handle easily, and older compression can blur fine detail. Their system, trained end to end, squeezes visible and infrared imagery from a weather satellite instrument.

The method cut files to a small fraction of their starting size, roughly a thirtieth on average, while keeping rebuilt images usable. Large scenes are split into small square blocks, compressed separately, then stitched back together. Faster downlinks mean fresher maps for weather tracking, land surveys, and disaster response.
plos-pone-0355734:
Abubakar Sani Halilu and coauthors published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on solving systems of nonlinear equations, the linked unknowns appearing across engineering and finance. Classic solvers can be slow or fragile on hard systems. Their proposal blends a three-step Picard–Ishikawa iteration with a sped-up, derivative-free framework, replacing the costly Jacobian matrix with a simple diagonal estimate.

The authors prove the method converges globally, not just when started near the answer. On a battery of benchmark problems, the hybrid needed fewer iterations and less computer time than several established approaches, and it proved more robust on problems where rivals stumbled. The scheme is presented as a practical solver for large systems in real work, where exact derivatives are expensive or out of reach. Its cheap per-step cost, they argue, is what lets it scale.
plos-pone-0355934:
Salem Mgammal Al-Ameri and co-authors buried grounding rods with biodegradable farm wastes to test cheaper lightning protection. Good earthing needs low-resistance soil paths, and chemical additives are costly. Their 2026 field study in Sarawak, Malaysia, installed five systems using local waste materials and watched them for six months.

Palm oil decanter cake performed best among the waste options, followed by a wash ash and sea sand mix, coconut shell charcoal, and palm fibre. Resistance was tracked with the standard fall-of-potential method. Treated systems improved on plain soil, and booster slurries refreshed the gains. The authors present the wastes as low-cost, greener enhancers for grounding in tropical soils.
plos-pone-0356234:
Yordanos Getachew and colleagues checked drug-proof gut germs in samples sent to a private lab in Addis Ababa. Germs that shrug off many drugs, plus last-resort drugs too, are a growing threat in Ethiopian hospitals. Their 2026 study worked through more than a thousand samples in three months and tested the germs they found.

About one sample in four grew germs, and over half of those were in the target gut family. Close to four in five fought off many drug types at once. About one in five made enzymes that break the last-resort drugs. Most of those came from one lung germ type. Getachew and colleagues call for tighter drug control and cleaner wards.
plos-pone-0356734:
Wendy Akushika Dogbegah and three colleagues map what Africa knows, and does not know, about drug resistant germs, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Antimicrobial resistance is a growing threat across the continent, but tracking data sits scattered among drug company programs, global health systems, and scattered published studies. Their project pulls those sources into interactive map dashboards so gaps become visible at a glance.

They merged records spanning nearly two decades, aligning bacteria types, drugs tested, and places while keeping each source's structure. The dashboards, built in R Shiny, let users explore resistance patterns, trends over time, and which countries report well or barely at all. Exposing the patchiness itself is the point: policy makers can see where surveillance needs building before the next decisions are made.
plos-pone-0357034:
Shenming Qu led a team of five authors building a light AI model to spot maize pests, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pests eat into maize harvests across millions of small farms, and early spotting limits the damage. Their model, WSD-YOLO, is built for enhanced feature reading while staying small enough for modest devices.

Qu's design aims to bring AI pest scouting directly to the cornfield, on phones or cheap cameras farmers can afford. A model that needs a server farm helps no one in a remote field. Lightweight detection also allows frequent scanning, catching infestations while they are still patches. The study joins a growing body of work making farm AI practical where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0357834:
Bonaventure Aman Omondi and coauthors published a 2026 field study in PLOS ONE on banana bunchy top disease, a virus that stunts banana plants and is spread by aphids. They surveyed just over a hundred banana gardens in disease-affected smallholder regions, three years after those gardens had been replanted with virus-free tissue-culture plants. The question was which landscape, garden design, and management factors went along with the virus coming back.

Re-infection was more likely where banana plants crowded the area around a garden, aphids were plentiful, many varieties were grown, and planting material came from local sources. Higher altitude, hedgerows, and frequent removal of sick plants went along with less disease. The authors argue for coordinated community replanting with certified clean material, steady removal of infected plants, and barrier hedges to slow aphid spread. Their results point to specific factors worth testing in controlled trials.
plos-pone-0358034:
Tong Tang and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on predicting the tipping force in a shiplift, the giant elevator that raises ships between water levels. Water sloshing in the chamber, the chamber itself, and the ship interact strongly, so full three-dimensional simulations are expensive, while simpler two-dimensional models ignore the ship and can understate the danger. The team ran detailed fluid simulations at many scales, then trained a hybrid learning model on the results.

Their simulations matched a published alternative method within a few percent, building confidence in the data. Under a standard earthquake shaking record, the three-dimensional model predicted much higher peak tipping moments than the two-dimensional shortcut, for both light and full ship loads. The trained surrogate, mixing image-style, sequence, and tree-based learners with outlier cleaning, then forecasts the next moment quickly, making safety checks more realistic.
plos-pone-0358334: Sajjad and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on reading tuberculosis from stained tissue images. Deep learning sorted the immune patterns in bright, multi-dye microscope images. The images came from diversity outbred mice, bred to vary genetically like people do. Telling disease states apart from tissue patterns could speed lab research on why TB turns severe in some hosts.
plos-pone-0358534:
Juan Carlos Magaña leads a team of eight comparing exercise programs for people with Parkinson's disease in the PARKEX trial, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Twenty-four participants were assigned to basic physical training, to that training plus dual task exercises, or to no intervention. Dual task work pairs movement with a mental or functional challenge. Sessions ran three times a week for twelve weeks. Leg strength, walking mobility, mood, and quality of life were measured throughout.

Both training groups beat the control group on the physical tests. Chair rising and the timed walk both improved significantly in each exercise arm.
