Tierney, Stewart, Ghersi, and co-authors give practical methods for adding time-to-event data into pooled analyses. Outcomes such as survival are best compared using hazard ratios, which weigh risk over time. Reviewers often lack the original patient-level records behind published trials.

The authors show how to recover hazard ratios and related figures by carefully working from published summaries and curves. That lets reviewers include trials that report results in awkward forms, instead of dropping them. Including more trials fairly makes pooled survival estimates stronger and less biased for treatment decisions.  Worked examples show how to handle curves reported in differing formats.
pmc-3142234:
Ludvigsson, Andersson, Ekbom, and co-authors carry out an external review of the Swedish National Inpatient Register. The register, or Hospital Discharge Register, serves as a principal data source for many research projects. It forms part of the wider National Patient Register.

The register began in 1964, with psychiatric diagnoses added from 1973. The team checked its coverage and accuracy against external records. Knowing how far register data can be trusted matters because hundreds of studies on disease patterns and care quality rest on it.  Hundreds of later studies on Swedish care quality rest on this validation exercise.
pmc-3197634:
Eddy presents faster methods for profile hidden Markov model searches of sequence databases. Profile models capture the pattern of a whole family of related sequences. They had contributed much to the theory of searching for distant relatives among sequences.

In practice, though, the methods were held back by how much computing existing software needed. Eddy's accelerated approach cuts that cost, making sensitive searches practical on large databases. Faster profile searches let researchers spot remote evolutionary links that simple pairwise comparison misses, guiding work on protein function.  Database centres adopted the faster search to keep annotation pipelines on schedule.
pmc-3365034:
Peterson, Weber, Kay, and co-authors present double digest RADseq, a cheap method for finding SNPs and genotyping. Finding gene types fast and well is a keystone of modern genetics. It supports clinical diagnosis, trait association studies, and reconstruction of ancestry and selection.

High-capacity methods at the time were costly or narrow. Their approach cuts DNA with two enzymes before sequencing, giving a steady subset of the genome at low cost. It works in model and non-model species alike, opening population genetics to organisms without reference genomes.  Field teams can genotype hundreds of samples without a sequenced reference genome.
pmc-3395634:
Murrell, Wertheim, Moola, and co-authors present a method for detecting single sites in proteins under episodic diversifying selection. Natural selection leaves an imprint on protein-coding genes, but that signal is often hard to identify. Selection is frequently brief, affecting only some branches of a family tree.

Older techniques were designed to find sites under constant selection across all lineages. The new method, called MEME, can catch short bursts on a subset of branches. Catching episodic change matters for viruses and immunity genes, where brief arms races shape proteins.  Immune genes in humans show exactly the episodic pattern the method targets.
pmc-4751634:
Schubert, Lindgreen, and Orlando presented AdapterRemoval version two in 2016. As sequencers produce longer reads, DNA from short inserts increasingly runs into adapter sequences at the read end. Short inserts are typical of fossil and degraded material, where DNA is broken into small pieces.

The program trims adapters rapidly, identifies them, and merges paired reads that overlap. Efficient trimming is needed so adapter pieces do not corrupt genome assembly or variant calls. Ancient DNA labs rely on such care, since their samples cannot be replaced. Version two kept pace with longer reads and higher data volumes.
pmc-5695134:
Gregory Gloor, Jean Macklaim, Vera Pawlowsky-Glahn, and coauthors wrote this methods paper in 2017. It deals with data from high-throughput sequencing of microbes in the gut and other places. Such data are now common in studies of disease and the environment.

The authors argue that sequencing counts are parts of a whole, not absolute amounts. Treating them as plain numbers can produce false results. They show how methods built for parts-of-a-whole data avoid those traps. Anyone who analyzes microbiome data needs this warning, because the choice of math shapes every claim that follows from the numbers.
pmc-5850834:
Jaime Huerta-Cepas and colleagues presented eggNOG-mapper for fast genome annotation in 2017. Genes that descend from a shared ancestor often keep the same job, so ancestry can predict function. Working out that ancestry for whole genomes is slow with older pipelines.

The mapper assigns genes to known orthology groups using precomputed data, which makes the job much faster. It then transfers careful functional notes from well-studied relatives. Accuracy stays close to slower expert methods in the authors tests. For teams facing thousands of genomes, the tool turns annotation from a bottleneck into a routine step.
pmc-5976434:
Gibran Hemani, Jie Zheng, Ben Elsworth, and many colleagues presented the MR-Base platform in 2018. Large genetic studies can be used to test causal links between traits. The method uses summary results only, so no private individual data are needed.

MR-Base gathers results from many studies into one place and runs the causal tests in a uniform way. Users can probe thousands of trait pairs in a systematic scan. Built-in checks probe for bias from pleiotropy. The platform turned a specialist method into a routine screen that many groups now run before deeper work.
pmc-6086934:
Amit Zeisel, Hannah Hochgerner, Peter Lönnerberg, and a large team mapped the mouse nervous system in 2018. The nervous system runs complex behavior through many specialized cell types. Their locations and partnerships matter as much as their names.

Sequencing RNA from about half a million single cells, the team built a census of cell types across brain regions. They charted where each type sits and how types relate. Rare types that bulk sampling had missed came into view. The atlas gives neuroscience a shared parts list for studying circuits, disease models, and drug action.
pmc-6602434:
Kai Blin, Simon Shaw, Kai Steinke, and coauthors described antiSMASH version 5.0 in 2019. Bacteria and fungi make secondary metabolites that include many antibiotics and other useful compounds. Genome mining hunts the gene clusters that build them.

antiSMASH scans a genome and flags clusters likely to produce such compounds. It compares each cluster with known ones and predicts the product family. The update speeds the pipeline and adds new cluster types. Natural product researchers use it as the first sieve when a new genome might hide a new drug lead each year.
pmc-6939334:
Ruei-Min Lu, Yu-Chen Hwang, I-Ju Liu, and coauthors reviewed therapeutic antibodies in 2020. More than three decades have passed since the first monoclonal antibody drug approval. Engineering since then has made antibodies safer and more precise.

The review follows that progress, from mouse-based antibodies to fully human designs. It surveys formats such as bispecific antibodies and antibody-drug pairs that carry a toxic payload. Approved uses now span cancer, autoimmunity, and infection. Readers see how a once fragile drug class became a mainstay of modern medicine. Safety data from approved products are reviewed to show how newer designs lowered immune reactions.
pmc-7615134:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled worldwide measurements in 2016 to chart how adult body weight changed across four decades. Their analysis combined nearly seventeen hundred population based studies, covering close to twenty million participants in two hundred countries from 1975 to 2014. From height and weight records they estimated body-mass index trends, the standard yardstick for sorting people from underweight through severe obesity.

The results show obesity rising across most of the world while underweight slowly receded, with sharp differences between regions. Both ends of the scale carry raised risks of serious illness and early death. Because the study used measured bodies rather than self reports, its trends became a benchmark for tracking one of the defining health shifts of the modern era.
pmc-9617234:
Laura Damschroder and colleagues published in 2022 an updated version of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, a widely used guide for putting health programs into practice. Many well planned efforts fail because the setting pushes back: staffing, culture, money, and workflow can overpower a good plan. The framework, known as CFIR, is among the most common tools for analyzing those contextual forces in advance.

The update was shaped by feedback from people who use the framework in real projects. The authors describe what users found unclear or missing and how the revised version answers them. Implementation scientists and health system leaders use CFIR to design rollouts and to diagnose why a program that worked in one hospital stumbles in another.
pmc-9825434:
Damian Szklarczyk and colleagues presented the 2023 edition of the STRING database, which maps associations between proteins for any sequenced genome. Much of a cell's complexity comes from proteins interacting and regulating one another. The core of that interaction web is increasingly known, yet new links still surface constantly, and the records are scattered across many databases.

STRING gathers those associations into one network resource and pairs it with enrichment analysis, which tests what a set of proteins does collectively. The update extends coverage to newly sequenced organisms and refreshes the underlying evidence. Researchers use it to move from a list of genes to a picture of the machinery those genes run.
poems-pg1034: The war poems of Wilfred Owen, killed in 1918 at twenty-five, one week before the Armistice. "Dulce et Decorum Est" and "Anthem for Doomed Youth" turned the pity of war into immortal verse. Published after his death, they remain the greatest English poetry of the First World War.
pope-essay-on-man-1734:
Alexander Pope published An Essay on Man in parts during 1733 and 1734, without his name at first. He addressed it to his friend Henry St. John, Lord Bolingbroke, whose ideas shaped its argument. The poem aims at nothing less than a system of the moral universe.

Across four letters, Pope argues that the world forms one great chain of being, with man in the middle. Human pride, passion, and self-love all serve purposes we only partly see. Whatever is, is right became its most quoted and most argued-over line. The essay sums up Enlightenment optimism in polished heroic couplets of remarkable force and balance.
pushkin-queen-of-spades-1834:
Alexander Pushkin wrote The Queen of Spades in 1834. It is a short tale of greed, cards, and a ghost. Hermann is a young German officer in St. Petersburg. He hears of an old countess who knows a sure run of three cards.

He forces his way to her rooms at night and scares her to death in his plea. Her ghost then gives him the three cards, with a price on the gift. At the faro table the last card turns to the queen of spades. The tale is the crown piece of Russian tales of the strange.
quran-sale-1734: George Sale's 1734 English translation of the Koran, the first direct from Arabic. Its preliminary discourse shaped European views of Islam for a century. This edition preserves that landmark translation. Later readers can locate it. The paper lived through the years.
rumi-mathnawi-vol-6-nicholson-1934:
Reynold A. Nicholson translated Rumi's Mathnawi, and this sixth volume came out in 1934 in London. The E. J. W. Gibb Memorial volume gives Books Five and Six in Nicholson's landmark English version. It completes the library's Mathnawi set, the fruit of Nicholson's life work on Rumi's great poem.

Jalalu'ddin Rumi's Mathnawi, a vast Persian poem of the 1200s, teaches Sufi faith through tale and discourse. Kings, fools, lovers, and animals act out lessons on love, pride, prayer, and the soul's return. Nicholson's prose, with its notes, aims at sense and order over the music of the Persian original. Book Six breaks off with Rumi's death, its last tale left, fittingly, without an end in time. Scholars still start with Nicholson when they approach Rumi's ocean of stories in English.
sale-koran-1734:
George Sale, an English lawyer with a fine grasp of Arabic, made this English Koran in 1734. It was the first English form made straight from the Arabic text. With it stands his Preliminary Discourse, a long first word on the faith of Islam and its Prophet.

Sale's text held the field for a hundred years as the Koran of the English world. His notes draw on the best Arabic sources of his day, with care and calm. The pair of text and first word shaped how the West saw Islam for a long age.
tob-10034:
Virgil wrote the Georgics as a poem about farming in four books, at the height of his powers. Mackail's translation is the version named for this entry. It treats the land as serious work fit for great verse.

Book one covers crops and weather signs, book two vines and trees, book three cattle and horses, and book four bees. Virgil mixes plain farming advice with myth, praise of country life, and dark notes on plague and loss. Farmers, poets, and rulers read it for centuries, and it remains the finest farming poem in Latin.
tob-10234:
William Gemmell's translation presents the Diamond Sutra, a short Mahayana Buddhist scripture cast as instruction from the Buddha to his disciple Subhuti. Its central teaching is emptiness: all things lack a fixed, separate self. Even Buddhist concepts must not be clung to as final possessions.

Images make the point vivid. Phenomena are like stars at dawn, a bubble in a stream, a flash of lightning, or a dream. The sutra's fame also rests on its copies: a printed version dated 868 AD ranks among the world's oldest surviving printed books. Readers get a demanding text in brief compass, built to cut attachment.
tob-4134:
Isaac Myer's Qabbalah, published in 1888, joined two subjects: the philosophy of Solomon ibn Gebirol and the roots of Jewish Kabbalah. Gebirol, an eleventh-century Spanish Jewish thinker, wrote the Fountain of Life, a Neoplatonic account of matter, form, and the divine will. Myer prints and explains his system.

Around it he builds one of the first American studies of Kabbalah's sources and growth. The book opened Jewish philosophy to English readers who had no other road in. Verified from the 1919 edition, Myer's work is dated in spots, yet its pioneering scope still earns respect from historians of mysticism.
tob-4185-78134:
Goodwin's edition of Plutarch's Moralia opens with volume one, devoted largely to essays on character and conduct. Plutarch writes as a practical counselor. He tells readers how to master anger, check curiosity about others, and find calm of mind amid trouble.

Other pieces advise on education, health, and listening well to lectures. The tone is friendly, the examples drawn from Greek and Roman history. English readers who knew only the Lives met a different Plutarch here: a philosopher of daily life. Goodwin's complete Victorian translation of the essays begins with this humane, useful volume.
tob-9334:
Early Christians passed down a short manual called the Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. Philotheos Bryennios edited the text after finding its only full copy in 1873, ending a loss that had lasted about a thousand years. Scholars date the manual to the church's first generations.

In a few brief chapters it tells believers how to baptize, how to fast and pray, and how to share the Eucharist meal. It also warns how to test traveling prophets and spot false ones. No other text shows so plainly how the earliest churches ran their common life, day by day.
un-ga-res-34: Three states joined the United Nations in a single vote on 9 November 1946. Resolution 34 acts on the advice of the Security Council and the report of the First Committee, which had backed all three bids without dissent. The new members were Afghanistan, the Republic of Iceland, and Sweden, admitted in the Assembly's first year of work.
un-ga-res-a-69-34:
Mines buried in fields and roads kill and maim long after wars end. Resolution A/69/34, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, renews the long fight against anti-personnel mines. Such mines kill or wound thousands each year, women, girls, boys, and men. They put whole towns at risk and hold back the growth of the lands where they lie.

The Assembly states its will to end that suffering in full. States must do their utmost, in joint and well-steered work, to clear the mines sown across the world and to see them destroyed. Care and healing for the hurt, and help to fit them back into daily life, stand as part of the same duty.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 34 was adopted on 9 November 1946, at the forty-seventh plenary meeting. It is a short admission decision. The Assembly noted the membership bids, the Security Council's backing, and a matching report from its First Committee. It then voted that Afghanistan, the Republic of Iceland, and Sweden be admitted as members of the United Nations.

Resolution 69/34 of the General Assembly backs implementation of the Convention banning anti-personnel mines. The Assembly notes that 162 states have accepted the convention. It notes that the 2014 Maputo review conference adopted an action plan for 2014–2019. It regrets that mines are still used in some conflicts. It invites states outside the convention to join without delay. It urges full reporting under article 7. It renews calls for mine clearance, risk education, and care and reintegration for mine victims worldwide.
un-sc-res-1034:
Bosnia's war crimes evidence was laid before the Council on 21 December 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 27 November, made under resolution 1019 (1995), told of Srebrenica, Zepa, Banja Luka, and Sanski Most. It found overwhelming proof of summary executions, rape, mass expulsion, detention, forced labour, and large-scale disappearances. The Dayton peace had been initialled a month earlier.

The Council strongly condemned every breach of humanitarian law and human rights in the former Yugoslavia. It condemned in the strongest terms the Bosnian Serb forces' crimes in particular. The unknown but large number of men missing from Srebrenica caused the utmost concern. The Bosnian Serb party had to give the Red Cross instant access to the displaced, the detained, and the missing. The Council noted that the Hague tribunal had indicted the Bosnian Serb leadership on 16 November 1995. No indicted person could hold public office under the peace.
un-sc-res-1334:
Sierra Leone's ceasefire was young and shaky in December 2000. The government and the Revolutionary United Front had signed it in Abuja in November. On 22 December 2000 the Security Council took note of the deal. It voiced concern that the RUF was not meeting its duties. The situation in Sierra Leone and its neighbors stayed fragile. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission days earlier.

UNAMSIL's main tasks stayed as set that August. They centered on helping the ceasefire hold and the peace process move. The Council praised the Secretary-General's hunt for more troops. It urged states able to give soldiers to think hard about doing so. The mission's strength had become the weak point of the peace.
un-sc-res-134:
Killings of unarmed demonstrators in South Africa brought the Security Council into the apartheid question on 1 April 1960. Twenty-nine member states had complained about the large-scale shootings of peaceful protesters against racial discrimination. The Council linked the crisis to Pretoria's racial policies and its long disregard of General Assembly calls to change them. World feeling on the killings ran strong.

The Council held that the situation had led to international friction and could endanger peace and security if it went on. It deplored the loss of so many African lives and sent its deepest sympathy to the victims' families. It deplored the policies that had caused the crisis. South Africa was called to start measures toward racial harmony based on equality and to abandon apartheid and racial discrimination. The Secretary-General was asked to arrange, with Pretoria, steps that would uphold the Charter, and to report as needed.
un-sc-res-1434:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's border mission gained six more months in September 2002. On 6 September 2002 the Security Council extended UNMEE until 15 March 2003. The force levels set in 2000 stayed in place. The Council restated its support for the peace process. The Algiers agreements of 2000 formed its base. A boundary commission was drawing the disputed border.

The Council would review progress often. It would check the parties' steps under the Algiers deals. It would also weigh what those steps meant for the mission. The text stresses that the mission's end is tied to the border process. Delimitation and demarcation had to be completed. That link later became a point of deep dispute.
un-sc-res-1534: Under number 1534, the Security Council placed a formal decision in its record, transcribed here from English Wikisource. The body's fifteen members include five permanent ones whose no vote can stop any text. What survives that test becomes a resolution, and this entry preserves one in full, from its first recital to its last instruction.
un-sc-res-1634: Resolution 1634, a 2005 Security Council act, survives in this collection through a transcription of the official record. The Council's work product is text: negotiated, voted, and filed under a number. This entry is one such file, complete with the preamble's reasoning and the numbered orders that give the reasoning practical effect.
un-sc-res-1734:
Resolution 1734, adopted on 22 December 2006, took up Sierra Leone. The country was rebuilding after a brutal civil war that ended in 2002. A small United Nations office, UNIOSIL, helped with peace and reform. National elections were set for July 2007, the first since the war's end without peacekeepers in charge.

The text extends UNIOSIL for twelve months, until 31 December 2007. Extra staff would join for most of 2007 to support the elections. All parties are told to keep the vote peaceful, free, and fair. The Council also praises the Special Court and urges states to fund its work, including a major war crimes trial then ahead.
un-sc-res-1834:
Chad and the Central African Republic are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1834. The Council adopted it on 24 September 2008. War in Darfur, next door in Sudan, spilled across the border. Armed groups attacked towns and threatened camps full of refugees and displaced people.

The text extends the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad until 15 March 2009. That mission, called MINURCAT, trained local police to guard the camps. The Council also plans a United Nations military force to take over from European troops that same day. It demands that armed groups stop their violence at once.
un-sc-res-1934: Resolution 1934, from 2010, is a Council decision kept in this collection in its record wording, copied by English Wikisource from the UN text. A reader can watch the body think on paper: facts are lined up, rules are named, and then a decision is set down in numbered lines. Those lines were meant to be acted on as written.
un-sc-res-2034: A vacancy on the International Court of Justice was set down for election on 19 January 2012. Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh had resigned, with effect from 31 December 2011. His seat stood empty for the rest of his term. Under the Court's Statute, the Council fixes the election date. The Council decided that the election would take place on 27 April 2012. It would be held at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly at its sixty-sixth session.
un-sc-res-2334:
Resolution 2334, adopted in December 2016, restated the Council's position that Israeli settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967 have no legal validity. The United States, which usually blocked such texts, abstained this time and let it pass. The vote drew huge attention worldwide.

The text calls settlements a major obstacle to the two-state solution and demands a halt to building, while also condemning violence against civilians on both sides. It asks the Secretary-General to report every three months on compliance. Few single resolutions show the Council's Middle East role, and its limits, as sharply as this one.
un-sc-res-234:
The Six-Day War was still raging when the Council met again on 7 June 1967. Its appeal of the day before had not stopped the fighting. Military activity in the Near East went on. The Council said the continued fighting could make the situation even more dangerous. The members acted with those facts in front of them.

This time the Council set an hour. It demanded that the governments concerned cease fire at 2000 hours GMT that same day. All military activity had to stop as a first step. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed at once. The deadline passed with the war still under way.
un-sc-res-334: This library holds Resolution 334 as an official Council record, dated 1964 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-34: Greece's border fight left the Security Council's desk under Resolution 34, passed on 15 September 1947. The dispute had set Greece against Albania, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria, over raids and unrest in the north of Greece. The Council rules that the case be struck from the list of matters before it. All files and papers in the case go to the General Assembly, which had its own team on Greek aid at work. The vote passed nine to two, with Poland and the Soviet Union against.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1034, adopted on 21 December 1995, confronts the crimes reported from Srebrenica, Zepa, Banja Luka, and Sanski Most in Bosnia and Herzegovina. A report by the Secretary-General found strong proof of a steady pattern of summary executions, rape, mass expulsion, forced detention, forced labour, and large-scale disappearances. Many men from the Srebrenica area were listed as executed at named sites.

The Council condemns these acts in the strongest terms and demands that the Bosnian Serb side give the Red Cross and aid agencies free access to displaced, detained, and missing people. It orders that proof of crimes be kept intact and that all detention camps close at once. It notes the war crimes tribunal's November 1995 indictments of Bosnian Serb leaders over Srebrenica. It also condemns looting and house wrecking by HVO forces and demands an end to new mine-laying.

Sierra Leone's peace hung by a thread at Christmas 2000. A truce had been signed in Abuja on 10 November. The RUF rebels had not kept their word in full. The UN force, UNAMSIL, was too weak for its vast task. The chief's report of 15 December urged more strength. Resolution 1334 passed with no dissent on 22 December 2000.

UNAMSIL's term ran to 31 March 2001. Its core jobs stayed the same. Help the state rule the whole land. Bring back law and calm, town by town. Aid the path to fresh arms hand-ins. The Council begged states with troops to spare to send them. More help for the chief's own plans was pledged fast. The force's size and shape would get a fresh look with the men who sent them.

South Africa's racial order faced one of its first Council rebukes in Resolution 134, adopted on 1 April 1960 by nine votes to none with two abstentions. Twenty-nine member states had complained after the large-scale killing of unarmed, peaceful demonstrators protesting racial discrimination and segregation. The Council said the situation had created international friction and could endanger peace if it continued.

The Council deplored the loss of so many African lives and sent sympathy to the victims' families. It deplored the policies that produced the crisis. It then called on South Africa to start measures aimed at racial harmony based on equality and to abandon apartheid and racial discrimination, an early marker on the long road to sanctions.

Peace held, just barely, between Ethiopia and Eritrea in 2002. Their border war had ended with the Algiers deals of 2000. A boundary team had drawn the new line that April. Both states called the ruling final. UN troops, the UNMEE force, patrolled the tense frontier. Resolution 1434 passed with no dissent on 6 September 2002.

The Council kept UNMEE in place to 15 March 2003. It would watch how both sides kept their word. Eritrea had just freed 279 captives of war. Ethiopia was urged to free its own captives and detainees. Reports of cross-border raids and seizures drew worry. Both states had to end such acts and help UN probes. Land transfers tied to the new line loomed ahead.

Staying on schedule is demanded of the war crimes tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda on 26 March 2004. A completion strategy was already set: investigations done by the end of 2004, first-instance trials by the end of 2008, and all work finished in 2010. Both tribunals had reported their plans.

Prosecutors are called on to review their case loads and decide which cases to keep and which to send to national courts. New indictments are to focus on the most senior leaders bearing the greatest responsibility for the crimes. Each tribunal must assess its progress twice a year in reports, so delays in the completion strategy can be caught early.

In August 2005 the POLISARIO Front released the last 404 Moroccan prisoners of war, ending a long humanitarian chapter of the Western Sahara conflict. The political dispute itself remained deadlocked. Against that background, MINURSO is extended on 28 October 2005, until 30 April 2006.

The prisoner release is welcomed, and the parties are called on to keep working with the Red Cross on people still unaccounted for. The call for a mutually acceptable political solution giving the people of Western Sahara self-determination is repeated. States are asked to fund confidence-building measures such as family visits, and the Secretary-General is to report on the situation before the mandate expires.

Sierra Leone's July 2007 elections loom over Resolution 1734, adopted on 22 December 2006. The United Nations Integrated Office in Sierra Leone, UNIOSIL, had helped the country recover from war. The Peacebuilding Commission had named four priority areas for support. The Special Court for Sierra Leone was at work, with the trial of a former Liberian president ahead. Wide acceptance of the election outcome would show that peace could last.

The Council extends UNIOSIL until 31 December 2007. It approves more staff from January to October 2007 to strengthen election support. It calls on all sides in Sierra Leone to show full loyalty to the vote and keep it calm, open, free, and fair. It asks the government to fund and back the election bodies and urges states to fill the budget gap. The Secretary-General must study UNIOSIL's role near the vote and shape an exit plan.

Refugees caught between Darfur's war and raids in Chad and the Central African Republic are the focus of Resolution 1834, adopted on 24 September 2008. The EU force EUFOR Chad/CAR had been guarding the east since March. The UN Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, MINURCAT, was training a special Chadian police unit, the DIS, to protect camps. Armed group attacks still put civilians and aid work at risk.

The Council extends MINURCAT until 15 March 2009, matching EUFOR's end date. It states its plan to approve a UN military force to take over from EUFOR in both countries, so safe terms for refugee return can be built. It asks the Secretary-General to plan that handover, seek troops and helicopters, and report by 15 November 2008 with options. It demands that armed groups stop violence at once and backs the Dakar Accord between Sudan and Chad.

A small United Nations force watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria on the Golan Heights. Resolution 1934, adopted on 30 June 2010, renews that force, the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force. Renewals like this one had become routine, coming every six months. The Council had just considered a new report on the force's work.

The Council called on both sides to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That older text demanded a cease-fire and talks after the October 1973 war. The observer force's mandate was renewed until 31 December 2010, and a report was due at the end of that period. The Council also praised the force's efforts to enforce a zero tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse by its own personnel.

Resolution 2034, adopted on 19 January 2012, is a brief scheduling decision. Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh had resigned from the International Court of Justice, the UN's main court, effective 31 December 2011, leaving a seat empty. The Council decides the election to fill the vacancy will take place on 27 April 2012, at meetings of both the Council and the General Assembly.

Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967 are the subject of Resolution 2334, adopted on 23 December 2016. The territory includes East Jerusalem. The Council said the growth of the settlements was putting the two-state solution in grave danger.

The Council reaffirmed that the settlements have no legal validity. It called them a flagrant violation of international law. It repeated its demand that Israel stop all settlement activity in the occupied territory at once and in full. The text also condemned all violence against civilians, including acts of terror. Both sides were called on to take steps that calm tensions. The aim was to restart a credible path to peace.

Resolution 234 is the UN Security Council's second ceasefire demand of the Six-Day War, adopted unanimously on 7 June 1967, the war's third day. The Council noted that despite its appeal in Resolution 233 the previous day, military activities in the Near East were continuing, and warned that events might create an even more menacing situation.

The resolution demands that the governments concerned stop firing and halt all military action, as a first step, by a fixed hour: 2000 hours Greenwich Mean Time that same day. It again asks the Secretary-General to keep it promptly informed. Israel and Jordan accepted; fighting with Syria ran two more days before the guns stopped.

Nine years after the Cyprus peacekeeping force was created, it received another term on 15 June 1973. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 31 May, said the force was still needed if peace was to hold. Cyprus agreed it should remain beyond 15 June. Resolution 334 records the renewal.

The Council reaffirmed its long series of Cyprus resolutions, starting with Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also told to keep speeding up their joint efforts toward the Council's objectives. The island's calmer climate was to be used in a constructive way. The extension runs to 15 December 1973. Progress toward a final solution might then allow the force to withdraw or be reduced.

A dispute that set Greece against Albania, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria was closed on the Council's books on 15 September 1947. Resolution 34 does two things only. It takes the dispute off the list of matters of which the Council is seized. It also asks the Secretary-General to place all the records and documents in the case at the disposal of the General Assembly. The Assembly could then deal with the question itself. The text is housekeeping from the Council's early years, not a ruling on the dispute.
